Example 3.12 (Simple linear regression). Let $\beta = ( \beta _ { 0 } , \beta _ { 1 } ) \in \mathcal { R } ^ { 2 }$ and $Z _ { i } = ( 1 , t _ { i } ) , t _ { i } \in \mathcal { R } , i = 1 , . . . , n$ . Then model (3.24) or (3.25) is called a simple linear regression model. It turns out that 

$$
Z ^ {\tau} Z = \left( \begin{array}{c c} n & \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} t _ {i} \\ \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} t _ {i} & \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} t _ {i} ^ {2} \end{array} \right).
$$

This matrix is invertible if and only if some $t _ { i } \mathrm { ^ { * } s }$ are diferent. Thus, if some $t _ { i } \mathrm { ^ { * } s }$ are diferent, then the unique unbiased LSE of $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ for any $l \in \mathcal { R } ^ { 2 }$ is $l ^ { \tau } ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - 1 } Z ^ { \tau } X$ , which has the normal distribution if assumption A1 holds. 

The result can be easily extended to the case of polynomial regression of order $p$ in which $\beta = ( \beta _ { 0 } , \beta _ { 1 } , . . . , \beta _ { p - 1 } )$ and $Z _ { i } = ( 1 , t _ { i } , . . . , t _ { i } ^ { p - 1 } )$ 

Example 3.13 (One-way ANOVA). Suppose that $\begin{array} { r } { n = \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { m } n _ { j } } \end{array}$ with m positive integers $n _ { 1 } , . . . , n _ { m }$ and that 

$$
X _ {i} = \mu_ {j} + \varepsilon_ {i}, \qquad i = k _ {j - 1} + 1,..., k _ {j}, j = 1,..., m,
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { k _ { 0 } = 0 , k _ { j } = \sum _ { l = 1 } ^ { j } n _ { l } , j = 1 , . . . , m } \end{array}$ , and $( \mu _ { 1 } , . . . , \mu _ { m } ) = \beta$ . Let $J _ { m }$ be the m-vector of ones. Then the matrix Z in this case is a block diagonal matrix with $J _ { n _ { j } }$ as the jth diagonal column. Consequently, $Z ^ { \tau } Z$ is an $m \times m$ diagonal matrix whose jth diagonal element is $n _ { j }$ . Thus, $Z ^ { \tau } Z$ is invertible and the unique LSE of $\beta$ is the m-vector whose jth component is $\begin{array} { r } { n _ { j } ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = k _ { j - 1 } + 1 } ^ { k _ { j } } X _ { i } , j = 1 , . . . , m . } \end{array}$ 

Sometimes it is more convenient to use the following notation: 

$$
X _ {i j} = X _ {k _ {i - 1} + j}, \varepsilon_ {i j} = \varepsilon_ {k _ {i - 1} + j}, \qquad j = 1, \dots , n _ {i}, i = 1, \dots , m,
$$

and 

$$
\mu_ {i} = \mu + \alpha_ {i}, \qquad i = 1, \dots , m.
$$

Then our model becomes 

$$
X _ {i j} = \mu + \alpha_ {i} + \varepsilon_ {i j}, \qquad j = 1, \dots , n _ {i}, i = 1, \dots , m,\tag{3.31}
$$

which is called a one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) model. Under model (3.31), $\beta = ( \mu , \alpha _ { 1 } , . . . , \alpha _ { m } ) \in \mathcal { R } ^ { m + 1 }$ . The matrix Z under model (3.31) is not of full rank (exercise). An LSE of $\beta$ under model (3.31) is 

$$
\hat {\beta} = \left(\bar {X}, \bar {X} _ {1}. - \bar {X},..., \bar {X} _ {m}. - \bar {X}\right),
$$

where $\bar { X }$ is still the sample mean of $X _ { i j }$ ’s and ${ \bar { X } } _ { i \cdot }$ is the sample mean of the ith group $\{ X _ { i j } , j = 1 , . . . , n _ { i } \}$ . The problem of finding the form of $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ under model (3.31) is left as an exercise. 

The notation used in model (3.31) allows us to generalize the one-way ANOVA model to any s-way ANOVA model with a positive integer s under the so-called factorial experiments. The following example is for the twoway ANOVA model. 

Example 3.14 (Two-way balanced ANOVA). Suppose that 

$$
X _ {i j k} = \mu + \alpha_ {i} + \beta_ {j} + \gamma_ {i j} + \varepsilon_ {i j k}, \quad i = 1, \dots , a, j = 1, \dots , b, k = 1, \dots , c,\tag{3.32}
$$

where $a , b ,$ and c are some positive integers. Model (3.32) is called a twoway balanced ANOVA model. If we view model (3.32) as a special case of model (3.25), then the parameter vector $\beta$ is 

$$
\beta = (\mu , \alpha_ {1},..., \alpha_ {a}, \beta_ {1},..., \beta_ {b}, \gamma_ {1 1},..., \gamma_ {1 b},..., \gamma_ {a 1},..., \gamma_ {a b}).\tag{3.33}
$$

One can obtain the matrix Z and show that it is $n \times p .$ , where $n = a b c$ and $p = 1 + a + b + a b . $ and is of rank $a b < p$ (exercise). It can also be shown (exercise) that an LSE of $\beta$ is given by the right-hand side of (3.33) with $\mu _ { ; }$ $\alpha _ { i } , \beta _ { j }$ , and $\gamma _ { i j }$ replaced by $\hat { \mu } , \hat { \alpha } _ { i } , \hat { \beta } _ { j }$ , and $\hat { \gamma } _ { i j }$ , respectively, where ${ \hat { \mu } } = { \bar { X } } . . .$ $\hat { \alpha } _ { i } = \bar { X } _ { i \cdot } - \bar { X } _ { \cdot \cdot \cdot } , \hat { \beta } _ { j } = \bar { X } _ { \cdot j \cdot } - \bar { X } _ { \cdot \cdot \cdot } , \hat { \gamma } _ { i j } = \bar { X } _ { i j \cdot } - \bar { X } _ { i \cdot \cdot } - \bar { X } _ { \cdot j \cdot } + \bar { X } _ { \cdot \cdot \cdot } .$ , and a dot is used to denote averaging over the indicated subscript, e.g., 

$$
\bar {X} _ {. j.} = \frac {1}{a c} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {a} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {c} X _ {i j k}
$$

with a fixed j. 

## 3.3.2 The UMVUE and BLUE

We now study UMVUE’s in model (3.25) with assumption A1. 

Theorem 3.7. Consider model (3.25) with assumption A1. 

(i) The LSE $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } }$ is the UMVUE of $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ for any estimable $l ^ { \tau } \beta .$ 

(ii) The UMVUE of $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ is $\hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 } = ( n - r ) ^ { - 1 } \| X - Z \hat { \beta } \| ^ { 2 }$ , where r is the rank of $Z$ . 

Proof. (i) Let $\hat { \beta }$ be an LSE of $\beta .$ . By (3.27), 

$$
(X - Z \hat {\beta}) ^ {\tau} Z (\hat {\beta} - \beta) = (X ^ {\tau} Z - X ^ {\tau} Z) (\hat {\beta} - \beta) = 0
$$

and, hence, 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\| X - Z \beta \| ^ {2} = \| X - Z \hat {\beta} + Z \hat {\beta} - Z \beta \| ^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad = \| X - Z \hat {\beta} \| ^ {2} + \| Z \hat {\beta} - Z \beta \| ^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad = \| X - Z \hat {\beta} \| ^ {2} - 2 \beta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} X + \| Z \beta \| ^ {2} + \| Z \hat {\beta} \| ^ {2}.} \end{array}
$$

Using this result and assumption A1, we obtain the following joint Lebesgue p.d.f. of $X$ : 

$$
(2 \pi \sigma^ {2}) ^ {- n / 2} \exp \left\{\frac {\beta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} x}{\sigma^ {2}} - \frac {\| x - Z \hat {\beta} \| ^ {2} + \| Z \hat {\beta} \| ^ {2}}{2 \sigma^ {2}} - \frac {\| Z \beta \| ^ {2}}{2 \sigma^ {2}} \right\}.
$$

By Proposition 2.1 and the fact that $Z { \hat { \beta } } = Z ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau } X$ is a function of $Z ^ { \tau } X , ( Z ^ { \tau } X , \| X - Z \hat { \beta } \| ^ { 2 } )$ is complete and suficient for $\theta = ( \beta , \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ . Note that $\hat { \beta }$ is a function of $Z ^ { \tau } X$ and, hence, a function of the complete suficient statistic. If $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ is estimable, then $l ^ { \tau } { \dot { \beta } }$ is unbiased for $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ (Theorem 3.6) and, hence, $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } }$ is the UMVUE of $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ 

(ii) From $\| X - Z \beta \| ^ { 2 } = \| X - Z \hat { \beta } \| ^ { 2 } + \| Z \hat { \beta } - Z \beta \| ^ { 2 }$ and $E ( Z { \hat { \beta } } ) = Z \beta $ (Theorem 3.6), 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E \| X - Z \hat {\beta} \| ^ {2} = E (X - Z \beta) ^ {\tau} (X - Z \beta) - E (\beta - \hat {\beta}) ^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} Z (\beta - \hat {\beta}) \\ & \qquad = \mathrm{tr} \left(\mathrm{Var} (X) - \mathrm{Var} (Z \hat {\beta})\right) \\ & \qquad = \sigma^ {2} [ n - \mathrm{tr} \left(Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau}\right) ] \\ & \qquad = \sigma^ {2} [ n - \mathrm{tr} \left((Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} Z\right) ]. \end{array}
$$

Since each row of $Z \in \mathcal { R } ( Z ) , Z \hat { \beta }$ does not depend on the choice of $( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - }$ in $\hat { \beta } = ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau } X$ (Theorem 3.6). Hence, we can evaluate $\operatorname { t r } ( ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau } Z )$ using a particular $( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - }$ . From the theory of linear algebra, there exists a $p \times p$ matrix C such that $C C ^ { \tau } = I _ { p }$ and 

$$
C ^ {\tau} (Z ^ {\tau} Z) C = \left( \begin{array}{c c} \Lambda & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array} \right),
$$

where Λ is an $r \times r$ diagonal matrix whose diagonal elements are positive. Then, a particular choice of $( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - }$ is 

$$
(Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} = C \left( \begin{array}{c c} \Lambda^ {- 1} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array} \right) C ^ {\tau}\tag{3.34}
$$

and 

$$
(Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} Z = C \left( \begin{array}{c c} I _ {r} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{array} \right) C ^ {\tau}
$$

whose trace is $r .$ . Hence $\hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 }$ is the UMVUE of $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ , since it is a function of the complete suficient statistic and 

$$
E \hat {\sigma} ^ {2} = (n - r) ^ {- 1} E \| X - Z \hat {\beta} \| ^ {2} = \sigma^ {2}. \quad \blacksquare
$$

In general, 

$$
\operatorname{Var} (l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta}) = l ^ {\tau} (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} \operatorname{Var} (\varepsilon) Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} l.\tag{3.35}
$$

If $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ and $\mathrm { V a r } ( \varepsilon ) = \sigma ^ { 2 } I _ { n }$ (assumption A2), then the use of the generalized inverse matrix in (3.34) leads to Var $( l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } } ) = \sigma ^ { 2 } l ^ { \tau } ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } l$ , which attains the Cram´er-Rao lower bound under assumption A1 (Proposition 3.2). 

The vector $X - Z { \hat { \boldsymbol { \beta } } }$ is called the residual vector and $\| X - Z { \hat { \beta } } \| ^ { 2 }$ is called the sum of squared residuals and is denoted by SSR. The estimator $\hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 }$ is then equal to $S S R / ( n - r )$ 

Since $X - Z { \hat { \beta } } = [ I _ { n } - Z ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau } ] X$ and $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } } = l ^ { \tau } ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau } X$ are linear in X, they are normally distributed under assumption A1. Also, using the generalized inverse matrix in (3.34), we obtain that 

$$
[ I _ {n} - Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} ] Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} = Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} - Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} = 0,
$$

which implies that $\hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 }$ and $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } }$ are independent (Exercise 58 in 1.6) for any estimable $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ . Furthermore, 

$$
[ Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} ] ^ {2} = Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau}
$$

$( \mathrm { i . e . , ~ } Z ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau }$ is a projection matrix) and 

$$
S S R = X ^ {\tau} [ I _ {n} - Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} ] X.
$$

The rank of $Z ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau }$ is $\mathrm { t r } ( Z ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau } ) = r$ . Similarly, the rank of the projection matrix ${ \cal I } _ { n } - Z ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau }$ is $n - r$ . From 

$$
X ^ {\tau} X = X ^ {\tau} [ Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} ] X + X ^ {\tau} [ I _ {n} - Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} ] X
$$

and Theorem 1.5 (Cochran’s theorem), $S S R / \sigma ^ { 2 }$ has the chi-square distri bution $\chi _ { n - r } ^ { 2 } ( \delta )$ with 

$$
\delta = \sigma^ {- 2} \beta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} [ I _ {n} - Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} ] Z \beta = 0.
$$

Thus, we have proved the following result. 

Theorem 3.8. Consider model (3.25) with assumption A1. For any estimable parameter $l ^ { \tau } \beta .$ , the UMVUE’s $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } }$ and $\hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 }$ are independent; the distribution of $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } }$ is ${ \cal N } ( l ^ { \tau } \beta , \sigma ^ { 2 } l ^ { \tau } ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } l )$ ; and $( n - r ) \hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 } / \sigma ^ { 2 }$ has the chisquare distribution $\chi _ { n - r } ^ { 2 }$ 

Example 3.15. In Examples 3.12-3.14, UMVUE’s of estimable $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ are the LSE’s $\bar { l } ^ { \tau } \hat { \beta }$ , under assumption A1. In Example 3.13, 

$$
S S R = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {m} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n _ {i}} (X _ {i j} - \bar {X} _ {i.}) ^ {2};
$$

in Example 3.14, if $c > 1$ 

$$
S S R = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {a} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {b} \sum_ {k = 1} ^ {c} (X _ {i j k} - \bar {X} _ {i j.}) ^ {2}. \quad \blacksquare
$$

We now study properties of $l ^ { \tau } \hat { \beta }$ and $\hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 }$ under assumption A2, i.e., without the normality assumption on ε. From Theorem 3.6 and the proof of Theorem $3 . 7 ( \mathrm { i i } ) , \ : l ^ { \tau } \hat { \beta }$ (with an $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z ) )$ and $\hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 }$ are still unbiased without the normality assumption. In what sense are $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } }$ and $\hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 }$ optimal beyond being unbiased? We have the following result for the LSE $\bar { l } ^ { \tau } \hat { \beta }$ . Some discussion about $\hat { \sigma } ^ { 2 }$ can be found, for example, in Rao (1973, p. 228). 

Theorem 3.9. Consider model (3.25) with assumption A2. 

(i) A necessary and suficient condition for the existence of a linear unbiased estimator of $l ^ { \tau } \beta \ ( \mathrm { i . e . }$ , an unbiased estimator that is linear in X) is $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ (ii) (Gauss-Markov theorem). If $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ , then the LSE $l ^ { \tau } \hat { \beta }$ is the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) of $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ in the sense that it has the minimum variance in the class of linear unbiased estimators of $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ 

Proof. (i) The suficiency has been established in Theorem 3.6. Suppose now a linear function of $X , c ^ { \tau } X$ with $c \in \mathcal { R } ^ { n }$ , is unbiased for $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ . Then 

$$
l ^ {\tau} \beta = E (c ^ {\tau} X) = c ^ {\tau} E X = c ^ {\tau} Z \beta .
$$

Since this equality holds for all $\beta , l = Z ^ { \tau } c , \mathrm { i . e . , } l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ 

(ii) Let $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z ) = \mathcal { R } ( Z ^ { \tau } Z )$ . Then $l = ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) \zeta$ for some $\zeta$ and $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } } =$ $\zeta ^ { \tau } ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) \hat { \beta } = \zeta ^ { \tau } Z ^ { \tau } X$ by (3.27). Let $c ^ { \tau } X$ be any linear unbiased estimator of $l ^ { \tau } \beta .$ . From the proof of $( \mathrm { i } ) , Z ^ { \tau } c = l$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\mathrm{Cov} (\zeta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} X, c ^ {\tau} X - \zeta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} X) = E (X ^ {\tau} Z \zeta c ^ {\tau} X) - E (X ^ {\tau} Z \zeta \zeta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} X)} \\ & {\qquad = \sigma^ {2} \mathrm{tr} (Z \zeta c ^ {\tau}) + \beta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} Z \zeta c ^ {\tau} Z \beta} \\ & {\qquad \quad - \sigma^ {2} \mathrm{tr} (Z \zeta \zeta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau}) - \beta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} Z \zeta \zeta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} Z \beta} \\ & {\qquad = \sigma^ {2} \zeta^ {\tau} l + (l ^ {\tau} \beta) ^ {2} - \sigma^ {2} \zeta^ {\tau} l - (l ^ {\tau} \beta) ^ {2}} \\ & {\qquad = 0.} \end{array}
$$

Hence 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname{Var} (c ^ {\tau} X) = \operatorname{Var} (c ^ {\tau} X - \zeta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} X + \zeta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} X) \\ \qquad = \operatorname{Var} (c ^ {\tau} X - \zeta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} X) + \operatorname{Var} (\zeta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} X) \\ \qquad + 2 \operatorname{Cov} (\zeta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} X, c ^ {\tau} X - \zeta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} X) \\ \qquad = \operatorname{Var} (c ^ {\tau} X - \zeta^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau} X) + \operatorname{Var} (l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta}) \\ \qquad \geq \operatorname{Var} (l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta}). \quad \blacksquare \end{array}
$$

## 3.3.3 Robustness of LSE’s

Consider now model (3.25) under assumption A3. An interesting question is under what conditions on $\mathrm { V a r } ( \varepsilon )$ is the LSE of $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ with $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ still the BLUE. If $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } }$ is still the BLUE, then we say that $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } } ,$ considered as a BLUE, is robust against violation of assumption A2. In general, a statistical procedure having certain properties under an assumption is said to be robust against violation of the assumption if and only if the statistical procedure still has the same properties when the assumption is (slightly) violated. For example, the LSE of $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ with $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ , as an unbiased estimator, is robust against violation of assumption A1 or $\mathrm { A 2 }$ , since the LSE is unbiased as long as $E ( \varepsilon ) = 0$ , which can be always assumed without loss of generality. On the other hand, the LSE as a UMVUE may not be robust against violation of assumption A1 (see 3.5). 

Theorem 3.10. Consider model (3.25) with assumption A3. The following are equivalent. 

(a) $l ^ { \tau } \dot { \beta }$ is the BLUE of $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ for any $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ 

(b) $E ( l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } } \eta ^ { \tau } X ) = 0$ for any $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ and any η such that $E ( \eta ^ { \tau } X ) = 0$ (c) $Z ^ { \tau } \mathrm { V a r } ( \varepsilon ) U = 0$ , where U is a matrix such that $Z ^ { \tau } U = 0$ and ${ \mathcal { R } } ( U ^ { \tau } ) +$ $\mathcal { R } ( Z ^ { \tau } ) = \mathcal { R } ^ { n }$ 

(d) $\mathrm { V a r } ( \varepsilon ) = Z \Lambda _ { 1 } Z ^ { \tau } + U \Lambda _ { 2 } U ^ { \tau }$ for some $\Lambda _ { 1 }$ and $\Lambda _ { 2 }$ 

(e) The matrix $Z ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau } { \mathrm { V a r } } ( \varepsilon )$ is symmetric. 

Proof. We first show that (a) and (b) are equivalent, which is an analogue of Theorem 3.2(i). Suppose that (b) holds. Let $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ If $c ^ { \tau } X$ is unbiased for $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ , then $E ( \eta ^ { \tau } X ) = 0$ with $\eta = c - Z ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } l$ . Hence 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname{Var} (c ^ {\tau} X) = \operatorname{Var} (c ^ {\tau} X - l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta} + l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta}) \\ \qquad = \operatorname{Var} (c ^ {\tau} X - l ^ {\tau} (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} X + l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta}) \\ \qquad = \operatorname{Var} (\eta^ {\tau} X + l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta}) \\ \qquad = \operatorname{Var} (\eta^ {\tau} X) + \operatorname{Var} (l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta}) + 2 \operatorname{Cov} (\eta^ {\tau} X, l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta}) \\ \qquad = \operatorname{Var} (\eta^ {\tau} X) + \operatorname{Var} (l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta}) + 2 E (l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta} \eta^ {\tau} X) \\ \qquad = \operatorname{Var} (\eta^ {\tau} X) + \operatorname{Var} (l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta}) \\ \qquad \geq \operatorname{Var} (l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta}). \end{array}
$$

Suppose now that there are $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ and η such that $E ( \eta ^ { \tau } X ) = 0$ but $\delta = E ( l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } } \eta ^ { \tau } X ) \neq 0$ . Let $c _ { t } = t \eta + Z ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } l$ . From the previous proof, 

$$
\mathrm{Var} (c _ {t} ^ {\tau} X) = t ^ {2} \mathrm{Var} (\eta^ {\tau} X) + \mathrm{Var} (l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta}) + 2 \delta t.
$$

As long as $\delta \neq 0$ , there exists a t such that $\operatorname { V a r } ( c _ { t } ^ { \tau } X ) < \operatorname { V a r } ( l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } } )$ . This shows that $l ^ { \tau } \hat { \beta }$ cannot be a BLUE and, therefore, (a) implies (b). 

We next show that (b) implies (c). Suppose that (b) holds. Since $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z ) , l = Z ^ { \tau } \gamma$ for some $\gamma .$ . Let $\eta \in \mathcal { R } ( U ^ { \tau } )$ . Then $E ( \eta ^ { \tau } X ) = \eta ^ { \tau } Z \beta = 0$ and, hence, 

$$
0 = E \left(l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta} \eta^ {\tau} X\right) = E \left[ \gamma^ {\tau} Z \left(Z ^ {\tau} Z\right) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} X X ^ {\tau} \eta \right] = \gamma^ {\tau} Z \left(Z ^ {\tau} Z\right) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} \operatorname{Var} (\varepsilon) \eta .
$$

Since this equality holds for all $l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ , it holds for all $\gamma .$ . Thus, 

$$
Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} \mathrm{Var} (\varepsilon) U = 0,
$$

which implies 

$$
Z ^ {\tau} Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} \operatorname{Var} (\varepsilon) U = Z ^ {\tau} \operatorname{Var} (\varepsilon) U = 0,
$$

since $Z ^ { \tau } Z ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau } = Z ^ { \tau }$ . Thus, (c) holds. 

To show that (c) implies (d), we need to use the following facts from the theory of linear algebra: there exists a nonsingular matrix C such that $\operatorname { V a r } ( \varepsilon ) = C C ^ { \tau }$ and $C = Z C _ { 1 } + U C _ { 2 }$ for some matrices $C _ { j }$ (since $\mathcal { R } ( U ^ { \tau } ) + \mathcal { R } ( Z ^ { \tau } ) = \mathcal { R } ^ { n } )$ . Let $\Lambda _ { 1 } = C _ { 1 } C _ { 1 } ^ { \tau } , \Lambda _ { 2 } = C _ { 2 } C _ { 2 } ^ { \tau }$ , and $\Lambda _ { 3 } = C _ { 1 } C _ { 2 } ^ { \tau }$ Then 

$$
\operatorname{Var} (\varepsilon) = Z \Lambda_ {1} Z ^ {\tau} + U \Lambda_ {2} U ^ {\tau} + Z \Lambda_ {3} U ^ {\tau} + U \Lambda_ {3} ^ {\tau} Z ^ {\tau}\tag{3.36}
$$

and $Z ^ { \tau } \mathrm { V a r } ( \varepsilon ) U = Z ^ { \tau } Z \Lambda _ { 3 } U ^ { \tau } U$ , which is 0 if (c) holds. Hence, (c) implies 

$$
0 = Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} Z \Lambda_ {3} U ^ {\tau} U (U ^ {\tau} U) ^ {-} U ^ {\tau} = Z \Lambda_ {3} U ^ {\tau},
$$

which with (3.36) implies (d). 

If (d) holds, then $Z ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau } \mathrm { V a r } ( \varepsilon ) = Z \Lambda _ { 1 } Z ^ { \tau }$ , which is symmetric. Hence (d) implies (e). To complete the proof, we need to show that (e) implies (b), which is left as an exercise. 

As a corollary of this theorem, the following result shows when the UMVUE’s in model (3.25) with assumption A1 are robust against the violation of $\mathrm { V a r } ( \varepsilon ) = \sigma ^ { 2 } I _ { n }$ 

Corollary 3.3. Consider model (3.25) with a full rank $Z , \ : \varepsilon = N _ { n } ( 0 , \Sigma )$ and an unknown positive definite matrix Σ. Then $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } }$ is a UMVUE of $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ for any $l \in \mathcal { R } ^ { p }$ if and only if one of ${ ( \mathrm { b } ) } \mathrm { - ( e ) }$ in Theorem 3.10 holds. 

Example 3.16. Consider model (3.25) with $\beta$ replaced by a random vector $\beta$ that is independent of ε. Such a model is called a linear model with random coeficients. Suppose that $\mathrm { V a r } ( \varepsilon ) = \sigma ^ { 2 } I _ { n }$ and $E ( \beta ) = \beta$ . Then 

$$
X = Z \beta + Z (\boldsymbol {\beta} - \boldsymbol {\beta}) + \varepsilon = Z \beta + e,\tag{3.37}
$$

where $e = Z ( \beta - \beta ) + \varepsilon$ satisfies $E ( e ) = 0$ and 

$$
\operatorname{Var} (e) = Z \operatorname{Var} (\boldsymbol {\beta}) Z ^ {\tau} + \sigma^ {2} I _ {n}.
$$

Since 

$$
Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} \mathrm{Var} (e) = Z \mathrm{Var} (\pmb {\beta}) Z ^ {\tau} + \sigma^ {2} Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau}
$$

is symmetric, by Theorem 3.10, the LSE $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } }$ under model (3.37) is the BLUE for any $l ^ { \tau } \beta , l \in \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ . If Z is of full rank and ε is normal, then, by Corollary 3.3, $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } }$ is the UMVUE of $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ for any $l \in \mathcal { R } ^ { p }$ 1 

Example 3.17 (Random efects models). Suppose that 

$$
X _ {i j} = \mu + A _ {i} + e _ {i j}, \quad j = 1, \dots , n _ {i}, i = 1, \dots , m,\tag{3.38}
$$

where $\mu \in \mathcal R$ is an unknown parameter, $A _ { i } \mathrm { { ' } s }$ are i.i.d. random variables having mean 0 and variance $\sigma _ { a } ^ { 2 } , \ : e _ { i j } ^ { } \mathrm { { s } }$ are i.i.d. random errors with mean 0 and variance $\sigma ^ { 2 }$ , and $A _ { i } \mathrm { { ' } s }$ and $e _ { i j } { ' } \overset { } { \underset { } { \mathrm { \varepsilon } } }$ s are independent. Model (3.38) is called a one-way random efects model and $A _ { i } { ' } \mathrm { i }$ s are unobserved random efects. Let $\varepsilon _ { i j } = A _ { i } + e _ { i j }$ . Then (3.38) is a special case of the general model (3.25) with 

$$
\mathrm{Var} (\varepsilon) = \sigma_ {a} ^ {2} \Sigma + \sigma^ {2} I _ {n},
$$

where $\Sigma$ is a block diagonal matrix whose ith block is $J _ { n _ { i } } J _ { n _ { i } } ^ { \tau }$ and $J _ { k }$ is the kvector of ones. Under this model, $\begin{array} { r } { Z = J _ { n } , n = \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { m } n _ { i } } \end{array}$ , and ${ \cal Z } ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau } =$ $n ^ { - 1 } J _ { n } J _ { n } ^ { \tau }$ . Note that 

$$
J _ {n} J _ {n} ^ {\tau} \Sigma = \left( \begin{array}{c c c c} n _ {1} J _ {n _ {1}} J _ {n _ {1}} ^ {\tau} & n _ {2} J _ {n _ {1}} J _ {n _ {2}} ^ {\tau} & \dots & n _ {m} J _ {n _ {1}} J _ {n _ {m}} ^ {\tau} \\ n _ {1} J _ {n _ {2}} J _ {n _ {1}} ^ {\tau} & n _ {2} J _ {n _ {2}} J _ {n _ {2}} ^ {\tau} & \dots & n _ {m} J _ {n _ {2}} J _ {n _ {m}} ^ {\tau} \\ \dots \dots & \dots \dots & \dots & \dots \dots \\ n _ {1} J _ {n _ {m}} J _ {n _ {1}} ^ {\tau} & n _ {2} J _ {n _ {m}} J _ {n _ {2}} ^ {\tau} & \dots & n _ {m} J _ {n _ {m}} J _ {n _ {m}} ^ {\tau} \end{array} \right),
$$

which is symmetric if and only if $n _ { 1 } = n _ { 2 } = \cdot \cdot \cdot = n _ { m }$ . Since $J _ { n } J _ { n } ^ { \tau } \mathrm { V a r } ( \varepsilon )$ is symmetric if and only if $J _ { n } J _ { n } ^ { \tau } \Sigma$ is symmetric, a necessary and suficient condition for the LSE of $\mu$ to be the BLUE is that all $n _ { i } \mathrm { ^ { * } s }$ are the same. This condition is also necessary and suficient for the LSE of $\mu$ to be the UMVUE when $\varepsilon _ { i j } \mathrm { ^ { * } s }$ are normal. 1 

In some cases, we are interested in some (not all) linear functions of $\beta .$ For example, consider $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ with $l \in \mathcal { R } ( H )$ , where H is an $n \times p$ matrix such that $\mathcal { R } ( H ) \subset \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ . We have the following result. 

Proposition 3.4. Consider model (3.25) with assumption A3. Suppose that H is a matrix such that $\mathcal { R } ( H ) \subset \mathcal { R } ( Z )$ . A necessary and suficient condition for the LSE $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } }$ to be the BLUE of $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ for any $l \in \mathcal { R } ( H )$ is $H ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } Z ^ { \tau } \mathrm { V a r } ( \varepsilon ) U = 0$ , where $U$ is the same as that in (c) of Theorem 3.10. 

Example 3.18. Consider model (3.25) with assumption A3 and $Z =$ $\left( H _ { 1 } \ H _ { 2 } \right)$ , where $H _ { 1 } ^ { \tau } H _ { 2 } = 0$ . Suppose that under the reduced model

X = H _ {1} \beta_ {1} + \varepsilon ,
$$

X = H _ {2} \beta_ {2} + \varepsilon ,
$$

Let $H = \left( H _ { 1 } \mathrm { ~ 0 } \right)$ be $n \times p$ . Note that 

$$
H (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} \mathrm{Var} (\varepsilon) U = H _ {1} (H _ {1} ^ {\tau} H _ {1}) ^ {-} H _ {1} ^ {\tau} \mathrm{Var} (\varepsilon) U,
$$

which is 0 by Theorem 3.10 for the U given in (c) of Theorem 3.10, and

Z (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} Z ^ {\tau} \mathrm{Var} (\varepsilon) U = H _ {2} (H _ {2} ^ {\tau} H _ {2}) ^ {-} H _ {2} ^ {\tau} \mathrm{Var} (\varepsilon) U,

which is not 0 by Theorem 3.10. This implies that some LSE $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \boldsymbol { \beta } } }$ is not a BLUE of $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ but $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } }$ is the BLUE of $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ if $l \in \mathcal { R } ( H )$ 

Finally, we consider model (3.25) with $\mathrm { V a r } ( \varepsilon )$ being a diagonal matrix whose ith diagonal element is $\sigma _ { i } ^ { 2 } , \mathrm { i . e . , } \varepsilon _ { i }$ ’s are uncorrelated but have unequal variances. A straightforward calculation shows that condition (e) in Theorem 3.10 holds if and only if, for all $i \neq j , \sigma _ { i } ^ { 2 } \neq \sigma _ { j } ^ { 2 }$ only when $h _ { i j } = 0$ , where $h _ { i j }$ is the $( i , j )$ th element of the projection matrix $Z ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } \bar { Z ^ { \tau } }$ . Thus, an LSE is not a BLUE in general, although it is still unbiased for estimable $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ 

Suppose that the unequal variances of $\varepsilon _ { i } \mathrm { { ^ { s } } }$ are caused by some small perturbations, i.e., $\varepsilon _ { i } = e _ { i } + u _ { i }$ , where $\operatorname { V a r } ( e _ { i } ) = \sigma ^ { 2 } , \operatorname { V a r } ( u _ { i } ) = \delta _ { i }$ , and $e _ { i }$ and $u _ { i }$ are independent so that $\sigma _ { i } ^ { 2 } = \sigma ^ { 2 } + \delta _ { i }$ . From (3.35), 

$$
\mathrm{Var} (l ^ {\tau} \hat {\beta}) = l ^ {\tau} (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \sigma_ {i} ^ {2} Z _ {i} Z _ {i} ^ {\tau} (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {-} l.
$$

If $\delta _ { i } = 0$ for all i (no perturbations), then assumption A2 holds and $l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } }$ is the BLUE of any estimable $l ^ { \tau } \beta$ with Var $( l ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } } ) = \sigma ^ { 2 } l ^ { \tau } ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - } l$ . Suppose that $0 < \delta _ { i } \le \sigma ^ { 2 } \delta$ . Then

$$

This indicates that the LSE is robust in the sense that its variance increases slightly when there is a slight violation of the equal variance assumption (small δ).

Theorem 3.11. Consider model (3.25) with assumption A3.
