Thus, inequality (4.68) becomes 

$$
[ \nabla g (\theta) ] ^ {\tau} V _ {n} (\theta) \nabla g (\theta) \geq [ \tilde {I} _ {n} (\vartheta) ] ^ {- 1},
$$

where $\tilde { I } _ { n } ( \vartheta )$ is the Fisher information matrix about ϑ contained in X. If $p = k$ and g is one-to-one, then 

$$
[ \tilde {I} _ {n} (\vartheta) ] ^ {- 1} = [ \nabla g (\theta) ] ^ {\tau} [ I _ {n} (\theta) ] ^ {- 1} \nabla g (\theta)
$$

and, therefore, $\hat { \vartheta } _ { n }$ is asymptotically eficient if and only if $\hat { \theta } _ { n }$ is asymptotically eficient. For this reason, in the case of $p < k , \hat { \vartheta } _ { n }$ is considered to be asymptotically eficient if and only if $\hat { \theta } _ { n }$ is asymptotically eficient, and we can focus on the estimation of θ only. 

## 4.5.2 Asymptotic eficiency of MLE’s and RLE’s

We now show that under some regularity conditions, a root of the likelihood equation (RLE), which is a candidate for an MLE, is asymptotically eficient. 

Theorem 4.17. Assume the conditions of Theorem 4.16. 

(i) There is a sequence of estimators $\{ \hat { \theta } _ { n } \}$ such that 

$$
P \big (s _ {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {n}) = 0 \big) \rightarrow 1 \qquad \text { and } \qquad \hat {\theta} _ {n} \rightarrow_ {p} \theta ,\tag{4.74}
$$

where $s _ { n } ( \gamma ) = \partial \log \ell ( \gamma ) / \partial \gamma .$ 

(ii) Any consistent sequence ${ \ddot { \theta } } _ { n }$ of RLE’s is asymptotically eficient. 

Proof. (i) Let $B _ { n } ( c ) = \{ \gamma : \| [ I _ { n } ( \theta ) ] ^ { 1 / 2 } ( \gamma - \theta ) \| \le c \}$ for $c > 0$ . Since Θ is open, for each $c > 0 , B _ { n } ( c ) \subset \Theta$ for suficiently large n. Since $B _ { n } ( c )$ shrinks to $\{ \theta \}$ as $n \to \infty$ , the existence of $\hat { \theta } _ { n }$ satisfying (4.74) is implied by the fact that for any $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists $c > 0$ and $n _ { 0 } > 1$ such that 

$$
P \bigl (\log \ell (\gamma) - \log \ell (\theta) <   0 \quad \text { for   all } \gamma \in \partial B _ {n} (c) \bigr) \geq 1 - \epsilon , \quad n \geq n _ {0},\tag{4.75}
$$

where $\partial B _ { n } ( c )$ is the boundary of $B _ { n } ( c )$ . (For a proof of the measurability of $\hat { \theta } _ { n }$ , see Serfling (1980, pp. 147-148).) For $\gamma \in \partial B _ { n } ( c )$ , the Taylor expansion gives 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \log \ell (\gamma) - \log \ell (\theta) & = c \lambda^ {\tau} [ I _ {n} (\theta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} s _ {n} (\theta) \\ & \quad + (c ^ {2} / 2) \lambda^ {\tau} [ I _ {n} (\theta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} \nabla s _ {n} (\gamma^ {*}) [ I _ {n} (\theta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} \lambda , \end{array}\tag{4.76}
$$

where $\lambda = [ I _ { n } ( \theta ) ] ^ { 1 / 2 } ( \gamma - \theta ) / c$ satisfying $\lVert \lambda \rVert = 1 , \nabla s _ { n } ( \gamma ) = \partial s _ { n } ( \gamma ) / \partial \gamma$ , and $\gamma ^ { * }$ lies between $\gamma$ and θ. Note that 

$$
\begin{array}{l}E \frac {\| \nabla s _ {n} (\gamma^ {*}) - \nabla s _ {n} (\theta) \|}{n} \leq E \max _ {\gamma \in B _ {n} (c)} \frac {\| \nabla s _ {n} (\gamma) - \nabla s _ {n} (\theta) \|}{n}\\\leq E \max _ {\gamma \in B _ {n} (c)} \left\| \frac {\partial^ {2} \log f _ {\gamma} (X _ {1})}{\partial \gamma \partial \gamma^ {\tau}} - \frac {\partial^ {2} \log f _ {\theta} (X _ {1})}{\partial \theta \partial \theta^ {\tau}} \right\|\\\rightarrow 0,\end{array}\tag {4.7}\tag{4.77}
$$

which follows from $\mathrm { ( a ) } \ \partial ^ { 2 }$ log $f _ { \gamma } ( x ) / \partial \gamma \partial \gamma ^ { \tau }$ is continuous in a neighborhood of $\theta$ for any fixed $x ; ( \mathrm { b } ) \ B _ { n } ( c )$ shrinks to $\{ \theta \}$ ; and (c) for suficiently large $n ,$ 

$$
\max _ {\gamma \in B _ {n} (c)} \left\| \frac {\partial^ {2} \log f _ {\gamma} (X _ {1})}{\partial \gamma \partial \gamma^ {\tau}} - \frac {\partial^ {2} \log f _ {\theta} (X _ {1})}{\partial \theta \partial \theta^ {\tau}} \right\| \leq 2 h _ {\theta} (X _ {1})
$$

under condition (4.69). By the SLLN (Theorem 1.13) and Proposition 3.1, $n ^ { - 1 } \nabla s _ { n } ( \theta ) \to _ { a . s . } - I _ { 1 } ( \theta ) ( \mathrm { i . e . , ~ } \| n ^ { - 1 } \nabla s _ { n } ( \theta ) + I _ { 1 } ( \theta ) \| \to _ { a . s . } 0 )$ . These results, together with (4.76), imply that 

$$
\log \ell (\gamma) - \log \ell (\theta) = c \lambda^ {\tau} [ I _ {n} (\theta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} s _ {n} (\theta) - [ 1 + o _ {p} (1) ] c ^ {2} / 2.\tag{4.78}
$$

Note that max $\phantom { } _ { \lambda } \{ \lambda ^ { \tau } [ I _ { n } ( \theta ) ] ^ { - 1 / 2 } s _ { n } ( \theta ) \} = \| [ I _ { n } ( \theta ) ] ^ { - 1 / 2 } s _ { n } ( \theta ) \|$ . Hence, (4.75) follows from (4.78) and 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & P \big (\| [ I _ {n} (\theta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} s _ {n} (\theta) \| <   c / 4 \big) \geq 1 - (4 / c) ^ {2} E \| [ I _ {n} (\theta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} s _ {n} (\theta) \| ^ {2} \\ & \qquad = 1 - k (4 / c) ^ {2} \\ & \qquad \geq 1 - \epsilon \end{array}
$$

by choosing c suficiently large. This completes the proof of (i). (ii) Let $A _ { \epsilon } = \{ \gamma : \| \gamma - \theta \| \le \epsilon \}$ for $\epsilon > 0$ . Since Θ is open, $A _ { \epsilon } ~ \subset ~ \Theta$ for suficiently small ǫ. Let $\left\{ \theta _ { n } \right\}$ be a sequence of consistent RLE’s, i.e., $P ( s _ { n } ( \tilde { \theta } _ { n } ) = 0$ and $\tilde { \theta } _ { n } \in A _ { \epsilon } ) \stackrel { \cdot } {  } 1$ for any $\epsilon > 0$ . Hence, we can focus on the set on which $s _ { n } ( \widetilde { \theta } _ { n } ) = 0$ and $\tilde { \theta } _ { n } \in A _ { \epsilon }$ . Using the mean-value theorem for vector-valued functions, we obtain that 

$$
- s _ {n} (\theta) = \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {1} \nabla s _ {n} \bigl (\theta + t (\tilde {\theta} _ {n} - \theta) \bigr) d t \right] (\tilde {\theta} _ {n} - \theta).
$$

Note that 

$$
\frac {1}{n} \left\| \int_ {0} ^ {1} \nabla s _ {n} (\theta + t (\tilde {\theta} _ {n} - \theta)) d t - \nabla s _ {n} (\theta) \right\| \leq \max _ {\gamma \in A _ {\epsilon}} \frac {\| \nabla s _ {n} (\gamma) - \nabla s _ {n} (\theta) \|}{n}.
$$

Using the argument in proving $( 4 . 7 7 )$ and the fact that $P ( \tilde { \theta } _ { n } \in A _ { \epsilon } )  1$ for arbitrary $\epsilon > 0$ , we obtain that 

$$
\frac {1}{n} \left\| \int_ {0} ^ {1} \nabla s _ {n} (\theta + t (\tilde {\theta} _ {n} - \theta)) d t - \nabla s _ {n} (\theta) \right\|\rightarrow_ {p} 0.
$$

Since $n ^ { - 1 } \nabla s _ { n } ( \theta ) \longrightarrow a . s . - I _ { 1 } ( \theta )$ and $I _ { n } ( \theta ) = n I _ { 1 } ( \theta )$ , 

$$
- s _ {n} (\theta) = - I _ {n} (\theta) (\tilde {\theta} _ {n} - \theta) + o _ {p} \big (\| I _ {n} (\theta) (\tilde {\theta} _ {n} - \theta) \| \big).
$$

This and Slutsky’s theorem (Theorem 1.11) imply that $\sqrt { n } ( \tilde { \theta } _ { n } - \theta )$ has the same asymptotic distribution as 

$$
\sqrt {n} \left[ I _ {n} (\theta) \right] ^ {- 1} s _ {n} (\theta) = n ^ {- 1 / 2} \left[ I _ {1} (\theta) \right] ^ {- 1} s _ {n} (\theta) \rightarrow_ {d} N _ {k} \left(0, \left[ I _ {1} (\theta) \right] ^ {- 1}\right)
$$

by the CLT (Corollary 1.2), since $\operatorname { V a r } ( s _ { n } ( \theta ) ) = I _ { n } ( \theta )$ 

Theorem 4.17(i) shows the asymptotic existence of a sequence of consistent RLE’s, and Theorem 4.17(ii) shows the asymptotic eficiency of any sequence of consistent RLE’s. However, for a given sequence of RLE’s, its consistency has to be checked unless the RLE’s are unique for suficiently large n, in which case the consistency of the RLE’s is guaranteed by Theorem 4.17(i). 

RLE’s are not necessarily MLE’s. We still have to use the techniques discussed in 4.4 to check whether an RLE is an MLE. However, according to Theorem 4.17, when a sequence of RLE’s is consistent, then it is asymptotically eficient and, therefore, we may not need to search for $\mathrm { M L E } \mathrm { : }$ , if asymptotic eficiency is the only criterion to select estimators. The method of estimating θ by solving $s _ { n } ( \gamma ) = 0$ over $\gamma \in \Theta$ is called scoring and the function $s _ { n } ( \gamma )$ is called the score function. 

Example 4.39. Suppose that $X _ { i }$ has a distribution in a natural exponential family, i.e., the p.d.f. of $X _ { i }$ is 

$$
f _ {\eta} (x _ {i}) = \exp \{\eta^ {\tau} T (x _ {i}) - \zeta (\eta) \} h (x _ {i}).\tag{4.79}
$$

Since $\partial ^ { 2 }$ log $f _ { \eta } ( x _ { i } ) / \partial \eta \partial \eta ^ { \tau } = - \partial ^ { 2 } \zeta ( \eta ) / \partial \eta \partial \eta ^ { \tau }$ , condition (4.69) is satisfied. From Proposition 3.2, other conditions in Theorem 4.16 are also satisfied. For i.i.d. $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ , 

$$
s _ {n} (\eta) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \left[ T (X _ {i}) - \frac {\partial \zeta (\eta)}{\partial \eta} \right].
$$

If $\begin{array} { r } { \hat { \theta } _ { n } = n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } T ( X _ { i } ) \in \Theta } \end{array}$ , the range of $\theta = g ( \eta ) = \partial \zeta ( \eta ) / \partial \eta$ , then $\hat { \theta } _ { n }$ is a unique RLE of $\theta ,$ which is also a unique MLE of $\theta$ since $\partial ^ { 2 } \zeta ( \eta ) / \partial \eta \partial \eta ^ { \tau } =$ $\operatorname { V a r } ( T ( X _ { i } ) )$ is positive definite. Also, $\eta = g ^ { - 1 } ( \theta )$ exists and a unique RLE (MLE) of η is $\hat { \eta } _ { n } = g ^ { - 1 } ( \hat { \theta } _ { n } )$ 

However, $\hat { \theta } _ { n }$ may not be in Θ and the previous argument fails $( \mathrm { e . g . }$ , Example 4.29). What Theorem 4.17 tells us in this case is that as $n \to \infty$ $P ( \hat { \theta } _ { n } \in \Theta )  1$ and, therefore, $\hat { \theta } _ { n } \ \left( \mathrm { o r } \ \hat { \eta } _ { n } \right)$ is the unique asymptotically eficient RLE (MLE) of $\theta \ ( \mathrm { o r } \ \eta )$ in the limiting sense. 

In an example like this we can directly show that $P ( \hat { \theta } _ { n } \in \Theta )  1$ , using the fact that $\hat { \theta } _ { n } \longrightarrow _ { a . s . } { \cal E } [ T ( X _ { 1 } ) ] = g ( \eta )$ (the SLLN). 

The next theorem provides a similar result for the MLE or RLE in the GLM ( 4.4.2). 

Theorem 4.18. Consider the GLM (4.55)-(4.58) with $t _ { i } \mathrm { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ in a fixed interval $( t _ { 0 } , t _ { \infty } ) , 0 < t _ { 0 } \le t _ { \infty } < \infty$ . where $s _ { n } ( \gamma )$ is the score function defined to be the left-hand side of (4.59) with $\gamma = \beta$

Proof. (i) The proof of the existence of ${ \hat { \beta } } _ { n }$ satisfying (4.80) is the same as that of Theorem 4.17(i) with $\theta = \beta$ , except that we need to show 

$$

$$

and 

$$
\max _ {\gamma \in B _ {n} (c)} \left\| [ M _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} R _ {n} (\gamma) [ M _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} \right\|\rightarrow_ {p} 0.\tag{4.83}
$$

The left-hand side of (4.82) is bounded by 

$$
\sqrt {p} \max _ {\gamma \in B _ {n} (c), i \leq n} \left| 1 - \varphi (\gamma^ {\tau} Z _ {i}) / \varphi (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {i}) \right|,
$$

which converges to 0 since $\varphi$ is continuous and, for $\gamma \in B _ { n } ( c )$ 1 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} {| \gamma^ {\tau} Z _ {i} - \beta^ {\tau} Z _ {i} | ^ {2}} & = {| (\gamma - \beta) ^ {\tau} [ I _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {1 / 2} [ I _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} Z _ {i} | ^ {2}} \\ & \leq \| [ I _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {1 / 2} (\gamma - \beta) \| ^ {2} \| [ I _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} Z _ {i} \| ^ {2} \\ & \leq c ^ {2} \max _ {i \leq n} Z _ {i} ^ {\tau} [ I _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1} Z _ {i} \\ & \leq c ^ {2} \phi \big [ t _ {0} \inf _ {i} \varphi (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {i}) \big ] ^ {- 1} \max _ {i \leq n} Z _ {i} ^ {\tau} (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {- 1} Z _ {i} \\ & \to 0 \end{array}
$$

under the assumed conditions. This proves (4.82). 

$$
\text { Let } e _ {i} = X _ {i} - \mu (\psi (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {i})),
$$

$$
U _ {n} (\gamma) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} [ \mu (\psi (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {i})) - \mu (\psi (\gamma^ {\tau} Z _ {i})) ] \psi^ {\prime \prime} (\gamma^ {\tau} Z _ {i}) t _ {i} Z _ {i} Z _ {i} ^ {\tau},
$$

$$
V _ {n} (\gamma) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} e _ {i} [ \psi^ {\prime \prime} (\gamma^ {\tau} Z _ {i}) - \psi^ {\prime \prime} (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {i}) ] t _ {i} Z _ {i} Z _ {i} ^ {\tau},
$$

and 

$$
W _ {n} (\beta) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} e _ {i} \psi^ {\prime \prime} (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {i}) t _ {i} Z _ {i} Z _ {i} ^ {\tau}.
$$

Then $R _ { n } ( \gamma ) = U _ { n } ( \gamma ) + V _ { n } ( \gamma ) + W _ { n } ( \beta )$ . Using the same argument as that in proving (4.82), we can show that 

$$
\max _ {\gamma \in B _ {n} (c)} \left\| [ M _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} U _ {n} (\gamma) [ M _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} \right\| \to 0.
$$

Note that $\left\| [ M _ { n } ( \beta ) ] ^ { - 1 / 2 } V _ { n } ( \gamma ) [ M _ { n } ( \beta ) ] ^ { - 1 / 2 } \right\|$ is bounded by the product of 

$$
[ M _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} | e _ {i} | t _ {i} Z _ {i} Z _ {i} ^ {\tau} [ M _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} = O _ {p} (1)
$$

and 

$$
\max _ {\gamma \in B _ {n} (c), i \leq n} \left| \psi^ {\prime \prime} (\gamma^ {\tau} Z _ {i}) - \psi^ {\prime \prime} (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {i}) \right|,
$$

which can be shown to be $o ( 1 )$ using the same argument as that in proving (4.82). Hence, 

$$
\max _ {\gamma \in B _ {n} (c)} \left\| [ M _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} V _ {n} (\gamma) [ M _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} \right\|\rightarrow_ {p} 0
$$

and (4.83) follows from 

$$
\left| \right.\left[ M _ {n} (\beta) \right] ^ {- 1 / 2} W _ {n} (\beta) [ M _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} \left. \right\|\rightarrow_ {p} 0.
$$

To show this result, we apply Theorem 1.14(ii). Since $E ( e _ { i } ) = 0$ and $\boldsymbol { e } _ { i } { \ ' } _ { \mathrm { i } }$ s are independent, it sufices to show that 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} E \left| e _ {i} \psi^ {\prime \prime} \left(\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {i}\right) t _ {i} Z _ {i} ^ {\tau} \left[ M _ {n} (\beta) \right] ^ {- 1} Z _ {i} \right| ^ {1 + \delta} \rightarrow 0\tag{4.84}
$$

for some $\delta \in ( 0 , 1 )$ . Note that sup $E | e _ { i } | ^ { 1 + \delta } < \infty$ . Hence, there is a constant $C > 0$ such that the left-hand side of (4.84) is bounded by 

$$
C \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \left| Z _ {i} ^ {\tau} (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {- 1} Z _ {i} \right| ^ {1 + \delta} \leq p C \max _ {i \leq n} | Z _ {i} ^ {\tau} (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {- 1} Z _ {i} | ^ {\delta} \to 0.
$$

Hence, (4.84) follows from Theorem 1.14(ii). This proves (4.80). The uniqueness of ${ \hat { \beta } } _ { n }$ follows from (4.83) and the fact that $M _ { n } ( \gamma )$ is positive definite in a neighborhood of $\beta .$ . This completes the proof of (i). 

(ii) The proof of (ii) is very similar to that of Theorem 4.17(ii). Using the results in the proof of (i) and Taylor’s expansion, we can establish (exercise) that 

$$
[ I _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {1 / 2} (\hat {\beta} _ {n} - \beta) = [ I _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} s _ {n} (\beta) + o _ {p} (1).\tag{4.85}
$$

Using the CLT (e.g., Corollary 1.3) and Theorem 1.9(iii), we can show (exercise) that 

$$
[ I _ {n} (\beta) ] ^ {- 1 / 2} s _ {n} (\beta) \rightarrow_ {d} N _ {p} (0, I _ {p}).\tag{4.86}
$$

Result (4.81) follows from (4.85)-(4.86) and Slutsky’s theorem. 

(iii) The result is obvious if $\phi$ is known. When $\phi$ is unknown, it follows from (4.59) that 

$$
\frac {\partial}{\partial \phi} \left[ \frac {\partial \log \ell (\theta)}{\partial \beta} \right] = - \frac {s _ {n} (\beta)}{\phi}.
$$

Since $E [ s _ { n } ( \beta ) ] = 0$ , the Fisher information about $\theta = ( \beta , \phi )$ is 

$$
I _ {n} (\beta , \phi) = - E \left[ \frac {\partial^ {2} \log \ell (\theta)}{\partial \theta \partial \theta^ {\tau}} \right] = \left( \begin{array}{c c} I _ {n} (\beta) & 0 \\ 0 & \tilde {I} _ {n} (\phi) \end{array} \right),
$$

where $\tilde { I } _ { n } ( \phi )$ is the Fisher information about $\phi .$ The result then follows from (4.81) and the discussion in the end of 4.5.1. 

## 4.5.3 Other asymptotically eficient estimators

To study other asymptotically eficient estimators, we start with MRIE’s in location-scale families. Since MLE’s and RLE’s are invariant (see Exercise 109 in 4.6), MRIE’s are often asymptotically eficient; see, for example, Stone (1974). 

Assume the conditions in Theorem 4.16 and let $s _ { n } ( \gamma )$ be the score function. Let $\hat { \theta } _ { n } ^ { ( 0 ) }$ be an estimator of $\theta$ that may not be asymptotically eficient. The estimator 

$$
\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(1)} = \hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)} - [ \nabla s _ {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)}) ] ^ {- 1} s _ {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)})\tag{4.87}
$$

is the first iteration in computing an MLE (or RLE) using the Newton-Raphson iteration method with $\hat { \theta } _ { n } ^ { ( 0 ) }$ as the initial value (see (4.53)) and, therefore, is called the one-step MLE. Without any further iteration, $\hat { \theta } _ { n } ^ { ( 1 ) }$ can be used as a numerical approximation to an MLE or RLE; and $\hat { \theta } _ { n } ^ { ( 1 ) }$ is asymptotically eficient under some conditions, as the following result shows. 

Theorem 4.19. Assume that the conditions in Theorem 4.16 hold and that $\hat { \theta } _ { n } ^ { ( 0 ) }$ is $\sqrt { n } -$ -consistent for $\theta$ (Definition 2.10). 

(i) The one-step MLE $\hat { \theta } _ { n } ^ { ( 1 ) }$ is asymptotically eficient. 

(ii) The one-step MLE obtained by replacing $\nabla s _ { n } ( \gamma )$ in (4.87) with its expected value, $- I _ { n } ( \gamma )$ (the Fisher-scoring method), is asymptotically eficient. 

Proof. Since $\hat { \theta } _ { n } ^ { ( 0 ) }$ is $\sqrt { n } -$ -consistent, we can focus on the event $\hat { \theta } _ { n } ^ { ( 0 ) } \in A _ { \epsilon } =$ $\{ \gamma : \| \gamma - \theta \| \le \epsilon \}$ for a suficiently small ǫ such that $A _ { \epsilon } \subset \Theta$ . From the mean-value theorem, 

$$
s _ {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)}) = s _ {n} (\theta) + \left[ \int_ {0} ^ {1} \nabla s _ {n} \big (\theta + t (\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)} - \theta) \big) d t \right] (\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)} - \theta).
$$

Substituting this into (4.87) we obtain that 

$$
\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(1)} - \theta = - [ \nabla s _ {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)}) ] ^ {- 1} s _ {n} (\theta) + [ I _ {k} - G _ {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)}) ] (\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)} - \theta),
$$

where 

$$
G _ {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)}) = [ \nabla s _ {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)}) ] ^ {- 1} \int_ {0} ^ {1} \nabla s _ {n} \big (\theta + t (\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)} - \theta) \big) d t.
$$

From $( 4 . 7 7 ) , \| [ I _ { n } ( \theta ) ] ^ { 1 / 2 } [ \nabla s _ { n } ( \hat { \theta } _ { n } ^ { ( 0 ) } ) ] ^ { - 1 } [ I _ { n } ( \theta ) ] ^ { 1 / 2 } + I _ { k } \| \to _ { p } 0$ . Using an argument similar to those in the proofs of (4.77) and (4.82), we can show that $\| G _ { n } ( \hat { \theta } _ { n } ^ { ( 0 ) } ) - I _ { k } \| \to _ { p } 0$ . These results and the fact that $\sqrt { n } (  { \hat { \theta } } _ { n } ^ { ( 0 ) } - \theta ) = O _ { p } ( 1 )$ imply 

$$
\sqrt {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(1)} - \theta) = \sqrt {n} [ I _ {n} (\theta) ] ^ {- 1} s _ {n} (\theta) + o _ {p} (1).
$$

This proves (i). The proof for (ii) is similar. 

Example 4.40. Let $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ be i.i.d. from the Weibull distribution $W ( \theta , 1 )$ , where $\theta > 0$ is unknown. Note that 

$$
s _ {n} (\theta) = \frac {n}{\theta} + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \log X _ {i} - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} X _ {i} ^ {\theta} \log X _ {i}
$$

and 

$$
\nabla s _ {n} (\theta) = - \frac {n}{\theta^ {2}} - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} X _ {i} ^ {\theta} (\log X _ {i}) ^ {2}.
$$

Hence, the one-step MLE of θ is 

$$
\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(1)} = \hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)} \left[ 1 + \frac {n + \hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)} (\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \log X _ {i} - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} X _ {i} ^ {\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)}} \log X _ {i})}{n + (\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)}) ^ {2} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} X _ {i} ^ {\hat {\theta} _ {n} ^ {(0)}} (\log X _ {i}) ^ {2}} \right].
$$

Usually one can use a moment estimator ( 3.5.2) as the initial estimator $\hat { \theta } _ { n } ^ { ( 0 ) }$ . In this example, a moment estimator of $\theta$ is the solution of $\bar { X } =$ $\Gamma ( \theta ^ { - 1 } + 1 )$ 

Results similar to that in Theorem 4.19 can be obtained in non-i.i.d. cases, for example, the GLM discussed in 4.4.2 (exercise); see also 5.4. 

As we discussed in 4.1.3, Bayes estimators are usually consistent. The next result, due to Bickel and Yahav (1969) and Ibragimov and Has’minskii (1981), states that Bayes estimators are asymptotically eficient when $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathfrak { s }$ s are i.i.d. 

Theorem 4.20. Assume the conditions of Theorem 4.16. Let $\pi ( \gamma )$ be a prior p.d.f. (which may be improper) w.r.t. the Lebesgue measure on Θ and $p _ { n } ( \gamma )$ be the posterior p.d.f., given $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n } , n = 1 , 2 , . . . .$ . Assume that there exists an $n _ { 0 }$ such that $p _ { n _ { 0 } } ( \gamma )$ is continuous and positive for all $\gamma \in \Theta$ $\begin{array} { r } { \int p _ { n _ { 0 } } ( \gamma ) d \gamma = 1 } \end{array}$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \int \| \gamma \| p _ { n _ { 0 } } ( \gamma ) d \gamma < \infty } \end{array}$ . Suppose further that, for any $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists a $\delta > 0$ such that 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} P \left(\sup _ {\| \gamma - \theta \| \geq \epsilon} \frac {\log \ell (\gamma) - \log \ell (\theta)}{n} > - \delta\right) = 0\tag{4.88}
$$

and 

$$
\lim _ {n \to \infty} P \left(\sup _ {\| \gamma - \theta \| \leq \delta} \frac {\| \nabla s _ {n} (\gamma) - \nabla s _ {n} (\theta) \|}{n} \geq \epsilon\right) = 0,\tag{4.89}
$$

where $\ell ( \gamma )$ is the likelihood function and $s _ { n } ( \gamma )$ is the score function. (i) Let $p _ { n } ^ { * } ( \gamma )$ be the posterior p.d.f. of ${ \sqrt { n } } ( \gamma - T _ { n } )$ , where $T _ { n } ~ = ~ \theta +$ $[ I _ { n } ( \theta ) ] ^ { - 1 } s _ { n } ( \theta )$ and $\theta$ is the true parameter value, and let $\psi ( \gamma )$ be the p.d.f. of $N _ { k } ( 0 , [ I _ { 1 } ( \theta ) ] ^ { - 1 } )$ . Then 

$$
\int (1 + \| \gamma \|) \big | p _ {n} ^ {*} (\gamma) - \psi (\gamma) \big | d \gamma \rightarrow_ {p} 0.\tag{4.90}
$$

(ii) The Bayes estimator of $\theta$ under the squared error loss is asymptotically eficient. 

The proof of Theorem 4.20 is lengthy and is omitted; see Lehmann (1983, 6.7) for a proof of the case of univariate θ. 

A number of conclusions can be drawn from Theorem 4.20. First, result (4.90) shows that the posterior p.d.f. is approximately normal with mean $\dot { \theta } + [ I _ { n } ( \theta ) ] ^ { - 1 } s _ { n } ( \theta )$ and covariance matrix $\bar { [ \boldsymbol { I } _ { n } ( \theta ) ] ^ { - 1 } }$ . This result is useful in Bayesian computation; see Berger (1985, 4.9.3). Second, (4.90) shows that the posterior distribution and its first-order moments converge to the degenerate distribution at $\theta$ and its first-order moments, which implies the consistency and asymptotic unbiasedness of Bayes estimators such as the posterior means. Third, the Bayes estimator under the squared error loss is asymptotically eficient, which provides an additional support for the early suggestion that the Bayesian approach is a useful method for generating estimators. Finally, the results hold regardless of the prior being used, indicating that the efect of the prior declines as n increases. 

In addition to the regularity conditions in Theorem 4.16, Theorem 4.20 requires two more nontrivial regularity conditions, (4.88) and (4.89). Let us verify these conditions for natural exponential families (Example 4.39), i.e., $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are i.i.d. with p.d.f. (4.79). Since $\nabla s _ { n } ( \eta ) = - n \partial ^ { 2 } \zeta ( \eta ) / \partial \eta \partial \eta ^ { \tau }$ , (4.89) follows from the continuity of the second-order derivatives of $\zeta$ . To show (4.88), consider first the case of univariate $\eta .$ . Without loss of generality, we assume that $\gamma > \eta$ . Note that 

$$
\frac {\log \ell (\gamma) - \log \ell (\eta)}{n} = \left[ \bar {T} - \zeta^ {\prime} (\eta) + \zeta^ {\prime} (\eta) - \frac {\zeta (\gamma) - \zeta (\eta)}{\gamma - \eta} \right] (\gamma - \eta),\tag{4.91}
$$

where $\bar { T }$ is the average of $T ( X _ { i } ) \mathrm { { ' s } }$ . Since $\zeta ( \gamma )$ is strictly convex, $\gamma > \eta$ implies $\zeta ^ { \prime } ( \eta ) < [ \zeta ( \gamma ) - \zeta ( \eta ) ] / ( \gamma - \eta )$ . Also, $\bar { T } \longrightarrow _ { a . s . } \ \zeta ^ { \prime } ( \eta )$ . Hence, with probability tending to 1, the factor in front of $( \gamma - \eta )$ on the right-hand side of (4.91) is negative. Then (4.88) holds with 

$$
\delta = \frac {\epsilon}{2} \inf _ {\gamma \geq \eta + \epsilon} \left[ \frac {\zeta (\gamma) - \zeta (\eta)}{\gamma - \eta} - \zeta^ {\prime} (\eta) \right].
$$

To show how to extend this to multivariate $\eta ,$ consider the case of bivariate $\eta .$ . Let $\eta _ { j } , ~ \gamma _ { j }$ , and $\xi _ { j }$ be the jth components of $\eta , ~ \gamma ,$ and $\bar { T } - \nabla \zeta ( \eta )$ , respectively. Assume $\gamma _ { 1 } > \eta _ { 1 }$ and $\gamma _ { 2 } > \eta _ { 2 }$ . Let $\zeta _ { j } ^ { \prime }$ be the derivative of $\zeta$ w.r.t. the jth component of $\eta .$ . Then the left-hand side of (4.91) is the sum of 

$$
(\gamma_ {1} - \eta_ {1}) \xi_ {1} - [ \zeta (\eta_ {1}, \gamma_ {2}) - \zeta (\eta_ {1}, \eta_ {2}) - (\gamma_ {2} - \eta_ {2}) \zeta_ {2} ^ {\prime} (\eta_ {1}, \eta_ {2}) ]
$$

and 

$$
(\gamma_ {2} - \eta_ {2}) \xi_ {2} - [ \zeta (\gamma_ {1}, \gamma_ {2}) - \zeta (\eta_ {1}, \gamma_ {2}) - (\gamma_ {1} - \eta_ {1}) \zeta_ {1} ^ {\prime} (\eta_ {1}, \eta_ {2}) ],
$$

where the last quantity is bounded by 

$$
(\gamma_ {2} - \eta_ {2}) \xi_ {2} - [ \zeta (\gamma_ {1}, \gamma_ {2}) - \zeta (\eta_ {1}, \gamma_ {2}) - (\gamma_ {1} - \eta_ {1}) \zeta_ {1} ^ {\prime} (\eta_ {1}, \gamma_ {2}) ],
$$

since $\zeta _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ( \eta _ { 1 } , \eta _ { 2 } ) \leq \zeta _ { 1 } ^ { \prime } ( \eta _ { 1 } , \gamma _ { 2 } )$ . The rest of the proof is the same as the case of univariate η. 

When Bayes estimators have explicit forms under a specific prior, it is usually easy to prove the asymptotic eficiency of the Bayes estimators directly. For instance, in Example 4.7, the Bayes estimator of $\theta$ is 

$$
\frac {n \bar {X} + \gamma^ {- 1}}{n + \alpha - 1} = \bar {X} + \frac {\gamma^ {- 1} - (\alpha - 1) \bar {X}}{n + \alpha - 1} = \bar {X} + O \left(\frac {1}{n}\right) \text {a.s.,}
$$

where $\bar { X }$ is the MLE of $\theta .$ Hence the Bayes estimator is asymptotically eficient by Slutsky’s theorem. A similar result can be obtained for the Bayes estimator $\delta _ { t } ( X )$ in Example 4.7. Theorem 4.20, however, is useful in cases where Bayes estimators do not have explicit forms and/or the prior is not specified clearly. One such example is the problem in Example 4.40 (Exercises 153 and 154).

9. Consider the estimation problem in Example 4.1 with the loss function $L ( \theta , a ) = w ( \theta ) [ g ( \theta ) - a ] ^ { 2 }$ , where $w ( \theta ) \geq 0$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { \Theta } w ( \theta ) [ g ( \theta ) ] ^ { 2 } d \Pi < \infty } \end{array}$ Show that the Bayes action is

# Estimation in Nonparametric Models

Estimation methods studied in this chapter are useful for nonparametric models as well as for parametric models in which the parametric model assumptions might be violated (so that robust estimators are required) or the number of unknown parameters is exceptionally large. Some such methods have been introduced in Chapter 3; for example, the methods that produce UMVUE’s in nonparametric models, the U- and V-statistics, the LSE’s and BLUE’s, the Horvitz-Thompson estimators, and the sample (central) moments. 

The theoretical justification for estimators in nonparametric models, however, relies more on asymptotics than that in parametric models. This means that applications of nonparametric methods usually require large sample sizes. Also, estimators derived using parametric methods are asymptotically more eficient than those based on nonparametric methods when the parametric models are correct. Thus, to choose between a parametric method and a nonparametric method, we need to balance the advantage of requiring weaker model assumptions (robustness) against the drawback of losing eficiency, which results in requiring a larger sample size. 

It is assumed in this chapter that a sample $X = ( X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n } )$ is from a population in a nonparametric family, where $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are random vectors. 

## 5.1 Distribution Estimators

In many applications the c.d.f.’s of $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are determined by a single c.d.f. $F$ on $\mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ ; for example, $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are i.i.d. random d-vectors. In this section, we consider the estimation of $F$ or $F ( t )$ for several $t ^ { \gamma } \mathrm { s } .$ , under a nonparametric model in which very little is assumed about $F$ . 

## 5.1.1 Empirical c.d.f.’s in i.i.d. cases

For i.i.d. random variables $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ , the empirical c.d.f. $F _ { n }$ is defined in (2.28). The definition of the empirical c.d.f. based on $X = ( X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n } )$ in the case of $X _ { i } \in \mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ is analogously given by 

$$
F _ {n} (t) = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} I _ {(- \infty , t ]} (X _ {i}), \qquad t \in \mathcal {R} ^ {d},\tag{5.1}
$$

where $( - \infty , a ]$ denotes the set $( - \infty , a _ { 1 } ] \times \cdot \cdot \cdot \times ( - \infty , a _ { d } ]$ for any $a =$ $( a _ { 1 } , . . . , a _ { d } ) \in \mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ . Similar to the case of $d = 1$ (Example 2.26), $F _ { n } ( t )$ as an estimator of $F ( t )$ has the following properties. For any $t \in \mathcal { R } ^ { d } , n F _ { n } ( t )$ has the binomial distribution $B i ( F ( t ) , n ) ; F _ { n } ( t )$ is unbiased with variance $F ( t ) [ 1 - F ( t ) ] / n ; F _ { n } ( t )$ is the UMVUE under some nonparametric models; and $F _ { n } ( t )$ <sub>is</sub> √<sub>n-consistent for</sub> $F ( t )$ . For any m fixed distinct points $t _ { 1 } , . . . , t _ { m }$ in $\mathcal { R } ^ { d } .$ , it follows from the multivariate CLT (Corollary 1.2) and (5.1) that as $n \to \infty$ , 

$$
\sqrt {n} \left[\left(F _ {n} (t _ {1}),..., F _ {n} (t _ {m})\right) - \left(F (t _ {1}),..., F (t _ {m})\right)\right]\rightarrow_ {d} N _ {m} (0, \Sigma),\tag{5.2}
$$

where Σ is the $m \times m$ matrix whose $( i , j )$ th element is 

$$
P \left(X _ {1} \in (- \infty , t _ {i} ] \cap (- \infty , t _ {j} ]\right) - F (t _ {i}) F (t _ {j}).
$$

Note that these results hold without any assumption on $F .$ 

Considered as a function of $t , F _ { n }$ is a random element taking values in ${ \mathfrak { F } } ,$ the collection of all $\mathrm { c . d . f . ^ { \prime } s }$ on $\mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ . As $n  \infty , \sqrt { n } ( F _ { n } - F )$ converges in some sense to a random element defined on some probability space. A detailed discussion of such a result is beyond our scope and can be found, for example, in Shorack and Wellner (1986). To discuss some global properties of $F _ { n }$ as an estimator of $F \in { \mathfrak { F } }$ , we need to define a closeness measure between the elements (c.d.f.’s) in $\mathfrak { F }$ 

Definition 5.1. Let $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ be a collection of c.d.f.’s on $\mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ 

(i) A function $\varrho$ from $\mathbf { \mathcal { F } } _ { 0 } \times \mathbf { \mathcal { F } } _ { 0 }$ to $\lbrack 0 , \infty )$ is called a distance or metric on $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ if and only if for any $G _ { j }$ in $\mathbf { \mathcal { F } } _ { 0 } , \mathbf { \Psi } ( \mathrm { a } ) ~ \varrho ( G _ { 1 } , G _ { 2 } ) = 0$ if and only if $G _ { 1 } = G _ { 2 }$ (b) $\varrho ( G _ { 1 } , G _ { 2 } ) = \varrho ( G _ { 2 } , \dot { G } _ { 1 } )$ ; and (c) $\varrho ( G _ { 1 } , G _ { 2 } ) \leq \varrho ( G _ { 1 } , G _ { 3 } ) + \varrho ( G _ { 3 } , G _ { 2 } )$ (ii) Let $\mathbf { \mathcal { D } } = \{ c ( G _ { 1 } - G _ { 2 } ) : c \in \mathcal { R } , G _ { j } \in \mathfrak { F } _ { 0 } , j = 1 , 2 \}$ . A function $\| \cdot \|$ from D to $[ 0 , \infty )$ is called a norm on D if and only if $( \mathrm { a } ) \ \lVert \Delta \rVert = 0$ if and only if $\Delta = 0 ; ( \mathrm { b } ) \| c \Delta \| = | c | \| \Delta \|$ for any $\Delta \in \mathbf { \Delta } \mathbb { D }$ and $c \in \mathcal R ;$ and (c) $\| \Delta _ { 1 } + \Delta _ { 2 } \| \le \| \Delta _ { 1 } \| + \| \Delta _ { 2 } \|$ for any $\Delta _ { j } \in \mathbf { \mathcal { D } } , j = 1 , 2$ 

Any norm $\| \cdot \|$ on D induces a distance given by $\varrho ( G _ { 1 } , G _ { 2 } ) = \| G _ { 1 } - G _ { 2 } \|$ The most commonly used distance is the sup-norm distance $\varrho _ { \infty }$ , i.e., the distance induced by the sup-norm 

$$
\| G _ {1} - G _ {2} \| _ {\infty} = \sup _ {t \in \mathcal {R} ^ {d}} | G _ {1} (t) - G _ {2} (t) |, \quad G _ {j} \in \mathcal {F}.\tag{5.3}
$$

The following result concerning the sup-norm distance between $F _ { n }$ and $F$ is due to Dvoretzky, Kiefer, and Wolfowitz (1956). 

Lemma 5.1. (DKW’s inequality). Let $F _ { n }$ be the empirical c.d.f. based on i.i.d. $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ from a c.d.f. F on $\mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ 

(i) When $d = 1$ , there exists a positive constant C (not depending on F) such that 

$$
P \big (\varrho_ {\infty} (F _ {n}, F) > z \big) \leq C e ^ {- 2 n z ^ {2}}, \quad z > 0,   n = 1, 2,...
$$

(ii) When $d \geq 2$ , for any $\epsilon > 0$ , there exists a positive constant $C _ { \epsilon , d }$ (not depending on $F )$ such that 

$$
P \big (\varrho_ {\infty} (F _ {n}, F) > z \big) \leq C _ {\epsilon , d} e ^ {- (2 - \epsilon) n z ^ {2}}, \quad z > 0, n = 1, 2, \dots .
$$

The proof of this lemma is omitted. The following results useful in statistics are direct consequences of Lemma 5.1. 

Theorem 5.1. Let $F _ { n }$ be the empirical c.d.f. based on i.i.d. $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ from a c.d.f. F on $\mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ . Then 

(i) $\varrho _ { \infty } ( F _ { n } , F ) \to _ { a . s . } 0$ as $n \to \infty ;$ 

(ii) $E [ \sqrt { n } \varrho _ { \infty } ( F _ { n } , F ) ] ^ { s } = O ( 1 )$ for any $s > 0$ 

Proof. (i) From DKW’s inequality, 

$$
\sum_ {n = 1} ^ {\infty} P \big (\varrho_ {\infty} (F _ {n}, F) > z \big) <   \infty .
$$

Hence, the result follows from Theorem $1 . 8 ( \mathrm { v } )$ 

(ii) Using DKW’s inequality with $z = y ^ { 1 / s } / \sqrt { n }$ and the result in Exercise 55 of 1.6, we obtain that 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E [ \sqrt {n} \varrho_ {\infty} (F _ {n}, F) ] ^ {s} = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} P \big (\sqrt {n} \varrho_ {\infty} (F _ {n}, F) > y ^ {1 / s} \big) d y \\ \qquad \leq C _ {\epsilon , d} \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} e ^ {- (2 - \epsilon) y ^ {2 / s}} d y \\ \qquad = O (1) \end{array}
$$

as long as $2 - \epsilon > 0$ 

Theorem 5.1(i) means that $F _ { n } ( t ) \to _ { a . s . } F ( t )$ uniformly in $t \in \mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ , a result stronger than the strong consistency of $F _ { n } ( t )$ for every t. Theorem 5.1(ii) implies that $\sqrt { n } \varrho _ { \infty } ( F _ { n } , F ) = O _ { p } ( 1 )$ , a result stronger than the $\sqrt { n } -$ consistency of $F _ { n } ( t )$ . These results hold without any condition on $F$ 

Let $p \geq 1$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \pmb { \mathcal { F } } _ { p } = \{ G \in \pmb { \mathcal { F } } : \int \| t \| ^ { p } d G < \infty \} } \end{array}$ , which is the subset of c.d.f.’s in $\mathcal { F }$ having finite pth moments. Mallows’ distance between $G _ { 1 }$ and $G _ { 2 }$ in $\mathfrak { F } _ { p }$ is defined to be 

$$
\varrho_ {M _ {p}} (G _ {1}, G _ {2}) = \inf (E \| Y _ {1} - Y _ {2} \| ^ {p}) ^ {1 / p},\tag{5.4}
$$

where the infimum is taken over all pairs of $Y _ { 1 }$ and $Y _ { 2 }$ having $\mathrm { c . d . f . } ^ { \prime } \mathrm { s } G _ { 1 }$ and $G _ { 2 }$ , respectively. Let $\left\{ G _ { j } : j = 0 , 1 , 2 , \ldots \right\} \subset \mathcal { F } _ { p }$ . Then $\varrho _ { M _ { p } } ( G _ { j } , G _ { 0 } ) \to 0$ as $j \to \infty$ if and only if $\begin{array} { r } { \int \| t \| ^ { p } d G _ { j }  \int \| t \| ^ { p } d G _ { 0 } } \end{array}$ and $G _ { j } ( t )  G _ { 0 } ( t )$ for every $t \in \mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ at which $G _ { 0 }$ is continuous. It follows from Theorem 5.1 and the SLLN (Theorem 1.13) that $\varrho _ { M _ { p } } ( F _ { n } , F ) \to _ { a . s . } 0$ if $F \in \mathfrak { F } _ { p }$ 

When $d = 1$ , another useful distance for measuring the closeness between $F _ { n }$ and F is the $L _ { p }$ distance $\varrho _ { L _ { p } }$ induced by the $L _ { p ^ { - } } \mathrm { n o r m } \ ( p \geq 1 )$ 

$$
\left\| G _ {1} - G _ {2} \right\| _ {L _ {p}} = \left[ \int | G _ {1} (t) - G _ {2} (t) | ^ {p} d t \right] ^ {1 / p}, \quad G _ {j} \in \mathfrak {F} _ {1}.\tag{5.5}
$$

A result similar to Theorem 5.1 is given as follows. 

Theorem 5.2. Let $F _ { n }$ be the empirical c.d.f. based on i.i.d. random vari ables $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ from a c.d.f. $F \in { \mathfrak { F } } _ { 1 }$ . Then 

(i) $\varrho _ { L _ { v } } ( F _ { n } , F ) \to _ { a . s . } 0 ;$ 

(ii) $E [ \sqrt { n } \varrho _ { L _ { n } } ( F _ { n } , F ) ] = O ( 1 ) \mathrm { i f } 1 \leq p < 2$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \int \{ F ( t ) [ 1 - F ( t ) ] \} ^ { p / 2 } d t < \infty , } \end{array}$ p or $p \geq 2$ 

Proof. (i) Since $[ \varrho _ { L _ { v } } ( F _ { n } , F ) ] ^ { p } \leq [ \varrho _ { \infty } ( F _ { n } , F ) ] ^ { p - 1 } [ \varrho _ { L _ { 1 } } ( F _ { n } , F ) ]$ and, by Theorem $5 . 1 , \varrho _ { \infty } ( F _ { n } , F ) \stackrel { . } { \to } _ { a . s . } 0$ , it sufices to show the result for $p = 1$ . Let $\begin{array} { r } { Y _ { i } = \int _ { - \infty } ^ { 0 } [ I _ { ( - \infty , t ] } ( X _ { i } ) - F ( t ) ] d t } \end{array}$ . Then $Y _ { 1 } , . . . , Y _ { n }$ are i.i.d. and 

$$
E \left| Y _ {i} \right| \leq \int E \left| I _ {\left(- \infty , t \right]} \left(X _ {i}\right) - F (t) \right| d t = 2 \int F (t) [ 1 - F (t) ] d t,
$$

which is finite under the condition that $F \in { \mathfrak { F } } _ { 1 }$ . By the SLLN, 

$$
\int_ {- \infty} ^ {0} [ F _ {n} (t) - F (t) ] d t = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Y _ {i} \rightarrow_ {a. s.} E (Y _ {1}) = 0.\tag{5.6}
$$

Since $[ F _ { n } ( t ) - F ( t ) ] _ { - } \leq F ( t )$ and $\textstyle \int _ { - \infty } ^ { 0 } F ( t ) d t < \infty$ (Exercise 55 in $\ S 1 . 6 )$ −∞<sub>it follows from Theorem 5.1 and the dominated convergence theorem that</sub> $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { - \infty } ^ { 0 } [ F _ { n } ( t ) - F ( t ) ] _ { - } d t \longrightarrow _ { a . s . } 0 } \end{array}$ , which with (5.6) implies 

$$
\int_ {- \infty} ^ {0} | F _ {n} (t) - F (t) | d t \rightarrow_ {a. s.} 0.\tag{5.7}
$$

The result follows since we can similarly show that (5.7) holds with $\boldsymbol { \int } _ { - \infty } ^ { 0 }$ replaced by $\textstyle \int _ { 0 } ^ { \infty }$ 

(ii) When $1 \le p < 2$ , the result follows from 

$$
\begin{array}{l} E [ \varrho_ {L _ {p}} (F _ {n}, F) ] \leq \left\{\int E | F _ {n} (t) - F (t) | ^ {p} d t \right\} ^ {1 / p} \\ \quad \leq \left\{\int [ E | F _ {n} (t) - F (t) | ^ {2} ] ^ {p / 2} d t \right\} ^ {1 / p} \\ \quad = n ^ {- 1 / 2} \left\{\int \{F (t) [ 1 - F (t) ] \} ^ {p / 2} d t \right\} ^ {1 / p} \\ \quad = O (n ^ {- 1 / 2}), \end{array}
$$

where the two inequalities follow from Jensen’s inequality. When $p \geq 2$ 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & E [ \varrho_ {L _ {p}} (F _ {n}, F) ] \leq E \left\{[ \varrho_ {\infty} (F _ {n}, F) ] ^ {1 - 2 / p} [ \varrho_ {L _ {2}} (F _ {n}, F) ] ^ {2 / p} \right\} \\ & \quad \leq \left\{E [ \varrho_ {\infty} (F _ {n}, F) ] ^ {(1 - 2 / p) q} \right\} ^ {1 / q} \left\{E [ \varrho_ {L _ {2}} (F _ {n}, F) ] ^ {2} \right\} ^ {1 / p} \\ & \quad = \left\{O (n ^ {- (1 - 2 / p) q / 2}) \right\} ^ {1 / q} \left\{E \int | F _ {n} (t) - F (t) | ^ {2} d t \right\} ^ {1 / p} \\ & \quad = O (n ^ {- (1 - 2 / p) / 2}) \left\{\frac {1}{n} \int F (t) [ 1 - F (t) ] d t \right\} ^ {1 / p} \\ & \quad = O (n ^ {- 1 / 2}), \end{array}
$$

where $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { q } } + { \frac { 1 } { p } } = 1$ , the second inequality follows from H¨older’s inequality (see (1.40) in 1.3.2), and the first equality follows from Theorem 5.1(ii). 

## 5.1.2 Empirical likelihoods

In 4.4 and 4.5, we have shown that the method of using likelihoods pro vides some asymptotically eficient estimators. We now introduce some likelihoods in nonparametric models. This not only provides another justification for the use of the empirical c.d.f. in (5.1), but also leads to a useful method of deriving estimators in various (possibly non-i.i.d.) cases, some of which are discussed later in this chapter. 

Let $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ be i.i.d. with $F \in { \mathfrak { F } }$ and $P _ { G }$ be the probability measure corresponding to $G \in { \mathfrak { F } }$ . Given $X _ { 1 } = x _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n } = x _ { n }$ , the nonparametric likelihood function is defined to be the following functional from $\Im$ to $[ 0 , \infty )$ 

$$
\ell (G) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} P _ {G} (\{x _ {i} \}), \qquad G \in \mathfrak {F}.\tag{5.8}
$$

Apparently, $\ell ( G ) = 0$ if $P _ { G } ( \{ x _ { i } \} ) = 0$ for at least one i. The following result, due to Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956), shows that the empirical c.d.f. $F _ { n }$ is a nonparametric maximum likelihood estimator of $F$ 

Theorem 5.3. Let $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ be i.i.d. with $F \in { \mathfrak { F } }$ and $\ell ( G )$ be defined by (5.8). Then $F _ { n }$ maximizes $\ell ( G )$ over $G \in { \mathfrak { F } }$ Proof. We only need to consider $G \in { \mathfrak { F } }$ such that $\ell ( G ) > 0$ . Let $c \in ( 0 , 1 ]$ and $\mathfrak { F } ( c )$ be the subset of $\Im$ containing $G \mathrm { { s } }$ satisfying $p _ { i } = P _ { G } ( \{ x _ { i } \} ) > 0$ $i = 1 , . . . , n$ , and $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } p _ { i } \ = \ c .$ We now apply the Lagrange multiplier method to solve the problem of maximizing $\ell ( G )$ over $G \in { \mathcal { F } } ( c )$ . Define 

$$
H (p _ {1}, \dots , p _ {n}, \lambda) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} + \lambda \left(\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} - c\right),
$$

where λ is the Lagrange multiplier. Set 

$$
\frac {\partial H}{\partial \lambda} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} - c = 0, \quad \frac {\partial H}{\partial p _ {j}} = p _ {j} ^ {- 1} \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} + \lambda = 0, \quad j = 1, \dots , n.
$$

The solution is $p _ { i } = c / n , i = 1 , . . . , n , \lambda = - ( c / n ) ^ { n - 1 }$ . It can be shown (exercise) that this solution is a maximum of $H ( p _ { 1 } , . . . , p _ { n } , \lambda )$ over $p _ { i } > 0$ ， $\begin{array} { r } { i = 1 , . . . , n , \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } p _ { i } = c . } \end{array}$ . This shows that 

$$
\max _ {G \in \mathcal {F} (c)} \ell (G) = (c / n) ^ {n},
$$

which is maximized at $c = 1$ for any fixed n. The result follows from $P _ { F _ { n } } ( \{ x _ { i } \} ) = n ^ { - 1 }$ for given $X _ { i } = x _ { i } , i = 1 , . . . , n$ 

From the proof of Theorem 5.3, $F _ { n }$ maximizes the likelihood $\ell ( G )$ in (5.8) over $p _ { i } > 0 , i = 1 , . . . , n$ , and $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } p _ { i } = 1$ , where $p _ { i } = P _ { G } ( \{ x _ { i } \} )$ . This method of deriving an estimator of $F$ can be extended to various situations with some modifications of (5.8) and/or constraints on $p _ { i } \mathrm { ^ { * } s }$ . Modifications of the likelihood in (5.8) are called empirical likelihoods (Owen, 1988, 2001; Qin and Lawless, 1994). An estimator obtained by maximizing an empirical likelihood is then called a maximum empirical likelihood estimator (MELE). We now discuss several applications of the method of empirical likelihoods. 

Consider first the estimation of $F$ with auxiliary information about F (and i.i.d. $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n } )$ . For instance, suppose that there is a known Borel function u from $\mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ to $\mathcal { R } ^ { s }$ such that 

$$
\int u (x) d F = 0\tag{5.9}
$$

$( \mathrm { e . g . }$ , some components of the mean of $F$ are 0). It is then reasonable to expect that any estimate $\hat { F }$ of $F$ has property (5.9), i.e., $\textstyle \int u ( x ) d { \hat { F } } = 0$ , which is not true for the empirical c.d.f. $F _ { n }$ in (5.1), since 

$$
\int u (x) d F _ {n} = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} u (X _ {i}) \neq 0
$$

even if $E [ u ( X _ { 1 } ) ] = 0$ . Using the method of empirical likelihoods, a natural solution is to put another constraint in the process of maximizing the likelihood. That is, we maximize $\ell ( G )$ in (5.8) subject to 

$$
p _ {i} > 0, \quad i = 1, \dots , n, \quad \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} = 1, \quad \text { and } \quad \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} u (x _ {i}) = 0,\tag{5.10}
$$

where $p _ { i } = P _ { G } ( \{ x _ { i } \} )$ . Using the Lagrange multiplier method and an argument similar to the proof of Theorem 5.3, it can be shown (exercise) that an MELE of $F$ is n 

$$
\hat {F} (t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \hat {p} _ {i} I _ {(- \infty , t ]} (X _ {i}),\tag{5.11}
$$

where the notation $( - \infty , t ]$ is the same as that in (5.1), 

$$
\hat {p} _ {i} = n ^ {- 1} [ 1 + \lambda_ {n} ^ {\tau} u (X _ {i}) ] ^ {- 1}, \qquad i = 1, \dots , n,\tag{5.12}
$$

and $\lambda _ { n } \in \mathcal { R } ^ { s }$ is the Lagrange multiplier satisfying 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \hat {p} _ {i} u (X _ {i}) = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {u (X _ {i})}{1 + \lambda_ {n} ^ {\tau} u (X _ {i})} = 0.\tag{5.13}
$$

Note that $\hat { F }$ reduces to $F _ { n }$ if $u \equiv 0$ 

To see that (5.13) has a solution asymptotically, note that 

$$
\frac {\partial}{\partial \lambda} \left[ \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \log \bigl (1 + \lambda^ {\tau} u (X _ {i}) \bigr) \right] = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {u (X _ {i})}{1 + \lambda^ {\tau} u (X _ {i})}
$$

and 

$$
\frac {\partial^ {2}}{\partial \lambda \partial \lambda^ {\tau}} \left[ \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \log \bigl (1 + \lambda^ {\tau} u (X _ {i}) \bigr) \right] = - \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {u (X _ {i}) [ u (X _ {i}) ] ^ {\tau}}{[ 1 + \lambda^ {\tau} u (X _ {i}) ] ^ {2}},
$$

which is negative definite if $\mathrm { V a r } ( u ( X _ { 1 } ) )$ is positive definite. Also, 

$$
E \left\{\frac {\partial}{\partial \lambda} \left[ \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \log \bigl (1 + \lambda^ {\tau} u (X _ {i}) \bigr) \right] \Bigg | _ {\lambda = 0} \right\} = E [ u (X _ {1}) ] = 0.
$$

Hence, using the same argument as in the proof of Theorem 4.18, we can show that there exists a unique sequence $\{ \lambda _ { n } ( X ) \}$ such that as $n \to \infty$ , 

$$
P \left(\frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {u (X _ {i})}{1 + \lambda_ {n} ^ {\tau} u (X _ {i})} = 0\right)\rightarrow 1 \quad \text { and } \quad \lambda_ {n} \rightarrow_ {p} 0.\tag{5.14}
$$

Theorem 5.4. Let $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ be i.i.d. with $F \in { \mathfrak { F } }$ , u be a Borel function on $\mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ satisfying (5.9), and $\hat { F }$ be given by (5.11)-(5.13). Suppose that $U = \mathrm { V a r } ( u ( X _ { 1 } ) )$ ) is positive definite. Then, for any m fixed distinct $t _ { 1 } , . . . , t _ { m }$ in $\mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ 

$$
\sqrt {n} \left[\left(\hat {F} \left(t _ {1}\right), \dots , \hat {F} \left(t _ {m}\right)\right) - \left(F \left(t _ {1}\right), \dots , F \left(t _ {m}\right)\right)\right]\rightarrow_ {d} N _ {m} \left(0, \Sigma_ {u}\right),\tag{5.15}
$$

where 

$$
\Sigma_ {u} = \Sigma - W ^ {\tau} U ^ {- 1} W,
$$

$\Sigma$ is given in (5.2), $W = \bigl ( W ( t _ { 1 } ) , . . . , W ( t _ { m } ) \bigr ) , W ( t _ { j } ) = E [ u ( X _ { 1 } ) I _ { ( - \infty , t _ { j } ] } ( X _ { 1 } ) ]$ , and the notation $( - \infty , t ]$ is the same as that in (5.1). 

Proof. We prove the case of $m = 1$ . The case of $m \geq 2$ is left as an exercise. Let ${ \bar { u } } = n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } u ( X _ { i } )$ . It follows from (5.13), (5.14), and Taylor’s expansion that 

$$
\bar {u} = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} u (X _ {i}) [ u (X _ {i}) ] ^ {\tau} \lambda_ {n} [ 1 + o _ {p} (1) ].
$$

By the SLLN and CLT, 

$$
U ^ {- 1} \bar {u} = \lambda_ {n} + o _ {p} (n ^ {- 1 / 2}).
$$

Using Taylor’s expansion and the SLLN again, we have 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} I _ {(- \infty , t ]} (X _ {i}) (n \hat {p} _ {i} - 1) = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} I _ {(- \infty , t ]} (X _ {i}) \left[ \frac {1}{1 + \lambda_ {n} ^ {\tau} u (X _ {i})} - 1 \right] \\ \qquad = - \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} I _ {(- \infty , t ]} (X _ {i}) \lambda_ {n} ^ {\tau} u (X _ {i}) + o _ {p} (n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \\ \qquad = - \lambda_ {n} ^ {\tau} W (t) + o _ {p} (n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \\ \qquad = - \bar {u} ^ {\tau} U ^ {- 1} W (t) + o _ {p} (n ^ {- 1 / 2}). \end{array}
$$

Thus, 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \hat {F} (t) - F (t) = F _ {n} (t) - F (t) + \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} I _ {(- \infty , t ]} (X _ {i}) (n \hat {p} _ {i} - 1) \\ \qquad = F _ {n} (t) - F (t) - \bar {u} ^ {\tau} U ^ {- 1} W (t) + o _ {p} (n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \\ \qquad = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \left\{I _ {(- \infty , t ]} (X _ {i}) - F (t) - [ u (X _ {i}) ] ^ {\tau} U ^ {- 1} W (t) \right\} + o _ {p} (n ^ {- 1 / 2}). \end{array}
$$

The result follows from the CLT and the fact that 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} \mathrm{Var} \big ([ W (t) ] ^ {\tau} U ^ {- 1} u (X _ {i}) \big) & = [ W (t) ] ^ {\tau} U ^ {- 1} U U ^ {- 1} W (t) \\ & = [ W (t) ] ^ {\tau} U ^ {- 1} W (t) \\ & = E \{[ W (t) ] ^ {\tau} U ^ {- 1} u (X _ {i}) I _ {(- \infty , t ]} (X _ {i}) \} \\ & = \mathrm{Cov} \big (I _ {(- \infty , t ]} (X _ {i}), [ W (t) ] ^ {\tau} U ^ {- 1} u (X _ {i}) \big). \end{array}
$$

Comparing (5.15) with (5.2), we conclude that $\hat { F }$ is asymptotically more eficient than $F _ { n }$ 

Example 5.1 (Survey problems). An example of situations in which we have auxiliary information expressed as (5.9) is a survey problem (Example 2.3) where the population $\mathcal { P } = \{ y _ { 1 } , . . . , y _ { N } \}$ consists of two-dimensional $y _ { j } \mathrm { \dot { s } }$ $y _ { j } = ( y _ { 1 j } , y _ { 2 j } )$ , and the population mean $\begin{array} { r } { \bar { Y } _ { 2 } = N ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { j = 1 } ^ { N } y _ { 2 j } } \end{array}$ is known. For example, suppose that $y _ { 1 j }$ is the current year’s income of unit $j$ in the population and $y _ { 2 j }$ is the last year’s income. In many applications the population total or mean of $y _ { 2 j }$ ’s is known, for example, from tax return records. Let $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ be a simple random sample (see Example 2.3) selected from $\mathcal { P }$ with replacement. Then $X _ { i }$ ’s are i.i.d. bivariate random vectors whose c.d.f. is 

$$
F (t) = \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {N} I _ {(- \infty , t ]} (y _ {j}),\tag{5.16}
$$

where the notation $( - \infty , t ]$ is the same as that in (5.1). If $\bar { Y } _ { 2 }$ is known, then it can be expressed as (5.9) with $u ( x _ { 1 } , x _ { 2 } ) = x _ { 2 } - { \bar { Y } } _ { 2 }$ . In survey problems $X _ { i } \mathrm { { ^ { * } s } }$ are usually sampled without replacement so that $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ are not i.i.d. However, for a simple random sample without replacement, (5.8) can still be treated as an empirical likelihood, given $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ . Note that $F$ in (5.16) is the c.d.f. of $X _ { i }$ , regardless of whether $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are sampled with replacement. 

If $X = ( X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n } )$ is not a simple random sample, then the likelihood (5.8) has to be modified. Suppose that $\pi _ { i }$ is the probability that the ith unit is selected (see Theorem 3.15). Given $X = \{ y _ { i } , i \in s \}$ , an empirical likelihood is 

$$
\ell (G) = \prod_ {i \in \boldsymbol {\mathcal {S}}} [ P _ {G} (\{y _ {i} \}) ] ^ {1 / \pi_ {i}} = \prod_ {i \in \boldsymbol {\mathcal {S}}} p _ {i} ^ {1 / \pi_ {i}},\tag{5.17}
$$

where $p _ { i } = P _ { G } ( \{ y _ { i } \} )$ . With the auxiliary information (5.9), an MELE of $F$ in (5.16) can be obtained by maximizing $\ell ( G )$ in (5.17) subject to (5.10). In this case $F$ may not be the c.d.f. of $X _ { i }$ , but the c.d.f.’s of $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are determined by $F$ and $\pi _ { i } ^ { \cdot } \mathrm { s }$ . It can be shown (exercise) that an MELE is given by (5.11) with 

$$
\hat {p} _ {i} = \frac {1}{\pi_ {i} [ 1 + \lambda_ {n} ^ {\tau} u (y _ {i}) ]} \bigg / \sum_ {i \in \boldsymbol {S}} \frac {1}{\pi_ {i}}\tag{5.18}
$$

and 

$$
\sum_ {i \in \pmb {\mathscr {S}}} \frac {u (y _ {i})}{\pi_ {i} [ 1 + \lambda_ {n} ^ {\tau} u (y _ {i}) ]} = 0.\tag{5.19}
$$

If $\pi _ { i } = \mathrm { a }$ constant, then the MELE reduces to that in (5.11)-(5.13). If 

$u ( x ) = 0$ (no auxiliary information), then the MELE is 

$$
\hat {F} (t) = \sum_ {i \in \pmb {\mathscr {S}}} \frac {1}{\pi_ {i}} I _ {(- \infty , t ]} (y _ {i}) \bigg / \sum_ {i \in \pmb {\mathscr {S}}} \frac {1}{\pi_ {i}},
$$

which is a ratio of two Horvitz-Thompson estimators ( 3.4.2). Some asymptotic properties of the MELE $\hat { F }$ can be found in Chen and Qin (1993). 

The second part of Example 5.1 shows how to use empirical likelihoods in a non-i.i.d. problem. Applications of empirical likelihoods in non-i.i.d. problems are usually straightforward extensions of those in i.i.d. cases. The following is another example. 

Example 5.2 (Biased sampling). Biased sampling is often used in applications. Suppose that $n = n _ { 1 } + \cdot \cdot \cdot + n _ { k } , k \geq 2 ; X _ { i } \mathrm { ' s }$ s are independent random variables; $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n _ { 1 } }$ are i.i.d. with $F ;$ and $X _ { n _ { 1 } + \cdots + n _ { j } + 1 } , . . . , X _ { { n _ { 1 } + \cdots + n _ { j + 1 } } }$ are i.i.d. with the c.d.f. 

$$
\int_ {- \infty} ^ {t} w _ {j + 1} (s) d F (s) \bigg / \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} w _ {j + 1} (s) d F (s),
$$

$j = 1 , . . . , k - 1$ , where $w _ { j } \mathrm { ^ { * } s }$ are some nonnegative Borel functions. A simple example is that $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n _ { 1 } }$ are sampled from $F$ and $X _ { n _ { 1 } + 1 } , . . . , X _ { { n _ { 1 } + n _ { 2 } } }$ are sampled from $F$ but conditional on the fact that each sampled value exceeds a given value $x _ { 0 } ~ ( \mathrm { i . e . , } ~ w _ { 2 } ( s ) = I _ { ( x _ { 0 } , \infty ) } ( s ) )$ . For instance, $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are blood pressure measurements; $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n _ { 1 } }$ are sampled from ordinary people and $X _ { n _ { 1 } + 1 } , . . . , X _ { { n _ { 1 } + n _ { 2 } } }$ are sampled from patients whose blood pressures are higher than $x _ { 0 }$ . The name biased sampling comes from the fact that there is a bias in the selection of samples. 

For simplicity we consider the case of $k = 2$ , since the extension to $k \geq 3$ is straightforward. Denote $w _ { 2 }$ by $w .$ . An empirical likelihood is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \ell (G) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n _ {1}} P _ {G} (\{x _ {i} \}) \prod_ {i = n _ {1} + 1} ^ {n} \frac {w (x _ {i}) P _ {G} (\{x _ {i} \})}{\int w (s) d G (s)} \\ = \left[ \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} w (x _ {i}) \right] ^ {- n _ {2}} \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} \prod_ {i = n _ {1} + 1} ^ {n} w (x _ {i}), \end{array}\tag{5.20}
$$

where $p _ { i } = P _ { G } ( \{ x _ { i } \} )$ . An MELE of $F$ can be obtained by maximizing the empirical likelihood (5.20) subject to $p _ { i } > 0 , i = 1 , . . . , n$ , and $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } p _ { i } =$ 1. Using the Lagrange multiplier method we can show (exercise) that an MELE $\hat { F }$ is given by (5.11) with 

$$
\hat {p} _ {i} = [ n _ {1} + n _ {2} w (X _ {i}) / \hat {w} ] ^ {- 1}, \qquad i = 1, \dots , n,\tag{5.21}
$$

where $\hat { w }$ satisfies 

$$
\hat {w} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {w (X _ {i})}{n _ {1} + n _ {2} w (X _ {i}) / \hat {w}}.
$$

An asymptotic result similar to that in Theorem 5.4 can be established (Vardi, 1985; Qin, 1993). 

If the function $w$ depends on an unknown parameter vector $\theta ,$ then the method of profile empirical likelihood (see 5.1.4) can be applied. 

Our last example concerns an important application in survival analysis. 

Example 5.3 (Censored data). Let $T _ { 1 } , . . . , T _ { n }$ be survival times that are i.i.d. nonnegative random variables from a c.d.f. $F$ , and $C _ { 1 } , . . . , C _ { n }$ be i.i.d. nonnegative random variables independent of $T _ { i } \mathrm { { ' s } }$ . In a variety of applications in biostatistics and life-time testing, we are only able to observe the smaller of $T _ { i }$ and $C _ { i }$ and an indicator of which variable is smaller: 

$$
X _ {i} = \min \{T _ {i}, C _ {i} \}, \qquad \delta_ {i} = I _ {(0, C _ {i})} (T _ {i}), \qquad i = 1,..., n.
$$

This is called a random censorship model and $C _ { i } \mathrm { { ^ { 5 } s } }$ are called censoring times. We consider the estimation of the survival distribution $F ;$ see Kalbfleisch and Prentice (1980) for other problems involving censored data. 

An MELE of $F$ can be derived as follows. Let $x _ { ( 1 ) } \leq \cdots \leq x _ { ( n ) }$ be ordered values of $X _ { i }$ ’s and $\delta _ { ( i ) }$ be the δ-value associated with $\boldsymbol { x } _ { ( i ) }$ . Consider a c.d.f. G that assigns its mass to the points $x _ { ( 1 ) } , . . . , x _ { ( n ) }$ and the interval $( x _ { ( n ) } , \infty )$ . Let $p _ { i } = P _ { G } ( \{ x _ { ( i ) } \} ) , i = 1 , . . . , n .$ , and $p _ { n + 1 } = 1 - G ( x _ { ( n ) } )$ . An MELE of $F$ is then obtained by maximizing 

$$
\ell (G) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} ^ {\delta_ {(i)}} \left(\sum_ {j = i + 1} ^ {n + 1} p _ {j}\right) ^ {1 - \delta_ {(i)}}\tag{5.22}
$$

subject to 

$$
p _ {i} \geq 0, \quad i = 1,..., n + 1, \quad \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n + 1} p _ {i} = 1.\tag{5.23}
$$

It can be shown (exercise) that an MELE is 

$$
\hat {F} (t) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n + 1} \hat {p} _ {i} I _ {(0, t ]} (X _ {(i)}),\tag{5.24}
$$

where $X _ { ( 0 ) } = 0 , X _ { ( n + 1 ) } = \infty , X _ { ( 1 ) } \leq \cdots \leq X _ { ( n ) }$ are order statistics, and 

$$
\hat {p} _ {i} = \frac {\delta_ {(i)}}{n - i + 1} \prod_ {j = 1} ^ {i - 1} \left(1 - \frac {\delta_ {(j)}}{n - j + 1}\right), \quad i = 1, \dots , n, \quad \hat {p} _ {n + 1} = 1 - \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \hat {p} _ {j}.
$$

The $\hat { F }$ in (5.24) can also be written as (exercise) 

$$
\hat {F} (t) = 1 - \prod_ {X _ {(i)} \leq t} \left(1 - \frac {\delta_ {(i)}}{n - i + 1}\right),\tag{5.25}
$$

which is the well-known Kaplan-Meier (1958) product-limit estimator. Some asymptotic results for $\hat { F }$ in (5.25) can be found, for example, in Shorack and Wellner (1986). 

## 5.1.3 Density estimation

Suppose that $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ are i.i.d. random variables from $F$ and that $F$ is unknown but has a Lebesgue p.d.f. $f .$ . Estimation of $F$ can be done by estimating $f _ { : }$ , which is called density estimation. Note that estimators of $F$ derived in 5.1.1 and 5.1.2 do not have Lebesgue p.d.f.’s. 

Since $f ( t ) = F ^ { \prime } ( t )$ a.e., a simple estimator of $f ( t )$ is the diference quotient 

$$
f _ {n} (t) = \frac {F _ {n} (t + \lambda_ {n}) - F _ {n} (t - \lambda_ {n})}{2 \lambda_ {n}}, \qquad t \in \mathcal {R},\tag{5.26}
$$

where $F _ { n }$ is the empirical c.d.f. given by (2.28) or (5.1) with $d = 1$ , and $\left\{ \lambda _ { n } \right\}$ is a sequence of positive constants. Since $2 n \lambda _ { n } f _ { n } ( t )$ has the binomial distribution $B i ( F ( t + \lambda _ { n } ) - F ( t - \lambda _ { n } ) , n )$ , 

$$
E [ f _ {n} (t) ] \rightarrow f (t) \quad \text { if } \lambda_ {n} \rightarrow 0 \text { as } n \rightarrow \infty
$$

and 

$$
\operatorname{Var} \bigl (f _ {n} (t) \bigr) \to 0 \quad \text { if } \lambda_ {n} \to 0 \text { and } n \lambda_ {n} \to \infty .
$$

Thus, we should choose $\lambda _ { n }$ converging to 0 slower than $n ^ { - 1 }$ . If we assume that $\lambda _ { n } \to 0 , n \lambda _ { n } \to \infty$ , and $f$ is continuously diferentiable at t, then it can be shown (exercise) that 

$$
\mathrm{mse} _ {f _ {n} (t)} (F) = \frac {f (t)}{2 n \lambda_ {n}} + o \left(\frac {1}{n \lambda_ {n}}\right) + O (\lambda_ {n} ^ {2})\tag{5.27}
$$

and, under the additional condition that $n \lambda _ { n } ^ { 3 } \to 0$ , 

$$
\sqrt {n \lambda_ {n}} [ f _ {n} (t) - f (t) ] \rightarrow_ {d} N \bigl (0, \frac {1}{2} f (t) \bigr).\tag{5.28}
$$

A useful class of estimators is the class of kernel density estimators of the form 

$$
\hat {f} (t) = \frac {1}{n \lambda_ {n}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} w \left(\frac {t - X _ {i}}{\lambda_ {n}}\right),\tag{5.29}
$$

where w is a known Lebesgue p.d.f. on $\mathcal { R }$ and is called the kernel. If we choose $\begin{array} { r } { w ( t ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } I _ { [ - 1 , 1 ] } ( t ) } \end{array}$ , then ${ \hat { f } } ( t )$ in (5.29) is essentially the same as the so-called histogram. The bias of ${ \hat { f } } ( t )$ in (5.29) is 

$$
\begin{array}{c} E [ \hat {f} (t) ] - f (t) = \frac {1}{\lambda_ {n}} \int w \left(\frac {t - z}{\lambda_ {n}}\right) f (z) d z - f (t) \\ = \int w (y) [ f (t - \lambda_ {n} y) - f (t) ] d y. \end{array}
$$

If $f$ is bounded and continuous at t, then, by the dominated convergence theorem (Theorem $1 . 1 ( \mathrm { i i i } ) )$ , the bias of ${ \hat { f } } ( t )$ converges to 0 as $\lambda _ { n } \to 0 ;$ if $f ^ { \prime }$ is bounded and continuous at t and $\begin{array} { r } { \int | t | w ( t ) d t < \infty } \end{array}$ , then the bias of ${ \hat { f } } ( t )$ is $O ( \lambda _ { n } )$ . The variance of ${ \hat { f } } ( t )$ is 

$$
\begin{array}{l} \operatorname{Var} \big (\hat {f} (t) \big) = \frac {1}{n \lambda_ {n} ^ {2}} \operatorname{Var} \left(w \left(\frac {t - X _ {1}}{\lambda_ {n}}\right)\right) \\ \qquad = \frac {1}{n \lambda_ {n} ^ {2}} \int \left[ w \left(\frac {t - z}{\lambda_ {n}}\right) \right] ^ {2} f (z) d z \\ \qquad - \frac {1}{n} \left[ \frac {1}{\lambda_ {n}} \int w \left(\frac {t - z}{\lambda_ {n}}\right) f (z) d z \right] ^ {2} \\ \qquad = \frac {1}{n \lambda_ {n}} \int [ w (y) ] ^ {2} f (t - \lambda_ {n} y) d y + O \left(\frac {1}{n}\right) \\ \qquad = \frac {w _ {0} f (t)}{n \lambda_ {n}} + o \left(\frac {1}{n \lambda_ {n}}\right) \end{array}
$$

if $f$ is bounded and continuous at t and $\begin{array} { r } { w _ { 0 } = \int [ w ( t ) ] ^ { 2 } d t < \infty } \end{array}$ . Hence, if $\lambda _ { n } \to 0 , n \lambda _ { n } \to \infty$ , and $f ^ { \prime }$ is bounded and continuous at t, then 

$$
\mathrm{mse} _ {\hat {f} (t)} (F) = \frac {w _ {0} f (t)}{n \lambda_ {n}} + O (\lambda_ {n} ^ {2}).
$$

Using the CLT (Theorem 1.15), one can show (exercise) that if $\lambda _ { n } \to 0$ , $n \lambda _ { n } \to \infty$ , and $f$ is bounded and continuous at t, then 

$$
\sqrt {n \lambda_ {n}} \{\hat {f} (t) - E [ \hat {f} (t) ] \} \rightarrow_ {d} N \big (0, w _ {0} f (t) \big).\tag{5.30}
$$

Furthermore, if $f ^ { \prime }$ is bounded and continuous at t, $\textstyle \int | t | w ( t ) d t < \infty$ , and $n \lambda _ { n } ^ { 3 } \to 0$ , then 

$$
\sqrt {n \lambda_ {n}} \{E [ \hat {f} (t) ] - f (t) \} = O (\sqrt {n \lambda_ {n}} \lambda_ {n}) \rightarrow 0
$$

and, therefore, (5.30) holds with $E [ \hat { f } ( t ) ]$ replaced by $f ( t )$ 

Similar to the estimation of a c.d.f., we can also study global properties of $f _ { n }$ or $\hat { f }$ as an estimator of the density curve $f _ { ; }$ using a suitably defined distance between $f$ and its density estimator. For example, we may study the convergence of $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { s u p } _ { t \in { \mathcal { R } } } | \widehat { f } ( t ) - f ( t ) | \ \mathrm { o r } \ \int | \widehat { f } ( t ) - f ( t ) | ^ { 2 } d t } \end{array}$ . More details can be found, for example, in Silverman (1986).

Figure 5.1: Density estimates in Example 5.4


Example 5.4. An i.i.d. sample of size $n = 2 0 0$ was generated from $N ( 0 , 1 )$ Density curve estimates (5.26) and (5.29) are plotted in Figure 5.1 with the curve of the true p.d.f. For the kernel density estimator (5.29), $\begin{array} { r } { w ( t ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } e ^ { - | t | } } \end{array}$ is used and $\lambda _ { n } = 0 . 4$ . From Figure 5.1, it seems that the kernel estimate (5.29) is much better than the estimate (5.26). 

There are many other density estimation methods, for example, the nearest neighbor method (Stone, 1977), the smoothing splines (Wahba, 1990), and the method of empirical likelihoods described in 5.1.2 (see, e.g., Jones (1991)), which produces estimators of the form 

$$
\hat {f} (t) = \frac {1}{\lambda_ {n}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \hat {p} _ {i} w \left(\frac {t - X _ {i}}{\lambda_ {n}}\right).
$$

## 5.1.4 Semi-parametric methods

Suppose that the sample X is from a population in a family indexed by $( \theta , \xi )$ , where $\theta$ is a parameter vector, i.e., $\theta \in \Theta \subset \mathcal { R } ^ { k }$ with a fixed positive integer $k ,$ but $\xi$ is not vector-valued, e.g., $\xi$ is a c.d.f. Such a model is often called a semi-parametric model, although it is nonparametric according to our definition in 2.1.2. A semi-parametric method refers to a statistical inference method that combines a parametric method and a nonparametric method in making an inference about the parametric component θ and the nonparametric component $\xi .$ . In the following, we consider two important examples of semi-parametric methods. 

## Partial likelihoods and proportional hazards models

The idea of partial likelihood (Cox, 1972) is similar to that of conditional likelihood introduced in 4.4.3. To illustrate this idea, we assume that X has a p.d.f. $f _ { \theta , \xi }$ and $\xi$ is also a vector-valued parameter. Suppose that X can be transformed into a sequence of pairs $( V _ { 1 } , U _ { 1 } ) , . . . , ( V _ { m } , U _ { m } )$ such that 

$$
f _ {\theta , \xi} (x) = \left[ \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {m} g _ {\theta} (u _ {i} | v _ {1}, u _ {1},..., u _ {i - 1}, v _ {i}) \right] \left[ \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {m} h _ {\theta , \xi} (v _ {i} | v _ {1}, u _ {1},..., v _ {i - 1}, u _ {i - 1}) \right],
$$

where $g _ { \boldsymbol { \theta } } \big ( \cdot | v _ { 1 } , u _ { 1 } , . . . , u _ { i - 1 } , v _ { i } \big )$ is the conditional p.d.f. of $U _ { i }$ given $V _ { 1 } ~ =$ $v _ { 1 } , U _ { 1 } = u _ { 1 } , . . . , U _ { i - 1 } = u _ { i - 1 } , V _ { i } = v _ { i }$ , which does not depend on $\xi ,$ , and $h _ { \theta , \xi } ( \cdot | v _ { 1 } , u _ { 1 } , . . . , v _ { i - 1 } , u _ { i - 1 } )$ is the conditional p.d.f. of $V _ { i }$ given $V _ { 1 } = v _ { 1 } , U _ { 1 } =$ $u _ { 1 } , . . . , V _ { i - 1 } = v _ { i - 1 } , U _ { i - 1 } = u _ { i - 1 }$ . The first product in the previous expression for $f _ { \boldsymbol { \theta } , \boldsymbol { \xi } } ( \boldsymbol { x } )$ is called the partial likelihood for $\theta .$ 

When $\xi$ is a nonparametric component, the partial likelihood for $\theta$ can be similarly defined, in which case the full likelihood $f _ { \boldsymbol { \theta } , \boldsymbol { \xi } } ( \boldsymbol { x } )$ should be replaced by a nonparametric likelihood or an empirical likelihood. As long as the conditional distributions of $U _ { i }$ given $V _ { 1 } , U _ { 1 } , . . . , U _ { i - 1 } , V _ { i } , i = 1 , . . . , m$ , are in a parametric family (indexed by $\theta )$ , the partial likelihood is parametric. 

A semi-parametric estimation method consists of a parametric method (typically the maximum likelihood method in 4.4) for estimating θ and a nonparametric method for estimating ξ. 

To illustrate the application of the method of partial likelihoods, we consider the estimation of the c.d.f. of survival data in the random censorship model described in Example 5.3. Following the notation in Example 5.3, we assume that $\{ T _ { 1 } , . . . , T _ { n } \}$ (survival times) and $\{ C _ { 1 } , . . . , C _ { n } \}$ (censoring times) are two sets of independent nonnegative random variables and that $X _ { i } = \operatorname* { m i n } \{ T _ { i } , C _ { i } \}$ and $\delta _ { i } = I _ { ( 0 , C _ { i } ) } ( T _ { i } ) , \ i = 1 , . . . , n$ , are independent observations. In addition, we assume that there is a p-vector $Z _ { i }$ of covariate values associated with $X _ { i }$ and $\delta _ { i }$ . The situation considered in Example 5.3 can be viewed as a special homogeneous case with $Z _ { i } \equiv \mathrm { a }$ constant. 

The survival function when the covariate vector is equal to $z$ is defined to be $S _ { z } ( t ) = 1 - F _ { z } ( t )$ , where $F _ { z }$ is the c.d.f. of the survival time $T$ having the same distribution as $T _ { i }$ . Assume that $f _ { z } ( t ) = F _ { z } ^ { \prime } ( t )$ exists for all $t > 0$ The function $\lambda _ { z } ( t ) ~ = ~ f _ { z } ( t ) / S _ { z } ( t )$ is called the hazard function and the function $\begin{array} { r } { \Lambda _ { z } ( t ) = \int _ { 0 } ^ { t } \lambda _ { z } ( s ) d s } \end{array}$ is called the cumulative hazard function, when the covariate vector is equal to z. A commonly adopted model for $\lambda _ { z }$ is the following proportional hazards model: 

$$
\lambda_ {z} (t) = \lambda_ {0} (t) \phi (\beta^ {\tau} z),\tag{5.31}
$$

where $\phi$ is a known function (typically $\phi ( x ) = e ^ { x } ) , z$ is a value of the $p \mathrm { - }$ vector of covariates, $\beta \in \mathcal { R } ^ { p }$ is an unknown parameter vector, and $\lambda _ { 0 } ( t )$ is the unknown hazard function when the covariate vector is 0 and is referred to as the baseline hazard function. Under model (5.31), 

$$
1 - F _ {z} (t) = \exp \{- \Lambda_ {z} (t) \} = \exp \{- \phi (\beta^ {\tau} z) \Lambda_ {0} (t) \}.
$$

Thus, the estimation of the $\mathrm { c . d . f . } \ F _ { z }$ or the survival function $S _ { z }$ can be done through the estimation of $\beta _ { ; }$ , the parametric component of model (5.31), and $\Lambda _ { 0 }$ , the nonparametric component of model (5.31). 

Consider first the estimation of $\beta$ using the method of partial likelihoods. Suppose that there are l observed failures at times $T _ { ( 1 ) } < \cdots < T _ { ( l ) }$ , where (i) is the label for the ith failure ordered according to the time to failure. (Note that a failure occurs when $\delta _ { i } = 1 . )$ Suppose that there are $m _ { i }$ items censored at or after $T _ { ( i ) }$ but before $T _ { ( i + 1 ) }$ at times $T _ { ( i , 1 ) } , . . . , T _ { ( i , m _ { i } ) }$ (setting $T _ { ( 0 ) } = 0 )$ . Let $U _ { i } = ( \dot { i } )$ and $V _ { i } = ( T _ { ( i ) } , \dot { T } _ { ( i - 1 , 1 ) } , . . . , T _ { ( i - 1 , m _ { i - 1 } ) } ) , i = 1 , . . . , l .$ Then the partial likelihood is 

$$
\prod_ {i = 1} ^ {l} P (U _ {i} = (i) | V _ {1}, U _ {1},..., U _ {i - 1}, V _ {i}).
$$

Since $\begin{array} { r } { \lambda _ { z } ( t ) = \operatorname* { l i m } _ { \Delta > 0 , \Delta \to 0 } \Delta ^ { - 1 } P _ { z } ( t \leq T < t + \Delta | T > t ) } \end{array}$ , where $P _ { z }$ denotes the probability measure of $T$ when the covariate is equal to $z$ , 

$$
P (U _ {i} = (i) | V _ {1}, U _ {1}, \dots , U _ {i - 1}, V _ {i}) = \frac {\lambda_ {Z _ {(i)}} (t _ {i})}{\sum_ {j \in R _ {i}} \lambda_ {Z _ {j}} (t _ {i})} = \frac {\phi (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {(i)})}{\sum_ {j \in R _ {i}} \phi (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {j})},
$$

where $t _ { i }$ is the observed value of $T _ { ( i ) } , R _ { i } = \{ j : X _ { j } \geq t _ { i } \}$ is called the risk set, and the last equality follows from assumption (5.31). This leads to the partial likelihood 

$$
\ell (\beta) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {l} \frac {\phi (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {(i)})}{\sum_ {j \in R _ {i}} \phi (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {j})} = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \left[ \frac {\phi (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {i})}{\sum_ {j \in R _ {i}} \phi (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {j})} \right] ^ {\delta_ {i}},
$$

which is a function of the parameter $\beta ,$ given the observed data. The maximum likelihood method introduced for parametric models in $\ S 4 . 4$ can be applied to obtain a maximum partial likelihood estimator $\hat { \beta }$ of $\beta .$ . It is shown in Tsiatis (1981) that $\hat { \beta }$ is consistent for $\beta$ and is asymptotically normal under some regularity conditions. 

We now consider the estimation of $\Lambda _ { 0 }$ . First, assume that the covariate vector $Z _ { i }$ is random, $( T _ { i } , C _ { i } , Z _ { i } )$ are i.i.d., and $T _ { i }$ and $C _ { i }$ are conditionally independent given $Z _ { i }$ . Let $( T , C , Z )$ be the random vector having the same distribution as $( T _ { i } , C _ { i } , Z _ { i } ) , ~ X ~ = ~ \mathrm { m i n } \{ T , C \}$ , and $\delta = I _ { ( 0 , C ) } ( T )$ . Under assumption (5.31), it can be shown (exercise) that 

$$
Q (t) = P (X > t, \delta = 1) = \iint_ {t} ^ {\infty} \lambda_ {0} (s) \phi (\beta^ {\tau} z) H (s | z) d s d G (z),\tag{5.32}
$$

where $H ( s | z ) = P ( X > s | Z = z )$ and $G$ is the c.d.f. of $Z .$ . Then 

$$
\frac {d Q (t)}{d t} = - \lambda_ {0} (t) \int \phi (\beta^ {\tau} z) H (t | z) d G (z)\tag{5.33}
$$

and 

$$
\lambda_ {0} (t) = - \frac {d Q (t)}{d t} \frac {1}{K (t)},\tag{5.34}
$$

where $K ( t ) = E [ \phi ( \beta ^ { \tau } Z ) I _ { ( t , \infty ) } ( X ) ]$ (exercise). Consequently, 

$$
\Lambda_ {0} (t) = \int_ {0} ^ {t} \lambda_ {0} (s) d s = - \int_ {0} ^ {t} \frac {d Q (s)}{K (s)}.
$$

An estimator of $\Lambda _ { 0 }$ can then be obtained by substituting $Q$ and $K$ in the previous expression by their estimators 

$$
\hat {Q} (t) = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} I _ {\{X _ {i} > t, \delta_ {i} = 1 \}}
$$

and 

$$
\hat {K} (t) = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \phi (\hat {\beta} ^ {\tau} Z _ {i}) I _ {(t, \infty)} (X _ {i}).\tag{5.35}
$$

This estimator is known as Breslow’s estimator. When $Z _ { 1 } , . . . , Z _ { n }$ are nonrandom, we can still use Breslow’s estimator. Its asymptotic properties can be found, for example, in Fleming and Harrington (1991). 

## Profile likelihoods

Let $\ell ( \theta , \xi )$ be a likelihood (or empirical likelihood), where $\theta$ and $\xi$ are not necessarily vector-valued. It may be dificult to maximize the likelihood $\ell ( \theta , \xi )$ simultaneously over $\theta$ and $\xi .$ . For each fixed $\theta ,$ , let $\xi ( \theta )$ satisfy 

$$
\ell (\theta , \xi (\theta)) = \sup _ {\xi} \ell (\theta , \xi).
$$

The function 

$$
\ell_ {P} (\theta) = \ell (\theta , \xi (\theta))
$$

is called a profile likelihood function for $\theta .$ . Suppose that $\hat { \theta } _ { P }$ maximizes $\ell _ { P } ( \theta )$ . Then ${ \hat { \theta } } _ { P }$ is called a maximum profile likelihood estimator of $\theta .$ . Note that $\hat { \theta } _ { P }$ may be diferent from an MLE of $\theta .$ . Although this idea can be applied to parametric models, it is more useful in nonparametric models, especially when $\theta$ is a parametric component. 

For example, consider the empirical likelihood in (5.8) subject to the constraints in (5.10). Sometimes it is more convenient to allow the function u in (5.10) to depend on an unknown parameter vector $\theta \in \mathcal { R } ^ { k }$ , where $k \leq s$ This leads to the empirical likelihood $\ell ( G )$ in (5.8) subject to (5.10) with $u ( x )$ replaced by $\psi ( x , \theta )$ , where $\psi$ is a known function from $\mathcal { R } ^ { d } \times \mathcal { R } ^ { k }$ to $\mathcal { R } ^ { s }$ Maximizing this empirical likelihood is equivalent to maximizing 

$$
\ell (p _ {1}, \dots , p _ {n}, \omega , \lambda , \theta) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} + \omega \left(1 - \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i}\right) + \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} \lambda^ {\tau} \psi (x _ {i}, \theta),
$$

where $\omega$ and λ are Lagrange multipliers. It follows from (5.12) and (5.13) that $\omega = n , \tilde { p } _ { i } ( \theta ) = n ^ { - 1 } \{ 1 + [ \lambda _ { n } ( \theta ) ] ^ { \tau } \psi ( x _ { i } , \theta ) \} ^ { - 1 }$ with a $\lambda _ { n } ( \theta )$ satisfying 

$$
\frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {\psi (x _ {i} , \theta)}{1 + [ \lambda_ {n} (\theta) ] ^ {\tau} \psi (x _ {i} , \theta)} = 0
$$

maximize $\ell ( p _ { 1 } , . . . p _ { n } , \omega , \lambda , \theta )$ for any fixed θ. Substituting $\tilde { p } _ { i }$ with $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } { \tilde { p } } _ { i } =$ 1 into $\ell ( p _ { 1 } , . . . p _ { n } , \omega , \lambda , \theta )$ leads to the following profile empirical likelihood for $\theta \colon$ : 

$$
\ell_ {P} (\theta) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {1}{n \{1 + [ \lambda_ {n} (\theta) ] ^ {\tau} \psi (x _ {i} , \theta) \}}.\tag{5.36}
$$

If $\hat { \theta }$ is a maximum of $\ell _ { P } ( \theta )$ in (5.36), then $\hat { \theta }$ is a maximum profile empirical likelihood estimator of θ and the corresponding estimator of $p _ { i }$ is $\tilde { p } _ { i } ( \boldsymbol { \hat { \theta } } )$ . A result similar to Theorem 5.4 and a result on asymptotic normality of $\hat { \theta }$ are established in Qin and Lawless (1994), under some conditions on $\psi .$ 

Another example is the empirical likelihood (5.20) in the problem of biased sampling with a function $w ( x ) = w _ { \theta } ( x )$ depending on an unknown $\theta \in \mathcal { R } ^ { k }$ . The profile empirical likelihood for $\theta$ is then 

$$
\ell_ {P} (\theta) = \hat {w} _ {\theta} ^ {- n _ {2}} \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {1}{n _ {1} + n _ {2} w _ {\theta} (x _ {i}) / \hat {w} _ {\theta}} \prod_ {i = n _ {1} + 1} ^ {n} w _ {\theta} (x _ {i}),
$$

where $\hat { w } _ { \boldsymbol { \theta } }$ satisfies 

$$
\hat {w} _ {\theta} = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {w _ {\theta} (x _ {i})}{n _ {1} + n _ {2} w _ {\theta} (x _ {i}) / \hat {w} _ {\theta}}.
$$

Finally, we consider the problem of missing data. Assume that $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ are i.i.d. random variables from an unknown c.d.f. $F$ and some $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are missing. Let $\delta _ { i } = 1$ if $X _ { i }$ is observed and $\delta _ { i } = 0 { \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } } X _ { i }$ is missing. Suppose that $( X _ { i } , \delta _ { i } )$ are i.i.d. Let 

$$
\pi (x) = P (\delta_ {i} = 1 | X _ {i} = x).
$$
