If $X _ { i }$ and $\delta _ { i }$ are independent, $\operatorname { i . e . , } \pi ( x ) \equiv \pi$ does not depend on $x ,$ then the empirical c.d.f. based on observed data, i.e., the c.d.f. putting mass $r ^ { - 1 }$ to each observed $X _ { i }$ , where $r$ is the number of observed $X _ { i } { } ^ { \prime } \mathrm { s } .$ , is an unbiased and consistent estimator of $F$ , provided that $\pi > 0$ . On the other hand, if $\pi ( x )$ depends on $x _ { \ast }$ , then the empirical c.d.f. based on observed data is a biased and inconsistent estimator of $F$ . In fact, it can be shown (exercise) that the empirical c.d.f. based on observed data is an unbiased estimator of $P ( X _ { i } \leq x | \delta _ { i } = 1 )$ , which is generally diferent from the unconditional probability $F ( x ) = P ( X _ { i } \leq x )$ 

If both $\pi$ and F are in parametric models, then we can apply the method of maximum likelihood. For example, if $\pi ( x ) = \pi _ { \theta } ( x )$ and $F ( x ) = F _ { \vartheta } ( x )$ has a p.d.f. $f _ { \vartheta }$ , where $\theta$ and $\vartheta$ are vectors of unknown parameters, then a parametric likelihood of $( \theta , \vartheta )$ is 

$$
\ell (\theta , \vartheta) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} [ \pi_ {\theta} (x _ {i}) f _ {\vartheta} (x _ {i}) ] ^ {\delta_ {i}} (1 - \pi) ^ {1 - \delta_ {i}},
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \pi = \int \pi _ { \theta } ( x ) d F ( x ) } \end{array}$ ). Suppose now that $\pi ( x ) = \pi _ { \theta } ( x )$ is the parametric component and $F$ is the nonparametric component. Then an empirical likelihood can be defined as 

$$
\ell (\theta , G) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} [ \pi_ {\theta} (x _ {i}) P _ {G} (\{x _ {i} \}) ] ^ {\delta_ {i}} (1 - \pi) ^ {1 - \delta_ {i}}
$$

subject to $\begin{array} { r } { p _ { i } \geq 0 , \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \delta _ { i } p _ { i } = 1 , \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \delta _ { i } p _ { i } [ \pi _ { \theta } ( x _ { i } ) - \pi ] = 0 } \end{array}$ , where $p _ { i } =$ $P _ { G } ( \{ x _ { i } \} ) , i = 1 , . . . , n$ 

It can be shown (exercise) that the logarithm of the profile empirical likelihood for $( \theta , \pi )$ (with a Lagrange multiplier) is 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \left\{\delta_ {i} \log \left(\pi_ {\theta} (x _ {i})\right) + (1 - \delta_ {i}) \log (1 - \pi) - \delta_ {i} \log \left(1 + \lambda [ \pi_ {\theta} (x _ {i}) - \pi ]\right) \right\}.\tag{5.37}
$$

Under some regularity conditions, Qin, Leung, and Shao (2002) show that the estimators $\boldsymbol { \hat { \theta } } , \boldsymbol { \hat { \pi } }$ , and $\hat { \lambda }$ obtained by maximizing the likelihood in (5.37) are consistent and asymptotically normal and that the empirical c.d.f. putting mass $\hat { p } _ { i } = r ^ { - 1 } \lbrace 1 + \hat { \lambda } [ \pi _ { \hat { \theta } } ( X _ { i } ) - \hat { \pi } ] \rbrace ^ { - 1 }$ to each observed $X _ { i }$ is consistent for F. The results are also extended to the case where a covariate vector $Z _ { i }$ associated with $X _ { i }$ is observed for all i. 

## 5.2 Statistical Functionals

In many nonparametric problems, we are interested in estimating some characteristics (parameters) of the unknown population, not the entire population. We assume in this section that $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are i.i.d. from an unknown c.d.f. $F$ on $\mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ . Most characteristics of $F$ can be written as $\mathtt { T } ( F )$ , where T is a functional from $\mathcal { F }$ to $\mathcal { R } ^ { s }$ . If we estimate $F$ by the empirical c.d.f. $F _ { n }$ in (5.1), then a natural estimator of $\mathtt { T } ( F )$ is $\mathbb { T } ( F _ { n } )$ , which is called a statistical functional. 

Many commonly used statistics can be written as $\operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ for some T. Two simple examples are given as follows. Let $\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { T } ( F ) = \int \psi ( x ) d F ( x ) } \end{array}$ with an integrable function $\psi _ { ; }$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { T } ( F _ { n } ) = \int \psi ( x ) d F _ { n } ( x ) = \overline { { n ^ { - 1 } \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } \psi ( X _ { i } ) } } } \end{array}$ The sample moments discussed in 3.5.2 are particular examples of this kind of statistical functional. For $d = 1$ , let $\mathrm { T } ( F ) = F ^ { - 1 } ( p ) = \operatorname* { i n f } \left\{ x : F ( x ) \geq p \right\}$ where $p \in ( 0 , 1 )$ is a fixed constant. $F ^ { - 1 } ( p )$ is called the pth quantile of $F$ The statistical functional ${ \sf T } ( F _ { n } ) = F _ { n } ^ { - 1 } ( p )$ is called the pth sample quantile. More examples of statistical functionals are provided in 5.2.1 and 5.2.2. 

In this section, we study asymptotic distributions of $\operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ . We focus on the case of real-valued $\textbf { T } ( s = 1 )$ , since the extension to the case of $s \geq 2$ is straightforward. 

## 5.2.1 Diferentiability and asymptotic normality

Note that $\mathbb { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is a function of the “statistic” $F _ { n }$ . In Theorem 1.12 (and 3.5.1) we have studied how to use Taylor’s expansion to establish asymptotic normality of diferentiable functions of statistics that are asymptotically normal. This leads to the approach of establishing asymptotic normality of $\mathbb { T } ( F _ { n } )$ by using some generalized Taylor expansions for functionals and using asymptotic properties of $F _ { n }$ given in 5.1.1. 

First, we need a suitably defined diferential of T. Several versions of diferentials are given in the following definition. 

Definition 5.2. Let T be a functional on $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ , a collection of c.d.f.’s on $\mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ , and let $\mathbf { \mathcal { D } } = \{ c ( G _ { 1 } - G _ { 2 } ) : c \in \mathcal { R } , G _ { j } \in \mathcal { F } _ { 0 } , j = 1 , 2 \}$ 

(i) A functional T on $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ is Gˆateaux diferentiable at $G \in \mathcal F _ { 0 }$ if and only if there is a linear functional $\operatorname { L } _ { G }$ on $\begin{array} { r } { \textbf { \textmd D } ( \mathrm { i . e . , ~ L } _ { G } ( c _ { 1 } \Delta _ { 1 } + c _ { 2 } \Delta _ { 2 } ) = c _ { 1 } \mathrm { L } _ { G } ( \Delta _ { 1 } ) + } \end{array}$ $c _ { 2 } \mathrm { L } _ { G } ( \Delta _ { 2 } )$ for any $\Delta _ { j } \in \mathbf { \mathscr { D } }$ and $c _ { j } \in \mathcal { R } )$ such that $\Delta \in \mathbf { \mathbb { D } }$ and $G + t \Delta \in \mathfrak { F } _ { 0 }$ imply 

$$
\lim _ {t \to 0} \left[ \frac {\mathrm{T} (G + t \Delta) - \mathrm{T} (G)}{t} - \mathrm{L} _ {G} (\Delta) \right] = 0.
$$

(ii) Let $\varrho$ be a distance on $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ induced by a norm $\| \cdot \|$ on D. A functiona T on $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ is ̺-Hadamard diferentiable at $G \in \mathcal F _ { 0 }$ if and only if there is a linear functional $\operatorname { L } _ { G }$ on D such that for any sequence of numbers $t _ { j } \to 0$ and $\{ \Delta , \Delta _ { j } , j = 1 , 2 , \ldots \} \subset \mathbf { \mathscr { D } }$ satisfying $\| \Delta _ { j } - \Delta \| \to 0$ and $G + t _ { j } \Delta _ { j } \in \mathscr { F } _ { 0 }$ , 

$$
\lim _ {j \to \infty} \left[ \frac {\mathsf {T} (G + t _ {j} \Delta_ {j}) - \mathsf {T} (G)}{t _ {j}} - \mathsf {L} _ {G} (\Delta_ {j}) \right] = 0.
$$

(iii) Let $\varrho$ be a distance on $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ . A functional T on $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ is ̺-Fr´echet diferentiable at $G \in \mathcal F _ { 0 }$ if and only if there is a linear functional $\operatorname { L } _ { G }$ on D such that for any sequence $\{ G _ { j } \}$ satisfying $G _ { j } \in \mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ and $\varrho ( G _ { j } , G )  0$ , 

$$
\lim _ {j \to \infty} \frac {\mathsf {T} (G _ {j}) - \mathsf {T} (G) - \mathsf {L} _ {G} (G _ {j} - G)}{\varrho (G _ {j} , G)} = 0.
$$

The functional $\operatorname { L } _ { G }$ is called the diferential of T at $G .$ If we define $h ( t ) = \mathbb { T } ( G + t \Delta )$ , then the Gˆateaux diferentiability is equivalent to the diferentiability of the function $h ( t )$ at $t = 0$ , and $\mathtt { L } _ { G } ( \Delta )$ is simply $h ^ { \prime } ( 0 )$ . Let $\delta _ { x }$ denote the d-dimensional c.d.f. degenerated at the point x and $\phi _ { G } ( x ) =$ $\operatorname { L } _ { G } ( \delta _ { x } - G )$ . Then $\phi _ { F } ( x )$ is called the influence function of T at $F .$ , which is an important tool in robust statistics (see Hampel (1974)). 

If T is Gˆateaux diferentiable at F, then we have the following expansion (taking $t = n ^ { - 1 / 2 }$ and $\Delta = { \sqrt { n } } ( F _ { n } - F ) )$ : 

$$
\sqrt {n} \left[ \mathrm{T} \left(F _ {n}\right) - \mathrm{T} (F) \right] = \mathrm{L} _ {F} \left(\sqrt {n} \left(F _ {n} - F\right)\right) + R _ {n}.\tag{5.38}
$$

Since $\mathtt { L } _ { F }$ is linear, 

$$
\mathsf {L} _ {F} \big (\sqrt {n} (F _ {n} - F) \big) = \frac {1}{\sqrt {n}} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \phi_ {F} (X _ {i}) \rightarrow_ {d} N (0, \sigma_ {F} ^ {2})\tag{5.39}
$$

by the CLT, provided that 

$$
E [ \phi_ {F} (X _ {1}) ] = 0 \qquad \mathrm{and} \qquad \sigma_ {F} ^ {2} = E [ \phi_ {F} (X _ {1}) ] ^ {2} <   \infty\tag{5.40}
$$

(which is usually true when $\phi _ { F }$ is bounded or when $F$ has some finite moments). By Slutsky’s theorem and (5.39), 

$$
\sqrt {n} [ \mathbf {T} (F _ {n}) - \mathbf {T} (F) ] \rightarrow_ {d} N (0, \sigma_ {F} ^ {2})\tag{5.41}
$$

if $R _ { n }$ in (5.38) is $o _ { p } ( 1 )$ 

Unfortunately, Gˆateaux diferentiability is too weak to be useful in establishing $R _ { n } ~ = ~ o _ { p } ( 1 )$ (or (5.41)). This is why we need other types of diferentiability. Hadamard diferentiability, which is also referred to as compact diferentiability, is clearly stronger than Gˆateaux diferentiability but weaker than Fr´echet diferentiability (exercise). For a given functional 

T, we can first find $\operatorname { L } _ { G }$ by diferentiating $h ( t ) = \mathbb { T } ( G + t \Delta )$ at $t = 0$ and then check whether T is ̺-Hadamard (or ̺-Fr´echet) diferentiable with a given $\varrho .$ The most commonly used distances on $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ are the sup-norm distance $\varrho _ { \infty }$ and the $L _ { p }$ distance $\varrho _ { L _ { p } }$ . Their corresponding norms are given by (5.3) and (5.5), respectively. 

Theorem 5.5. Let $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ be i.i.d. from a c.d.f. F on $\mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ 

(i) If T is ̺ -Hadamard diferentiable at $F$ , then $R _ { n }$ in (5.38) is $o _ { p } ( 1 )$ 

(ii) If T is ̺-Fr´echet diferentiable at $F$ with a distance $\varrho$ satisfying 

$$
\sqrt {n} \varrho (F _ {n}, F) = O _ {p} (1),\tag{5.42}
$$

then $R _ { n }$ in (5.38) is $o _ { p } ( 1 )$ 

(iii) In either (i) or (ii), if (5.40) is also satisfied, then (5.41) holds. Proof. Part (iii) follows directly from (i) or (ii). The proof of (i) involves some high-level mathematics and is omitted; see, for example, Fernholz (1983). We now prove (ii). From Definition 5.2(iii), for any $\epsilon > 0$ , there is a $\delta > 0$ such that $| R _ { n } | < \epsilon \sqrt { n } \varrho ( F _ { n } , F )$ whenever $\varrho ( F _ { n } , F ) < \delta$ . Then 

$$
P \left(\left| R _ {n} \right| > \eta\right) \leq P \left(\sqrt {n} \varrho (F _ {n}, F) > \eta / \epsilon\right) + P \left(\varrho (F _ {n}, F) \geq \delta\right)
$$

for any $\eta > 0$ , which implies 

$$
\operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n} P \left(| R _ {n} | > \eta\right) \leq \operatorname * {l i m s u p} _ {n} P \left(\sqrt {n} \varrho (F _ {n}, F) > \eta / \epsilon\right).
$$

The result follows from (5.42) and the fact that ǫ can be made arbitrarily small. 

Since ̺-Fr´echet diferentiability implies ̺-Hadamard diferentiability, Theorem 5.5(ii) is useful when $\varrho$ is not the sup-norm distance. There are functionals that are not $\varrho _ { \infty } { \mathrm { - H a d a m a r d } }$ diferentiable (and hence not $\varrho _ { \infty } \mathrm { - F r e c h e t }$ diferentiable). For example, if $d = 1$ and $\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { T } ( G ) = g ( \int x d G ) } \end{array}$ with a diferentiable function $g _ { \mathrm { : } }$ , then $T$ is not necessarily $\varrho _ { \infty } { \mathrm { - H a d a m a r d } }$ diferentiable, but is $\varrho _ { L _ { 1 } } \mathrm { - F r e c h e t }$ diferentiable (exercise). 

From Theorem 5.2, condition (5.42) holds for $\varrho _ { L _ { p } }$ under the moment conditions on $F$ given in Theorem 5.2. 

Note that if $\varrho$ and $\tilde { \varrho }$ are two distances on $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ satisfying $\tilde { \varrho } ( G _ { 1 } , G _ { 2 } ) \leq$ $c \varrho ( G _ { 1 } , G _ { 2 } )$ for a constant c and all $G _ { j } \in \mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ , then ˜̺-Hadamard (Fr´echet) diferentiability implies ̺-Hadamard (Fr´echet) diferentiability. This suggests the use of the distance $\varrho _ { \infty + p } = \varrho _ { \infty } + \varrho _ { L _ { v } }$ , which also satisfies (5.42) under the moment conditions in Theorem 5.2. The distance $\varrho _ { \infty + p }$ is useful in some cases (Theorem 5.6). 

A ̺ -Hadamard diferentiable T having a bounded and continuous influence function $\phi _ { F }$ is robust in Hampel’s sense (see, e.g., Huber (1981)). 

This is motivated by the fact that the asymptotic behavior of $\operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is determined by that of $\mathtt { L } _ { F } ( F _ { n } - F )$ , and a small change in the sample, i.e., small changes in all $x _ { i } \mathrm { { ^ { * } s } }$ (rounding, grouping) or large changes in a few $x _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ (gross errors, blunders), will result in a small change of $\mathbb { T } ( F _ { n } )$ if and only if $\phi _ { F }$ is bounded and continuous. 

We now consider some examples. For the sample moments related to functionals of the form $\begin{array} { r } { \mathrm { T } ( G ) = \int \psi ( x ) d G ( x ) } \end{array}$ , it is clear that T is a linear functional. Any linear functional is trivially ̺-Fr´echet diferentiable for any $\varrho .$ Next, if F is one-dimensional and $F ^ { \prime } ( x ) > 0$ for all $x ,$ then the quantile functional $\operatorname { T } ( G ) = G ^ { - 1 } ( p )$ is ̺ -Hadamard diferentiable at $F$ (Fernholz, 1983). Hence, Theorem 5.5 applies to these functionals. But the asymptotic normality of sample quantiles can be established under weaker conditions, which are studied in 5.3.1. 

Example 5.5 (Convolution functionals). Suppose that $F$ is on $\mathcal { R }$ and for a fixed $z \in \mathcal { R }$ , 

$$
\mathrm{T} (G) = \int G (z - y) d G (y), \qquad G \in \mathfrak {F}.
$$

If $X _ { 1 }$ and $X _ { 2 }$ are i.i.d. with c.d.f. $G ,$ , then $\mathrm { T } ( G )$ is the c.d.f. of $X _ { 1 } + X _ { 2 }$ (Exercise 47 in 1.6), and is also called the convolution of G evaluated at z. For $t _ { j } \to 0$ and $\| \Delta _ { j } - \Delta \| _ { \infty } \to 0$ , 

$$
\mathsf {T} (G + t _ {j} \Delta_ {j}) - \mathsf {T} (G) = 2 t _ {j} \int \Delta_ {j} (z - y) d G (y) + t _ {j} ^ {2} \int \Delta_ {j} (z - y) d \Delta_ {j} (y)
$$

(for $\Delta = c _ { 1 } G _ { 1 } + c _ { 2 } G _ { 2 } , G _ { j } \in \mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ , and $c _ { j } \in \mathcal R$ 5 $d \Delta$ denotes $c _ { 1 } d G _ { 1 } + c _ { 2 } d G _ { 2 } )$ Using Lemma 5.2, one can show (exercise) that 

$$
\int \Delta_ {j} (z - y) d \Delta_ {j} (y) = O (1).\tag{5.43}
$$

Hence T is $\varrho _ { \infty }$ -Hadamard diferentiable at any $G \in { \mathfrak { F } }$ with $\operatorname { L } _ { G } ( \Delta ) \ =$ $2 \textstyle \int \Delta ( z - y ) d G ( y )$ . The influence function, $\begin{array} { r } { \phi _ { F } ( x ) = 2 \int ( \delta _ { x } - F ) ( z - y ) d F ( y ) } \end{array}$ • is a bounded function and clearly satisfies (5.40). Thus, (5.41) holds. If $F$ is continuous, then T is robust in Hampel’s sense (exercise). 

Three important classes of statistical functionals, i.e., L-estimators, Mestimators, and rank statistics and R-estimators, are considered in 5.2.2. 

Lemma 5.2. Let $\Delta \in \mathbf { \mathbb { D } }$ and h be a continuous function on $\mathcal { R }$ such that $\textstyle \int h ( x ) d \Delta ( x )$ is finite. Then 

$$
\left| \int h (x) d \Delta (x) \right| \leq \| h \| _ {V} \| \Delta \| _ {\infty},
$$

where $\| h \| _ { V }$ is the variation norm defined by 

$$
\| h \| _ {V} = \lim _ {a \rightarrow - \infty , b \rightarrow \infty} \left[ \sup \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {m} | h (x _ {j}) - h (x _ {j - 1}) | \right]
$$

with the supremum being taken over all partitions $a = x _ { 0 } < \cdot \cdot \cdot < x _ { m } = b$ of the interval [a, b]. 

The proof of Lemma 5.2 can be found in Natanson (1961, p. 232). 

The diferentials in Definition 5.2 are first-order diferentials. For some functionals, we can also consider their second-order diferentials, which provides a way of defining the order of the asymptotic biases via expansion (2.37). 

Definition 5.3. Let T be a functional on $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ and $\varrho$ be a distance on $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ (i) T is second-order ̺-Hadamard diferentiable at $G \in \mathcal F _ { 0 }$ if and only if there is a functional Q on D such that for any sequence of numbers $t _ { j } \to 0$ and $\{ \Delta , \Delta _ { j } , j = 1 , 2 , \ldots \} \subset \mathbf { \mathscr { D } }$ satisfying $\| \Delta _ { j } - \Delta \| \to 0$ and $G + t _ { j } \Delta _ { j } \in \mathscr { F } _ { 0 }$ 

$$
\lim _ {j \to \infty} \frac {\mathsf {T} (G + t _ {j} \Delta_ {j}) - \mathsf {T} (G) - \mathbb {Q} _ {G} (t _ {j} \Delta_ {j})}{t _ {j} ^ {2}} = 0,
$$

where $\begin{array} { r } { \mathsf { Q } _ { G } ( \Delta ) = \int \int \psi _ { G } ( x , y ) d ( G + \Delta ) ( x ) d ( G + \Delta ) ( y ) } \end{array}$ for a function $\psi _ { G }$ satisfying $\begin{array} { r } { \psi _ { G } ( x , y ) = \psi _ { G } ( y , x ) , \int \int \psi _ { G } ( x , y ) d G ( x ) d G ( y ) = 0 } \end{array}$ , and D and $\| \cdot \|$ are the same as those in Definition 5.2(ii). 

(ii) T is second-order ̺-Fr´echet diferentiable at $G \in \mathcal F _ { 0 }$ if and only if, for any sequence $\{ G _ { j } \}$ satisfying $G _ { j } \in \mathfrak { F } _ { 0 }$ and $\varrho ( G _ { j } , G )  0$ , 

$$
\lim _ {j \to \infty} \frac {T (G _ {j}) - T (G) - \mathbb {Q} _ {G} (G _ {j} - G)}{[ \varrho (G _ {j} , G) ] ^ {2}} = 0,
$$

where $\mathsf Q _ { G }$ is the same as that in (i). 

For a second-order diferentiable T, we have the following expansion: 

$$
n [ \mathrm{T} (F _ {n}) - \mathrm{T} (F) ] = n V _ {n} + R _ {n},\tag{5.44}
$$

where 

$$
V _ {n} = \mathbb {Q} _ {F} (F _ {n} - F) = \int \int \psi_ {F} (x, y) d F _ {n} (x) d F _ {n} (y) = \frac {1}{n ^ {2}} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \psi_ {F} (X _ {i}, X _ {j})
$$

is a “V-statistic” ( 3.5.3) whose asymptotic properties are given by Theorem 3.16. If $R _ { n }$ in (5.44) is $o _ { p } ( 1 )$ , then the asymptotic behavior of $\mathbb { T } ( F _ { n } ) - \mathbb { T } ( F )$ is the same as that of $V _ { n }$ 

Proposition 5.1. Let $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ be i.i.d. from $F$ . 

(i) If T is second-order $\varrho _ { \infty }$ -Hadamard diferentiable at $F$ , then $R _ { n }$ in (5.44) is $o _ { p } ( 1 )$ 

(ii) If T is second-order ̺-Fr´echet diferentiable at $F$ with a distance $\varrho$ satisfying (5.42), then $R _ { n }$ in (5.44) is $o _ { p } ( 1 )$ 

Combining Proposition 5.1 with Theorem 3.16, we conclude that if 

$$
\zeta_ {1} = \operatorname{Var} \left(\int \psi_ {F} (X _ {1}, y) d F (y)\right) > 0,
$$

then (5.41) holds with $\sigma _ { F } ^ { 2 } = 4 \zeta _ { 1 }$ and $\mathrm { a m s e } _ { T ( F _ { n } ) } ( P ) = \sigma _ { F } ^ { 2 } / n ; \mathrm { i f } \zeta _ { 1 } = 0$ , then 

$$
n [ \mathsf {T} (F _ {n}) - \mathsf {T} (F) ] \to_ {d} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {\infty} \lambda_ {j} \chi_ {1 j} ^ {2}
$$

and $\mathrm { a m s e } _ { T ( F _ { n } ) } ( P ) = \{ 2 \mathrm { V a r } ( \psi _ { F } ( X _ { 1 } , X _ { 2 } ) ) + [ E \psi _ { F } ( X _ { 1 } , X _ { 1 } ) ] ^ { 2 } \} / n ^ { 2 } $ . In any case, expansion (2.37) holds and the $n ^ { - 1 }$ order asymptotic bias of $T ( F _ { n } )$ is $E \psi _ { F } ( X _ { 1 } , X _ { 1 } ) / n$ 

If T is also first-order diferentiable, then it can be shown (exercise) that 

$$
\phi_ {F} (x) = 2 \int \psi_ {F} (x, y) d F (y).\tag{5.45}
$$

Then $\zeta _ { 1 } = 4 ^ { - 1 } \mathrm { V a r } ( \phi _ { F } ( X _ { 1 } ) )$ and $\zeta _ { 1 } = 0$ corresponds to the case of $\phi _ { F } ( x ) \equiv$ 0. However, second-order ̺-Hadamard (Fr´echet) diferentiability does not imply first-order ̺-Hadamard (Fr´echet) diferentiability (exercise). 

The technique in this section can be applied to non-i.i.d. $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ when the $\mathrm { c . d . f . ^ { \prime } s }$ of $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are determined by an unknown c.d.f. F, provided that results similar to (5.39) and (5.42) (with $F _ { n }$ replaced by some other estimator $\hat { F } )$ can be established. 

## 5.2.2 L-, M-, and R-estimators and rank statistics

Three large classes of statistical functionals based on i.i.d. $X _ { i } ^ { , }$ s are studied in this section. 

## L-estimators

Let J(t) be a Borel function on [0, 1]. An L-functional is defined as 

$$
\mathrm{T} (G) = \int x J (G (x)) d G (x), \quad G \in \mathfrak {F} _ {0},\tag{5.46}
$$

where $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ contains all c.d.f.’s on for which T is well defined. For $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ i.i.d. from $F \in \mathcal { F } _ { 0 } , \operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is called an L-estimator of $\mathtt { T } ( F )$ 

Example 5.6. The following are some examples of commonly used Lestimators. 

(i) When $J \equiv 1 , \mathsf { T } ( F _ { n } ) = \bar { X }$ , the sample mean. 

(ii) When $J ( t ) = 4 t - 2 , \mathsf { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is proportional to Gini’s mean diference. 

(iii) When $J ( t ) = ( \beta - \alpha ) ^ { - 1 } I _ { ( \alpha , \beta ) } ( t )$ for some constants $\alpha < \beta , \thinspace \thinspace \mathrm { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is called the trimmed sample mean. 

For an L-functional T, it can be shown (exercise) that 

$$
\mathsf {T} (G) - \mathsf {T} (F) = \int \phi_ {F} (x) d (G - F) (x) + R (G, F),\tag{5.47}
$$

where 

$$
\phi_ {F} (x) = - \int (\delta_ {x} - F) (y) J (F (y)) d y,\tag{5.48}
$$

$$
R (G, F) = - \int W _ {G} (x) [ G (x) - F (x) ] d x,
$$

and 

$$
W _ {G} (x) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} [ G (x) - F (x) ] ^ {- 1} \int_ {F (x)} ^ {G (x)} J (t) d t - J (F (x)) & \quad G (x) \neq F (x) \\ 0 & \quad G (x) = F (x). \end{array} \right.
$$

A suficient condition for (5.40) in this case is that J is bounded and $F$ has a finite variance (exercise). However, (5.40) is also satisfied if $\phi _ { F }$ is bounded. The diferentiability of T can be verified under some conditions on $J .$ 

Theorem 5.6. Let T be an L-functional defined by (5.46). 

(i) Suppose that J is bounded, $J ( t ) = 0$ when $t \in [ 0 , \alpha ] \cup [ \beta , 1 ]$ for some constants $\alpha < \beta .$ and that the set $D = \{ x : J$ is discontinuous at $F ( x ) \}$ has Lebesgue measure 0. Then T is $\varrho _ { \infty } \mathrm { - F r e c h e t }$ diferentiable at $F$ with the influence function $\phi _ { F }$ given by (5.48), and $\phi _ { F }$ is bounded and continuous and satisfies (5.40). 

(ii) Suppose that J is bounded, the set D in (i) has Lebesgue measure 0, and J is continuous on $[ 0 , \alpha ] \cup [ \beta , 1 ]$ for some constants $\alpha < \beta$ . Then T is $\varrho _ { \infty + 1 }$ -Fr´echet diferentiable at $F$ 

(iii) Suppose that $| J ( t ) - J ( s ) | \leq C | t - s | ^ { p - 1 }$ , where $C > 0$ and $p > 1$ are some constants. Then T is $\varrho _ { L _ { p } }$ -Fr´echet diferentiable at $F .$ 

(iv) If, in addition to the conditions in part (i), $J ^ { \prime }$ is continuous on $[ \alpha , \beta ]$ , then T is second-order $\varrho _ { \infty } – \mathrm { F 1 }$ r´echet diferentiable at $F$ with 

$$
\psi_ {F} (x, y) = \phi_ {F} (x) + \phi_ {F} (y) - \int (\delta_ {x} - F) (z) (\delta_ {y} - F) (z) J ^ {\prime} (F (z)) d z.
$$

(v) Suppose that $J ^ { \prime }$ is continuous on [0, 1]. Then T is second-order ${ \varrho _ { L _ { 2 } } } ^ { - }$ Fr´echet diferentiable at $F$ with the same $\psi _ { F }$ given in (iv). 

Proof. We prove (i)-(iii). The proofs for (iv) and (v) are similar and are left to the reader. 

(i) Let $G _ { j } \in \mathcal { F }$ and $\varrho _ { \infty } ( G _ { j } , F ) \to 0$ . Let c and d be two constants such that $F ( c ) > \beta$ and $F ( d ) < \alpha$ . Then, for suficiently large $j , G _ { j } ( x ) \in [ 0 , \alpha ] \cup [ \beta , 1 ]$ if $x > c { \mathrm { ~ o r ~ } } x < d .$ . Hence, for suficiently large $j .$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{c} | R (G _ {j}, F) | = \left| \int_ {d} ^ {c} W _ {G _ {j}} (x) (G _ {j} - F) (x) d x \right| \\ \leq \varrho_ {\infty} (G _ {j}, F) \int_ {d} ^ {c} | W _ {G _ {j}} (x) | d x. \end{array}
$$

Since J is continuous at $F ( x )$ when $x \notin D$ and D has Lebesgue measure 0, $W _ { G _ { i } } ( x )  0$ a.e. Lebesgue. By the dominated convergence theorem, $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { d } ^ { c } | W _ { G _ { j } } ( x ) | d x  0 } \end{array}$ . This proves that T is $\varrho _ { \infty } \mathrm { - F r e c h e t }$ diferentiable. The assertions on $\phi _ { F }$ can be proved by noting that 

$$
\phi_ {F} (x) = - \int_ {d} ^ {c} (\delta_ {x} - F) (y) J (F (y)) d y.
$$

(ii) From the proof of (i), we only need to show that 

$$
\left| \int_ {A} W _ {G _ {j}} (x) (G _ {j} - F) (x) d x \right| / \varrho_ {\infty + 1} (G _ {j}, F) \rightarrow 0,\tag{5.49}
$$

where $A = \{ x : F ( x ) \leq \alpha$ or $F ( x ) > \beta \}$ . The quantity on the left-hand side of (5.49) is bounded by $\operatorname* { s u p } _ { x \in A } \left| W _ { G _ { j } } ( x ) \right|$ , which converges to 0 under the continuity assumption of J on $[ 0 , \alpha ] \cup [ \beta , 1 ]$ . Hence (5.49) follows. (iii) The result follows from 

$$
| R (G, F) | \leq C \int | G (x) - F (x) | ^ {p} d x = O \left(\left[ \varrho_ {L _ {p}} (G, F) \right] ^ {p}\right)
$$

and the fact that $p > 1$ 

An L-estimator with $J ( t ) = 0$ when $t \in [ 0 , \alpha ] \cup [ \beta , 1 ]$ is called a trimmed L-estimator. Theorem $5 . 6 ( \mathrm { i } )$ shows that trimmed L-estimators satisfy (5.41) and are robust in Hampel’s sense. In cases (ii) and (iii) of Theorem 5.6, (5.41) holds if $\mathrm { V a r } ( X _ { 1 } ) < \infty$ , but $\operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ may not be robust in Hampel’s sense. It can be shown (exercise) that one or several of ${ \mathrm { ( i ) } } - { \mathrm { ( v ) } }$ of Theorem 5.6 can be applied to each of the L-estimators in Example 5.6. 

## M-estimators

Let $\rho ( x , t )$ be a Borel function on $\mathcal { R } ^ { d } \times \mathcal { R }$ and Θ be an open subset of $\mathcal { R }$ An M-functional is defined to be a solution of 

$$
\int \rho (x, \mathsf {T} (G)) d G (x) = \min _ {t \in \Theta} \int \rho (x, t) d G (x), \qquad G \in \mathfrak {F} _ {0},\tag{5.50}
$$

where $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 }$ contains all c.d.f.’s on $\mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ for which the integrals in (5.50) are well defined. For $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ i.i.d. from $F \in \mathfrak { F } _ { 0 } , \mathrm { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is called an M-estimator of $\mathtt { T } ( F )$ . Assume that $\psi ( x , t ) = \partial \rho ( x , t ) / \partial t$ exists a.e. and 

$$
\lambda_ {G} (t) = \int \psi (x, t) d G (x) = \frac {\partial}{\partial t} \int \rho (x, t) d G (x).\tag{5.51}
$$

Then $\lambda _ { G } ( \mathbb { T } ( G ) ) = 0$ 

Example 5.7. The following are some examples of M-estimators. 

(i) If $\rho ( x , t ) = ( x - t ) ^ { 2 } / 2$ , then $\begin{array} { r } { \psi ( x , t ) = t - x ; \operatorname { T } ( G ) = \int x d G ( x ) } \end{array}$ is the mean functional; and $\mathbb { T } ( F _ { n } ) = { \bar { X } }$ is the sample mean. 

(ii) If $\rho ( x , t ) = | x - t | ^ { p } / p .$ , where $p \in [ 1 , 2 )$ , then 

$$
\psi (x, t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} | x - t | ^ {p - 1} & \quad x \leq t \\ - | x - t | ^ {p - 1} & \quad x > t. \end{array} \right.
$$

When $p = 1 , \operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is the sample median. When $1 < p < 2 , T ( F _ { n } )$ is called the pth least absolute deviations estimator or the minimum $L _ { p }$ distance estimator. 

(iii) Let $\mathcal { F } _ { 0 } = \{ f _ { \theta } : \theta \in \Theta \}$ be a parametric family of p.d.f.’s with $\Theta \subset \mathcal { R }$ and $\rho ( x , t ) = - \log f _ { t } ( x )$ . Then $\operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is an MLE. This indicates that Mestimators are extensions of MLE’s in parametric models. 

(iv) Let $C > 0$ be a constant. Huber (1964) considers 

$$
\rho (x, t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {1}{2} (x - t) ^ {2} & | x - t | \leq C \\ \frac {1}{2} C ^ {2} & | x - t | > C \end{array} \right.
$$

with 

$$
\psi (x, t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} t - x & | x - t | \leq C \\ 0 & | x - t | > C. \end{array} \right.
$$

The corresponding $\operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is a type of trimmed sample mean. 

(v) Let $C > 0$ be a constant. Huber (1964) considers 

$$
\rho (x, t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \frac {1}{2} (x - t) ^ {2} & | x - t | \leq C \\ C | x - t | - \frac {1}{2} C ^ {2} & | x - t | > C \end{array} \right.
$$

with 

$$
\psi (x, t) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} C & t - x > C \\ t - x & | x - t | \leq C \\ - C & t - x <   - C. \end{array} \right.
$$

The corresponding $\operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is a type of Winsorized sample mean. 

(vi) Hampel (1974) considers $\psi ( x , t ) = \psi _ { 0 } ( t - x )$ with $\psi _ { 0 } ( s ) = - \psi _ { 0 } ( - s )$ and 

$$
\psi_ {0} (s) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} s & 0 \leq s \leq a \\ a & a <   s \leq b \\ \frac {a (c - s)}{c - b} & b <   s \leq c \\ 0 & s > c, \end{array} \right.
$$

where $0 < a < b < c$ are constants. A smoothed version of $\psi _ { 0 }$ is 

$$
\psi_ {1} (s) = \left\{ \begin{array}{l l} \sin (a s) & 0 \leq s <   \pi / a \\ 0 & s > \pi / a. \end{array} \right.
$$

For bounded and continuous $\psi _ { ; }$ , the following result shows that T is $\varrho _ { \infty } -$ Hadamard diferentiable with a bounded and continuous influence function and, hence, $\operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ satisfies (5.41) and is robust in Hampel’s sense. 

Theorem 5.7. Let T be an M-functional defined by (5.50). Assume that $\psi$ is a bounded and continuous function on $\mathcal { R } ^ { d } \times \mathcal { R }$ and that $\lambda _ { F } ( t )$ is continuously diferentiable at $\mathtt { T } ( F )$ and $\lambda _ { F } ^ { \prime } ( \mathrm { T } ( F ) ) ~ \ne ~ 0$ . Then T is $\varrho _ { \infty } -$ Hadamard diferentiable at $F$ with 

$$
\phi_ {F} (x) = - \psi (x, \mathbf {T} (F)) / \lambda_ {F} ^ {\prime} (\mathbf {T} (F)).
$$

Proof. Let $t _ { j } \to 0 , \Delta _ { j } \in \pmb { \mathbb { D } } , \| \Delta _ { j } - \Delta \| _ { \infty } \to 0$ , and $G _ { j } = F + t _ { j } \Delta _ { j } \in \mathfrak { F }$ Since $\lambda _ { G } ( \mathbb { T } ( G ) ) = 0$ 2 

$$
| \lambda_ {F} (\mathrm{T} (G _ {j})) - \lambda_ {F} (\mathrm{T} (F)) | = \left| t _ {j} \int \psi (x, \mathrm{T} (G _ {j})) d \Delta_ {j} (x) \right|\rightarrow 0
$$

by $\| \Delta _ { j } - \Delta \| _ { \infty } \to 0$ and the boundedness of $\psi .$ . Note that $\lambda _ { F } ^ { \prime } ( \mathsf { T } ( F ) ) \neq 0$ Hence, the inverse of $\lambda _ { F } ( t )$ exists and is continuous in a neighborhood of $0 = \lambda _ { F } ( \mathbf { T } ( F ) )$ . Therefore, 

$$
\mathrm{T} (G _ {j}) - \mathrm{T} (F) \rightarrow 0.\tag{5.52}
$$

Let $h _ { F } ( \mathtt { T } ( F ) ) = \lambda _ { F } ^ { \prime } ( \mathtt { T } ( F ) ) , h _ { F } ( t ) = [ \lambda _ { F } ( t ) - \lambda _ { F } ( \mathtt { T } ( F ) ) ] / [ t - \mathtt { T } ( F ) ] \mathrm { ~ i f ~ } t \neq$ $\mathtt { T } ( F )$ 

$$
R _ {1 j} = \int \psi (x, \mathsf {T} (F)) d \Delta_ {j} (x) \left[ \frac {1}{\lambda_ {F} ^ {\prime} (\mathsf {T} (F))} - \frac {1}{h _ {F} (\mathsf {T} (G _ {j}))} \right],
$$

$$
R _ {2 j} = \frac {1}{h _ {F} (\mathsf {T} (G _ {j}))} \int [ \psi (x, \mathsf {T} (G _ {j})) - \psi (x, \mathsf {T} (F)) ] d \Delta_ {j} (x),
$$

and 

$$
\mathrm{L} _ {F} (\Delta) = - \frac {1}{\lambda_ {F} ^ {\prime} (\mathrm{T} (F))} \int \psi (x, \mathrm{T} (F)) d \Delta (x), \qquad \Delta \in \mathcal {D}.
$$

Then 

$$
\mathbf {T} (G _ {j}) - \mathbf {T} (F) = - \mathbf {L} _ {F} (t _ {j} \Delta_ {j}) + t _ {j} (R _ {1 j} - R _ {2 j}).
$$

By (5.52), $\| \Delta _ { j } - \Delta \| _ { \infty } \to 0$ , and the boundedness of $\psi , \ R _ { j 1 } \to 0$ . The result then follows from $R _ { 2 j }  0$ , which follows from $\| \Delta _ { j } - \Delta \| _ { \infty } \to 0$ and the boundedness and continuity of $\psi$ (exercise). 

Some $\psi$ functions in Example 5.7 satisfy the conditions in Theorem 5.7 (exercise). Under more conditions on $\psi ,$ it can be shown that an Mfunctional is $\varrho _ { \infty } \mathrm { - F r e c h e t }$ diferentiable at $F$ (Clarke, 1986; Shao, 1993). Some M-estimators that satisfy (5.41) but are not diferentiable functionals are studied in 5.4. 

## Rank statistics and R-estimators

Assume that $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ are i.i.d. from a c.d.f. F on $\mathcal { R }$ . The rank of $X _ { i }$ among $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ , denoted by $R _ { i }$ , is defined to be the number of $X _ { j } \mathrm { { ' s } }$ satisfying $X _ { j } \leq X _ { i } , i = 1 , . . . , n$ . The rank of $| X _ { i } |$ among $\left| X _ { 1 } \right| , . . . , \left| X _ { n } \right|$ is similarly defined and denoted by $\tilde { R } _ { i }$ . A statistic that is a function of $R _ { i } { ' }$ ’s or $\tilde { R } _ { i } \mathrm { : s }$ is called a rank statistic. For $G \in { \mathfrak { F } }$ , let 

$$
\tilde {G} (x) = G (x) - G \big ((- x) - \big), \quad x > 0,
$$

where $g ( x - )$ denotes the left limit of the function g at x. Define a functional T by 

$$
\mathrm{T} (G) = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} J (\tilde {G} (x)) d G (x), \qquad G \in \mathfrak {F},\tag{5.53}
$$

where J is a function on [0, 1] with a bounded derivative $J ^ { \prime }$ . Then 

$$
\mathsf {T} (F _ {n}) = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} J (\tilde {F} _ {n} (x)) d F _ {n} (x) = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} J \left(\frac {\tilde {R} _ {i}}{n}\right) I _ {(0, \infty)} (X _ {i})
$$

is a (one-sample) signed rank statistic. If $J ( t ) = t$ , then $\mathbb { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is the wellknown Wilcoxon signed rank test statistic ( 6.5.1). 

Statistics based on ranks (or signed ranks) are robust against changes in values of $x _ { i } \mathrm { { ^ { * } s } }$ , but may not provide eficient inference procedures, since the values of $x _ { i } \mathrm { { ^ { * } s } }$ are discarded after ranks (or signed ranks) are determined. 

It can be shown (exercise) that T in (5.53) is $\varrho _ { \infty }$ -Hadamard diferentiable at $F$ with the diferential 

$$
\mathrm{L} _ {F} (\Delta) = \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} J ^ {\prime} (\tilde {F} (x)) \tilde {\Delta} (x) d F (x) + \int_ {0} ^ {\infty} J (\tilde {F} (x)) d \Delta (x),\tag{5.54}
$$

where $\Delta \in \mathbf { \mathbb { D } }$ and $\tilde { \Delta } ( x ) = \Delta ( x ) - \Delta ( ( - x ) - )$ 

These results can be extended to the case where $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ are i.i.d. from a c.d.f. F on $\mathcal { R } ^ { 2 }$ . For any c.d.f. G on $\mathcal { R } ^ { 2 }$ , let $J$ be a function on [0, 1] with $J ( 1 - t ) = - J ( t )$ and a bounded $J ^ { \prime }$ , 

$$
\bar {G} (y) = [ G (y, \infty) + G (\infty , y) ] / 2, \qquad y \in \mathcal {R},
$$

and 

$$
\mathrm{T} (G) = \int J (\bar {G} (y)) d G (y, \infty).\tag{5.55}
$$

Let $X _ { i } ~ = ~ ( Y _ { i } , Z _ { i } )$ $R _ { i }$ be the rank of $Y _ { i }$ , and $U _ { i }$ be the number of $Z _ { j } { } ^ { : }$ ’s satisfying $Z _ { j } \le Y _ { i } , i = 1 , . . . , n$ . Then 

$$
\mathrm{T} (F _ {n}) = \int J (\bar {F} _ {n} (y)) d F _ {n} (y, \infty) = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} J \left(\frac {R _ {i} + U _ {i}}{2 n}\right)
$$

is called a two-sample linear rank statistic. It can be shown (exercise) that T in (5.55) is $\varrho _ { \infty }$ -Hadamard diferentiable at $F$ with the diferential 

$$
\mathsf {L} _ {F} (\Delta) = \int J ^ {\prime} (\bar {F} (y)) \bar {\Delta} (y) d F (y, \infty) + \int J (\bar {F} (y)) d \Delta (y, \infty),\tag{5.56}
$$

where $\bar { \Delta } ( y ) = [ \Delta ( y , \infty ) + \Delta ( \infty , y ) ] / 2 .$ 

Rank statistics (one-sample or two-sample) are asymptotically normal and robust in Hampel’s sense (exercise). These results are useful in testing hypotheses ( 6.5). 

Let $F$ be a continuous c.d.f. on $\mathcal { R }$ symmetric about an unknown parameter $\theta \in \mathcal { R }$ . An estimator of $\theta$ closely related to a rank statistic can be derived as follows. Let $X _ { i }$ be i.i.d. from $F$ and $W _ { i } = ( X _ { i } , 2 t - X _ { i } )$ with a fixed $t \in \mathcal { R }$ . The functional T in (5.55) evaluated at the c.d.f. of $W _ { i }$ is equal to 

$$
\lambda_ {F} (t) = \int J \left(\frac {F (x) + 1 - F (2 t - x)}{2}\right) d F (x).\tag{5.57}
$$

If J is strictly increasing and $F$ is strictly increasing in a neighborhood of $\theta ,$ then $\lambda _ { F } ( t ) = 0$ if and only if $t = \theta$ (exercise). For $G \in { \mathfrak { F } }$ , define $\mathrm { T } ( G )$ to be a solution of 

$$
\int J \left(\frac {G (x) + 1 - G (2 \mathrm{T} (G) - x)}{2}\right) d G (x) = 0.\tag{5.58}
$$

$\operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is called an R-estimator of $\operatorname { T } ( F ) = \theta$ . When $\begin{array} { r } { J ( t ) = t - \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ (which is related to the Wilcoxon signed rank test), $\operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is the well-known Hodges-Lehmann estimator and is equal to any value between the two middle points of the values $( X _ { i } + X _ { j } ) / 2 , i = 1 , . . . , n , j = 1 , . . . , n .$ 

Theorem 5.8. Let T be the functional defined by (5.58). Suppose that $F$ is continuous and symmetric about $\theta ,$ , the derivatives $F ^ { \prime }$ and $J ^ { \prime }$ exist, and $J ^ { \prime }$ is bounded. Then T is $\varrho _ { \infty }$ -Hadamard diferentiable at $F$ with the influence function 

$$
\phi_ {F} (x) = \frac {J (F (x))}{\int J ^ {\prime} (F (x)) F ^ {\prime} (x) d F (x)}.
$$

Proof. Since $F$ is symmetric about $\theta ,$ $F ( x ) + F ( 2 \theta - x ) = 1$ . Under the assumed conditions, $\lambda _ { F } ( t )$ is continuous and $\begin{array} { r } { \int J ^ { \prime } ( F ( x ) ) F ^ { \prime } ( x ) d F ( x ) = } \end{array}$ $- \lambda _ { F } ^ { \prime } ( \theta ) \neq 0$ (exercise). Hence, the inverse of $\lambda _ { F }$ exists and is continuous at $0 = \lambda _ { F } ( \theta )$ Suppose that $t _ { j } \ \to \ 0 , \ \Delta _ { j } \ \in \ \mathbf { \mathcal { D } } , \ \lVert \Delta _ { j } - \Delta \rVert _ { \infty } \ \to \ 0$ , and $G _ { j } = F + t _ { j } \Delta _ { j } \in \mathscr { F }$ . Then 

$$
\int [ J (G _ {j} (x, t)) - J (F (x, t)) ] d G _ {j} (x) \rightarrow 0
$$

uniformly in t, where $G ( x , t ) = [ G ( x ) + 1 - G ( 2 t - x ) ] / 2$ , and 

$$
\int J (F (x, t)) d (G _ {j} - F) (x) = \int (F - G _ {j}) (x) J ^ {\prime} (F (x, t)) d F (x, t) \rightarrow 0
$$

uniformly in t. Let $\lambda _ { G } ( t )$ be defined by (5.57) with F replaced by $G$ . Then 

$$
\lambda_ {G _ {j}} (t) - \lambda_ {F} (t) \rightarrow 0
$$

uniformly in t. Thus, $\lambda _ { F } ( \operatorname { T } ( G _ { j } ) ) \to 0$ , which implies 

$$
\mathrm{T} (G _ {j}) \rightarrow \mathrm{T} (F) = \theta .\tag{5.59}
$$

Let $\begin{array} { r } { \xi _ { G } ( t ) = \int J ( F ( x , t ) ) d G ( x ) , h _ { F } ( t ) = [ \lambda _ { F } ( t ) - \lambda _ { F } ( \theta ) ] / ( t - \theta ) } \end{array}$ if $t \neq \theta ,$ and $h _ { F } ( \theta ) = \lambda _ { F } ^ { \prime } ( \theta )$ . Then $\begin{array} { r } { \Sigma ( G _ { j } ) - \Sigma ( F ) - \int \phi _ { F } ( x ) d ( G _ { j } - F ) ( x ) } \end{array}$ is equal to 

$$
\xi_ {G _ {j}} (\theta) \left[ \frac {1}{\lambda_ {F} ^ {\prime} (\theta)} - \frac {1}{h _ {F} (\mathsf {T} (G _ {j}))} \right] + \frac {\lambda_ {F} (\mathsf {T} (G _ {j})) - \xi_ {G _ {j}} (\theta)}{h _ {F} (\mathsf {T} (G _ {j}))}.\tag{5.60}
$$

Note that 

$$
\xi_ {G _ {j}} (\theta) = \int J (F (x)) d G _ {j} (x) = t _ {j} \int J (F (x)) d \Delta_ {j} (x).
$$

By (5.59), Lemma 5.2, and $\| \Delta _ { j } - \Delta \| _ { \infty } \to 0$ , the first term in (5.60) is $o ( t _ { j } )$ The second term in (5.60) is the sum of 

$$
- \frac {t _ {j}}{h _ {F} (\mathsf {T} (G _ {j}))} \int [ J (F (x, \mathsf {T} (G _ {j}))) - J (F (x)) ] d \Delta_ {j} (x)\tag{5.61}
$$

and 

$$
\frac {1}{h _ {F} (\mathsf {T} (G _ {j}))} \int [ J (F (x, \mathsf {T} (G _ {j}))) - J (G _ {j} (x, \mathsf {T} (G _ {j}))) ] d G _ {j} (x).\tag{5.62}
$$

From the continuity of J and $F _ { ; }$ , the quantity in (5.61) is $o ( t _ { j } )$ . Similarly, the quantity in (5.62) is equal to 

$$
\frac {1}{h _ {F} (\mathsf {T} (G _ {j}))} \int [ J (F (x, \mathsf {T} (G _ {j}))) - J (G _ {j} (x, \mathsf {T} (G _ {j}))) ] d F (x) + o (t _ {j}).\tag{5.63}
$$

From Taylor’s expansion, (5.59), and $\| \Delta _ { j } - \Delta \| _ { \infty } \to 0$ , the quantity in (5.63) is equal to 

$$
\frac {t _ {j}}{h _ {F} (\mathsf {T} (G _ {j}))} \int J ^ {\prime} (F (x)) \Delta (x, \theta) d F (x) + o (t _ {j}).\tag{5.64}
$$

Since $J ( 1 - t ) = - J ( t )$ , the integral in (5.64) is 0. This proves that the second term in (5.60) is $o ( t _ { j } )$ and thus the result. 

It is clear that the influence function $\phi _ { F }$ for an R-estimator is bounded and continuous if J and F are continuous. Thus, R-estimators satisfy (5.41) and are robust in Hampel’s sense. 

Example 5.8. Let $\begin{array} { r } { J ( t ) = t - \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ . Then $\operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ is the Hodges-Lehmann estimator. From Theorem 5.8, $\phi _ { F } ( \stackrel { \bf \bar { \boldsymbol { x } } } { x } ) = [ F ( x ) - \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } ] / \gamma$ , where $\begin{array} { r } { \gamma = \int F ^ { \prime } ( x ) d F ( x ) } \end{array}$ Since $F ( X _ { 1 } )$ has a uniform distribution on $[ 0 , 1 ] , \phi _ { F } ( X _ { 1 } )$ has mean 0 and variance $( 1 2 \gamma ^ { 2 } ) ^ { - 1 }$ . Thus, $\sqrt { n } [ \mathrm { T } ( F _ { n } ) - \mathrm { T } ( F ) ] { \overset { \cdot } { \longrightarrow } } _ { d } \cdot N ( 0 , ( 1 2 \gamma ^ { 2 } ) ^ { - 1 } )$ 

## 5.3 Linear Functions of Order Statistics

In this section, we study statistics that are linear functions of order statistics $X _ { ( 1 ) } \leq \cdots \leq X _ { ( n ) }$ based on independent random variables $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ (in 5.3.1 and $\ S 5 . 3 . 2 , X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ are assumed i.i.d.). Order statistics, first introduced in Example 2.9, are usually suficient and often complete (or minimal suficient) for nonparametric families (Examples 2.12 and 2.14). 

L-estimators defined in 5.2.2 are in fact linear functions of order statis tics. If T is given by (5.46), then 

$$
\mathsf {T} (F _ {n}) = \int x J (F _ {n} (x)) d F _ {n} (x) = \frac {1}{n} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} J \left(\frac {i}{n}\right) X _ {(i)},\tag{5.65}
$$

since $F _ { n } ( X _ { ( i ) } ) = i / n , i = 1 , . . . , n$ . If J is a smooth function, such as those given in Example 5.6 or those satisfying the conditions in Theorem 5.6, the corresponding L-estimator is often called a smooth L-estimator. Asymptotic properties of smooth L-estimators can be obtained using Theorem 5.6 and the results in 5.2.1. Results on L-estimators that are slightly diferent from that in (5.65) can be found in Serfling (1980, Chapter 8). 

In 5.3.1, we consider another useful class of linear functions of order statistics, the sample quantiles described in the beginning of 5.2. In 5.3.2, we study robust linear functions of order statistics (in Hampel’s sense) and their relative eficiencies w.r.t. the sample mean X<sup>¯</sup> , an eficient but nonrobust estimator. In 5.3.3, extensions to linear models are discussed. 

## 5.3.1 Sample quantiles

Recall that $G ^ { - 1 } ( p )$ is defined to be in $\{ x : G ( x ) \geq p \}$ for any c.d.f. G on , where $p \in ( 0 , 1 )$ is a fixed constant. For i.i.d. $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ from $F _ { ; }$ , let $\theta _ { p } = F ^ { - 1 } ( p )$ and $\hat { \theta } _ { p } = F _ { n } ^ { - 1 } ( p )$ denote the pth quantile of $F$ and the pth 

sample quantile, respectively. Then 

$$
\hat {\theta} _ {p} = c _ {n p} X _ {(m _ {p})} + (1 - c _ {n p}) X _ {(m _ {p} + 1)},\tag{5.66}
$$

where $m _ { p }$ is the integer part of $n p , c _ { n p } = 1$ if $n p$ is an integer, and $c _ { n p } = 0$ if $n p$ is not an integer. Thus, $\hat { \theta } _ { p }$ is a linear function of order statistics. 

Note that $F ( \theta _ { p } - ) \leq p \leq F ( \theta _ { p } )$ and F is not flat in a neighborhood of $\theta _ { p }$ if and only if $p < F ( \theta _ { p } + \epsilon )$ for any $\epsilon > 0$ 

Theorem 5.9. Let $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ be i.i.d. random variables from a c.d.f. F satisfying $p < F ( \theta _ { p } + \epsilon )$ for any $\epsilon > 0$ . Then, for every $\epsilon > 0$ and $n = 1 , 2 , \ldots ,$ 

$$
P \big (| \hat {\theta} _ {p} - \theta_ {p} | > \epsilon \big) \leq 2 C e ^ {- 2 n \delta_ {\epsilon} ^ {2}},\tag{5.67}
$$

where $\delta _ { \epsilon }$ is the smaller of $F ( \theta _ { p } + \epsilon ) - p$ and $p - F ( \theta _ { p } - \epsilon )$ and C is the same constant in Lemma 5.1(i). 

Proof. Let $\epsilon > 0$ be fixed. Note that $G ( x ) \geq t$ if and only if $x \geq G ^ { - 1 } ( t )$ for any c.d.f. G on $\mathcal { R }$ (exercise). Hence 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \big (\hat {\theta} _ {p} > \theta_ {p} + \epsilon \big) = P \big (p > F _ {n} (\theta_ {p} + \epsilon) \big) \\ \qquad = P \big (F (\theta_ {p} + \epsilon) - F _ {n} (\theta_ {p} + \epsilon) > F (\theta_ {p} + \epsilon) - p \big) \\ \qquad \leq P \big (\varrho_ {\infty} (F _ {n}, F) > \delta_ {\epsilon} \big) \\ \qquad \leq C e ^ {- 2 n \delta_ {\epsilon} ^ {2}}, \end{array}
$$

where the last inequality follows from DKW’s inequality (Lemma 5.1(i)). Similarly, 

$$
P \big (\hat {\theta} _ {p} <   \theta_ {p} - \epsilon \big) \leq C e ^ {- 2 n \delta_ {\epsilon} ^ {2}}.
$$

This proves (5.67). 

Result (5.67) implies that $\hat { \theta } _ { p }$ is strongly consistent for $\theta _ { p }$ (exercise) and that $\hat { \theta } _ { p }$ is $\sqrt { n } -$ -consistent for $\theta _ { p }$ if $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } - )$ and $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } + )$ (the left and right derivatives of $F$ at $\theta _ { p } )$ exist (exercise). 

The exact distribution of $\hat { \theta } _ { p }$ can be obtained as follows. Since $n F _ { n } ( t )$ has the binomial distribution $B i ( F ( t ) , n )$ for any $t \in \mathcal { R }$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{l} P \big (\hat {\theta} _ {p} \leq t \big) = P \big (F _ {n} (t) \geq p \big) \\ = \sum_ {i = l _ {p}} ^ {n} \binom {n} {i} [ F (t) ] ^ {i} [ 1 - F (t) ] ^ {n - i}, \end{array}\tag{5.68}
$$

where $l _ { p } = n p$ if np is an integer and $l _ { p } = 1 +$ the integer part of np if np is not an integer. If F has a Lebesgue p.d.f. f, then $\hat { \theta } _ { p }$ has the Lebesgue p.d.f. 

$$
\varphi_ {n} (t) = n \binom {n - 1} {l _ {p} - 1} [ F (t) ] ^ {l _ {p} - 1} [ 1 - F (t) ] ^ {n - l _ {p}} f (t).\tag{5.69}
$$

The following result provides an asymptotic distribution for $\sqrt { n } ( \hat { \theta } _ { p } - \theta _ { p } )$ 

Theorem 5.10. Let $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ be i.i.d. random variables from $F .$ 

(i) If $F ( \theta _ { p } ) = p $ , then $\begin{array} { r } { P ( \sqrt { n } ( \hat { \theta } _ { p } - \theta _ { p } ) \leq 0 )  \Phi ( 0 ) = \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ , where Φ is the c.d.f. of the standard normal. 

(ii) If $F$ is continuous at $\theta _ { p }$ and there exists $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } - ) > 0$ , then 

$$
P \big (\sqrt {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {p} - \theta_ {p}) \leq t \big) \rightarrow \Phi (t / \sigma_ {F} ^ {-}), \qquad t <   0,
$$

where $\sigma _ { F } ^ { - } = \sqrt { p ( 1 - p ) } / F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } - )$ 

(iii) If $F$ is continuous at $\theta _ { p }$ and there exists $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } + ) > 0$ , then 

$$
P \big (\sqrt {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {p} - \theta_ {p}) \leq t \big) \rightarrow \Phi (t / \sigma_ {F} ^ {+}), \qquad t > 0,
$$

where $\sigma _ { F } ^ { + } = \sqrt { p ( 1 - p ) } / F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } + )$ 

(iv) If $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } )$ exists and is positive, then 

$$
\sqrt {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {p} - \theta_ {p}) \rightarrow_ {d} N (0, \sigma_ {F} ^ {2}),\tag{5.70}
$$

where $\sigma _ { F } = \sqrt { p ( 1 - p ) } / F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } )$ 

Proof. The proof of (i) is left as an exercise. Part (iv) is a direct consequence of (i)-(iii) and the proofs of (ii) and (iii) are similar. Thus, we only give a proof for (iii). 

Let $t > 0 , p _ { n t } = F ( \theta _ { p } + t \sigma _ { F } ^ { + } n ^ { - 1 / 2 } ) , c _ { n t } = \sqrt { n } ( p _ { n t } - p ) / \sqrt { p _ { n t } ( 1 - p _ { n t } ) }$ , and $Z _ { n t } = [ B _ { n } ( p _ { n t } ) - n p _ { n t } ] / \sqrt { n p _ { n t } ( 1 - p _ { n t } ) }$ , where $B _ { n } ( q )$ denotes a random variable having the binomial distribution $B i ( q , n )$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{c} P \big (\hat {\theta} _ {p} \leq \theta_ {p} + t \sigma_ {F} ^ {+} n ^ {- 1 / 2} \big) = P \big (p \leq F _ {n} (\theta_ {p} + t \sigma_ {F} ^ {+} n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \big) \\ = P \big (Z _ {n t} \geq - c _ {n t} \big). \end{array}
$$

Under the assumed conditions on $F , \ p _ { n t } \to p$ and $c _ { n t } \ \to \ t$ . Hence, the result follows from 

$$
P \big (Z _ {n t} <   - c _ {n t} \big) - \Phi (- c _ {n t}) \rightarrow 0.
$$

But this follows from the CLT (Example 1.33) and P´olya’s theorem (Proposition 1.16). 

If both $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } - )$ and $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } + )$ exist and are positive, but $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } - { \bf \Big ) \ } \neq$ $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } + )$ , then the asymptotic distribution of $\sqrt { n } ( \hat { \theta } _ { p } - \theta _ { p } )$ has the c.d.f. $\Phi ( t / \sigma _ { F } ^ { - } ) I _ { ( - \infty , 0 ) } ( t ) + \Phi ( t / \sigma _ { F } ^ { + } ) I _ { [ 0 , \infty ) } ( t )$ , a mixture of two normal distributions. An example of such a case when $\begin{array} { r } { p = \frac { 1 } { 2 } } \end{array}$ is 

$$
F (x) = x I _ {[ 0, \frac {1}{2})} (x) + (2 x - \frac {1}{2}) I _ {[ \frac {1}{2}, \frac {3}{4})} (x) + I _ {[ \frac {3}{4}, \infty)} (x).
$$

When $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } - ) = F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } + ) = F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } ) > 0 , ( 5 . 7 0 )$ shows that the asymptotic distribution of $\sqrt { n } (  { \hat { \theta } } _ { p } - \theta _ { p } )$ is the same as that of $\sqrt { n } [ F _ { n } ( \theta _ { p } ) - F ( \theta _ { p } ) ] / F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } )$ (see (5.2)). The following result reveals a stronger relationship between sample quantiles and the empirical c.d.f. 

Theorem 5.11 (Bahadur’s representation). Let $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ be i.i.d. random variables from F. Suppose that $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } )$ exists and is positive. Then 

$$
\hat {\theta} _ {p} = \theta_ {p} + \frac {F (\theta_ {p}) - F _ {n} (\theta_ {p})}{F ^ {\prime} (\theta_ {p})} + o _ {p} \left(\frac {1}{\sqrt {n}}\right).\tag{5.71}
$$

Proof. Let $t \in \mathcal { R } , \theta _ { n t } = \theta _ { p } + t n ^ { - 1 / 2 } , Z _ { n } ( t ) = \sqrt { n } [ F ( \theta _ { n t } ) - F _ { n } ( \theta _ { n t } ) ] / F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } )$ and $U _ { n } ( t ) = \sqrt { n } [ F ( \theta _ { n t } ) - F _ { n } ( \hat { \theta } _ { p } ) ] / F ^ { \prime } ( \theta _ { p } )$ . It can be shown (exercise) that 

$$
Z _ {n} (t) - Z _ {n} (0) = o _ {p} (1).\tag{5.72}
$$

Note that $| p - F _ { n } ( \hat { \theta } _ { p } ) | \leq n ^ { - 1 }$ . Then 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} U _ {n} (t) & = \sqrt {n} [ F (\theta_ {n t}) - p + p - F _ {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {p}) ] / F ^ {\prime} (\theta_ {p}) \\ & = \sqrt {n} [ F (\theta_ {n t}) - p ] / F ^ {\prime} (\theta_ {p}) + O (n ^ {- 1 / 2}) \\ & \to t. \end{array}\tag{5.73}
$$

Let $\xi _ { n } = \sqrt { n } (  { \hat { \theta } } _ { p } - \theta _ { p } )$ . Then, for any $t \in \mathcal { R }$ and $\epsilon > 0$ , 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} P \big (\xi_ {n} \leq t, Z _ {n} (0) \geq t + \epsilon \big) & = P \big (Z _ {n} (t) \leq U _ {n} (t), Z _ {n} (0) \geq t + \epsilon \big) \\ & \leq P \big (| Z _ {n} (t) - Z _ {n} (0) | \geq \epsilon / 2 \big) \\ & \quad + P \big (| U _ {n} (t) - t | \geq \epsilon / 2 \big) \\ & \to 0 \end{array}\tag{5.74}
$$

by (5.72) and (5.73). Similarly, 

$$
P \big (\xi_ {n} \geq t + \epsilon , Z _ {n} (0) \leq t \big) \rightarrow 0.\tag{5.75}
$$

It follows from the result in Exercise 128 of 1.6 that 

$$
\xi_ {n} - Z _ {n} (0) = o _ {p} (1),
$$

which is the same as (5.71). 

If F has a positive Lebesgue p.d.f., then $\hat { \theta } _ { p }$ viewed as a statistical functional ( 5.2) is ̺ -Hadamard diferentiable at $F$ (Fernholz, 1983) with the influence function 

$$
\phi_ {F} (x) = [ F (\theta_ {p}) - I _ {(- \infty , \theta_ {p} ]} (x) ] / F ^ {\prime} (\theta_ {p}).
$$

This implies result (5.71). Note that $\phi _ { F }$ is bounded and is continuous except when $x = \theta _ { p }$ 

Corollary 5.1. Let $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ be i.i.d. random variables from $F$ having positive derivatives at $\theta _ { p _ { j } }$ , where $0 < p _ { 1 } < \cdots < p _ { m } < 1$ are fixed constants. Then 

$$
\sqrt {n} [ (\hat {\theta} _ {p _ {1}}, \dots , \hat {\theta} _ {p _ {m}}) - (\theta_ {p _ {1}}, \dots , \theta_ {p _ {m}}) ] \rightarrow_ {d} N _ {m} (0, D),
$$

where D is the $m \times m$ symmetric matrix whose $( i , j )$ th element is 

$$
p _ {i} (1 - p _ {j}) / [ F ^ {\prime} (\theta_ {p _ {i}}) F ^ {\prime} (\theta_ {p _ {j}}) ], \qquad i \leq j. \quad ⅰ
$$

The proof of this corollary is left to the reader. 

Example 5.9 (Interquartile range). One application of Corollary 5.1 is the derivation of the asymptotic distribution of the interquartile range $\hat { \theta } _ { 0 . 7 5 } -$ $\hat { \theta } _ { 0 . 2 5 }$ . The interquartile range is used as a measure of the variability among $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ . It can be shown (exercise) that 

$$
\sqrt {n} [ (\hat {\theta} _ {0. 7 5} - \hat {\theta} _ {0. 2 5}) - (\theta_ {0. 7 5} - \theta_ {0. 2 5}) ] \rightarrow_ {d} N (0, \sigma_ {F} ^ {2})
$$

with 

$$
\sigma_ {F} ^ {2} = \frac {3}{1 6 [ F ^ {\prime} (\theta_ {0 . 7 5}) ] ^ {2}} + \frac {3}{1 6 [ F ^ {\prime} (\theta_ {0 . 2 5}) ] ^ {2}} - \frac {1}{8 F ^ {\prime} (\theta_ {0 . 7 5}) F ^ {\prime} (\theta_ {0 . 2 5})}.
$$

There are some applications of using extreme order statistics such as $X _ { ( 1 ) }$ and $X _ { ( n ) }$ . One example is given in Example 2.34. Some other examples and references can be found in Serfling (1980, pp. 89-91). 

## 5.3.2 Robustness and eficiency

Let F be a c.d.f. on $\mathcal { R }$ symmetric about $\theta \in \mathcal { R }$ with $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta ) > 0$ . Then $\theta = \theta _ { 0 . 5 }$ and is called the median of F. If F has a finite mean, then θ is also equal to the mean. In this section, we consider the estimation of θ based on i.i.d. $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ from F. 

If $F$ is normal, it has been shown in previous chapters that the sample mean $\bar { X }$ is the UMVUE, MRIE, and MLE of $\theta ,$ and is asymptotically eficient. On the other hand, if $F$ is the c.d.f. of the Cauchy distribution $C ( \theta , 1 )$ , it follows from Exercise 78 in 1.6 that X<sup>¯</sup> has the same distribution as X , i.e., X<sup>¯</sup> is as variable as $X _ { 1 }$ , and is inconsistent as an estimator of $\theta .$ 

Why does $\bar { X }$ perform so diferently? An important diference between the normal and Cauchy $\mathrm { p . d . f . ^ { \prime } s }$ is that the former tends to 0 at the rate $e ^ { - x ^ { 2 } / 2 } { \mathrm { ~ a s ~ } } | x |  \infty$ , whereas the latter tends to 0 at the much slower rate $x ^ { - 2 }$ , which results in $\textstyle \int | x | d F ( x ) = \infty$ . The poor performance of $\bar { X }$ in the Cauchy case is due to the high probability of getting extreme observations and the fact that $\bar { X }$ is sensitive to large changes in a few of the $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ . (Note that $\bar { X }$ is not robust in Hampel’s sense, since the functional $\textstyle \int x d G ( x )$ has an unbounded influence function at $F . )$ This suggests the use of a robust estimator that discards some extreme observations. The sample median, which is defined to be the 50%th sample quantile $\widehat { \theta } _ { 0 . 5 }$ described in 5.3.1, is insensitive to the behavior of $F$ as $| x | \to \infty$ 

Since both the sample mean and the sample median can be used to estimate $\theta ,$ a natural question is when is one better than the other, using a criterion such as the amse. Unfortunately, a general answer does not exist, since the asymptotic relative eficiency between these two estimators depends on the unknown distribution $F$ . If $F$ does not have a finite variance, then $\mathrm { V a r } ( { \bar { X } } ) = \infty$ and $\bar { X }$ may be inconsistent. In such a case the sample median is certainly preferred, since $\widehat { \theta } _ { 0 . 5 }$ is consistent and asymptotically normal as long as $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta ) > 0$ , and may have a finite variance (Exercise 60). The following example, which compares the sample mean and median in some cases, shows that the sample median can be better even if $\mathrm { V a r } ( X _ { 1 } ) < \infty$ 

Example 5.10. Suppose that $\mathrm { V a r } ( X _ { 1 } ) < \infty$ . Then, by the CLT, 

$$
\sqrt {n} (\bar {X} - \theta) \rightarrow_ {d} N (0, \operatorname{Var} (X _ {1})).
$$

By Theorem 5.10(iv), 

$$
\sqrt {n} (\hat {\theta} _ {0. 5} - \theta) \rightarrow_ {d} N (0, [ 2 F ^ {\prime} (\theta) ] ^ {- 2}).
$$

Hence, the asymptotic relative eficiency of $\hat { \theta } _ { 0 . 5 } ~ \mathrm { w . r . t . } ~ \bar { X }$ is 

$$
e (F) = 4 [ F ^ {\prime} (\theta) ] ^ {2} \mathrm{Var} (X _ {1}).
$$

(i) If $F$ is the c.d.f. of $N ( \theta , \sigma ^ { 2 } )$ , then $\operatorname { V a r } ( X _ { 1 } ) = \sigma ^ { 2 } , F ^ { \prime } ( \theta ) = ( { \sqrt { 2 \pi } } \sigma ) ^ { - 1 }$ and $e ( F ) = 2 / \pi = 0 . 6 3 7$ 

(ii) If F is the c.d.f. of the logistic distribution $L G ( \theta , \sigma )$ , then $\mathrm { V a r } ( X _ { 1 } ) =$ $\dot { \sigma } ^ { 2 } \pi ^ { 2 } / 3 , F ^ { \prime } ( \theta ) = ( 4 \sigma ) ^ { - 1 }$ , and $e ( F ) = \pi ^ { 2 } / 1 2 = 0 . 8 2 2 .$ 

(iii) If $F ( x ) = F _ { 0 } ( x - \theta )$ and $F _ { 0 }$ is the c.d.f. of the t-distribution $t _ { \nu }$ with $\nu \geq 3$ , then $\operatorname { V a r } ( X _ { 1 } ) = \nu / ( \nu - 2 ) , F ^ { \prime } ( \theta ) = \Gamma ( \textstyle { \frac { \nu + 1 } { 2 } } ) / [ \sqrt { \nu \pi } \Gamma ( \textstyle { \frac { \nu } { 2 } } ) ] , e ( F ) = 1 . 6 2$ when $\nu = 3 , e ( F ) = 1 . 1 2$ when $\nu = 4$ , and $e ( F ) = 0 . 9 6$ when $\nu = 5$ 

(iv) If F is the c.d.f. of the double exponential distribution $D E ( \theta , \sigma )$ , then $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta ) = ( 2 \sigma ) ^ { - 1 }$ and $e ( F ) = 2$ 

(v) Consider the Tukey model 

$$
F (x) = (1 - \epsilon) \Phi \left(\frac {x - \theta}{\sigma}\right) + \epsilon \Phi \left(\frac {x - \theta}{\tau \sigma}\right),\tag{5.76}
$$

where $\sigma > 0 , \tau > 0$ , and $0 < \epsilon < 1$ . Then Var $( X _ { 1 } ) = ( 1 - \epsilon ) \sigma ^ { 2 } + \epsilon \tau ^ { 2 } \sigma ^ { 2 }$ $F ^ { \prime } ( \theta ) = ( 1 - \epsilon + \epsilon / \tau ) / ( \sqrt { 2 \pi } \sigma )$ , and $e ( F ) = 2 ( 1 - \epsilon + \epsilon \tau ^ { 2 } ) ( 1 - \epsilon + \epsilon / \tau ) ^ { 2 } / \pi .$ Note that $\begin{array} { r } { \operatorname* { l i m } _ { \epsilon  0 } e ( F ) = 2 / \pi } \end{array}$ and lim $_ { \tau \to \infty } e ( F ) = \infty$ 

Since the sample median uses at most two actual values of $x _ { i } \mathrm { { ' s } }$ , it may go too far in discarding observations, which results in a possible loss of eficiency. The trimmed sample mean introduced in Example 5.6(iii) is a natural compromise between the sample mean and median. Since $F$ is symmetric, we consider $\beta = 1 - \alpha$ in the trimmed mean, which results in the following L-estimator: 

$$
\bar {X} _ {\alpha} = \frac {1}{(1 - 2 \alpha) n} \sum_ {j = m _ {\alpha} + 1} ^ {n - m _ {\alpha}} X _ {(j)},\tag{5.77}
$$

where $m _ { \alpha }$ is the integer part of nα and $\alpha \in ( 0 , \textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } } )$ . The estimator in (5.77) is called the α-trimmed sample mean. It discards the $m _ { \alpha }$ smallest and $m _ { \alpha }$ largest observations. The sample mean and median can be viewed as two extreme cases of $\bar { X } _ { \alpha }$ as $\alpha \to 0$ and $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } }$ , respectively. 

It follows from Theorem 5.6 that if $F ( x ) = F _ { 0 } ( x - \theta )$ , where $F _ { 0 }$ is symmetric about 0 and has a Lebesgue p.d.f. positive in the range of $X _ { 1 }$ then 

$$
\sqrt {n} (\bar {X} _ {\alpha} - \theta) \rightarrow_ {d} N (0, \sigma_ {\alpha} ^ {2}),\tag{5.78}
$$

where 

$$
\sigma_ {\alpha} ^ {2} = \frac {2}{(1 - 2 \alpha) ^ {2}} \left\{\int_ {0} ^ {F _ {0} ^ {- 1} (1 - \alpha)} x ^ {2} d F _ {0} (x) + \alpha [ F _ {0} ^ {- 1} (1 - \alpha) ] ^ {2} \right\}.
$$

Lehmann (1983, 5.4) provides various values of the asymptotic relative eficiency $e _ { \bar { X } _ { \alpha } , \bar { X } } ( F ) = \mathrm { V a r } ( X _ { 1 } ) / \sigma _ { \alpha } ^ { 2 }$ . For instance, when $F ( x ) = F _ { 0 } ( x - \theta )$ and $F _ { 0 }$ is the c.d.f. of the t-distribution $t _ { 3 } , e _ { \bar { X } _ { \alpha } , \bar { X } } ( F ) = 1 . 7 0 , 1 . 9 1$ , and 1.97 for $\alpha = 0 . 0 5 , 0 . 1 2 5$ , and 0.25, respectively; when $F$ is given by (5.76) with $\tau = 3$ and $\epsilon = 0 . 0 5 , e _ { \bar { X } _ { \alpha } , \bar { X } } ( F ) = 1 . 2 0 , 1 . 1 9$ , and 1.09 for $\alpha = 0 . 0 5 , 0 . 1 2 5$ 2 and 0.25, respectively; when $F$ is given by (5.76) with $\tau = 3$ and $\epsilon = 0 . 0 1$ $e _ { \bar { X } _ { \alpha } , \bar { X } } ( F ) = 1 . 0 4 , 0 . 9 8$ , and 0.89 for $\alpha = 0 . 0 5 , 0 . 1 2 5$ , and 0.25, respectively. 

Robustness and eficiency of other L-estimators can be discussed similarly. For an L-estimator $\operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ with T given by (5.46), if the conditions in one of (i)-(iii) of Theorem 5.6 are satisfied, then (5.41) holds with 

$$
\sigma_ {F} ^ {2} = \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} \int_ {- \infty} ^ {\infty} J (F (x)) J (F (y)) [ F (\min \{x, y \}) - F (x) F (y) ] d x d y,\tag{5.79}
$$

provided that $\sigma _ { F } ^ { 2 } < \infty \mathrm { ( e x e r c i s e ) }$ . If F is symmetric about $\theta , J$ is symmetric about $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } }$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } J ( t ) d t = 1 } \end{array}$ , then $\mathbb { T } ( F ) = \theta$ (exercise) and, therefore, the asymptotic relative eficiency of $\operatorname { T } ( F _ { n } )$ w.r.t. X<sup>¯</sup> is $\mathrm { V a r } \big ( X _ { 1 } \big ) / \sigma _ { F } ^ { 2 }$ 

## 5.3.3 L-estimators in linear models

In this section, we extend L-estimators to the following linear model: 

$$
X _ {i} = \beta^ {\tau} Z _ {i} + \varepsilon_ {i}, \qquad i = 1, \dots , n,\tag{5.80}
$$

with i.i.d. $\varepsilon _ { i } \mathrm { { ^ { s } } }$ having an unknown c.d.f. $F _ { 0 }$ and a full rank $Z$ whose ith row is the vector $Z _ { i }$ . Note that the c.d.f. of $X _ { i }$ is $F _ { 0 } ( x - \beta ^ { \tau } Z _ { i } )$ . Instead of assuming $E ( \varepsilon _ { i } ) = 0$ (as we did in Chapter 3), we assume that 

$$
\int x J (F _ {0} (x)) d F _ {0} (x) = 0,\tag{5.81}
$$

where J is a Borel function on [0, 1] (the same as that in (5.46)). Note that (5.81) may hold without any assumption on the existence of $E ( \varepsilon _ { i } )$ . For instance, (5.81) holds if $F _ { 0 }$ is symmetric about $0 , J$ is symmetric about $\textstyle { \frac { 1 } { 2 } }$ , and $\begin{array} { r } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { 1 } J ( t ) d t = 1 } \end{array}$ (Exercise 69). 

Since $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are not identically distributed, the use of the order statistics and the empirical c.d.f. based on $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ may not be appropriate. Instead, we consider the ordered values of residuals $r _ { i } = X _ { i } { - } Z _ { i } ^ { \tau } { \hat { \beta } } , i = 1 , . . . , n$ , and some empirical c.d.f.’s based on residuals, where $\hat { \beta } = ( Z ^ { \tau } Z ) ^ { - 1 } Z ^ { \tau } X$ is the LSE of $\beta$ ( 3.3.1). 

To illustrate the idea, let us start with the case where $\beta$ and $Z _ { i }$ are univariate. First, assume that $Z _ { i } \geq 0$ for all i (or $Z _ { i } \le 0$ for all i). Let $\hat { F } _ { 0 }$ be the c.d.f. putting mass $Z _ { i } / \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } Z _ { i }$ at $r _ { i } , i = 1 , . . . , n$ . An L-estimator of $\beta$ is defined to be 

$$
\hat {\beta} _ {L} = \hat {\beta} + \int x J (\hat {F} _ {0} (x)) d \hat {F} _ {0} (x) \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Z _ {i} \bigg / \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Z _ {i} ^ {2}.
$$

When $J ( t ) = ( 1 - 2 \alpha ) ^ { - 1 } I _ { ( \alpha , 1 - \alpha ) } ( t )$ with an $\alpha \in ( 0 , { \textstyle \frac { 1 } { 2 } } ) , \hat { \beta } _ { L }$ is similar to the α-trimmed sample mean in the i.i.d. case. 

If not all $Z _ { i } \mathrm { ^ { * } s }$ have the same sign, we can define L-estimators as follows. Let $Z _ { i } ^ { + } =$ max $\{ Z _ { i } , 0 \}$ and $Z _ { i } ^ { - } = Z _ { i } ^ { + } - Z _ { i }$ . Let $\hat { F } _ { 0 } ^ { \pm }$ be the c.d.f. putting mass $\textstyle { \bar { Z } } _ { i } ^ { \pm } / \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } Z _ { i } ^ { \pm }$ at $r _ { i } , i = 1 , . . . , n$ . An L-estimator of $\beta$ is defined to be 

$$
\begin{array}{r l} & {\hat {\beta} _ {L} = \hat {\beta} + \int x J (\hat {F} _ {0} ^ {+} (x)) d \hat {F} _ {0} ^ {+} (x) \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Z _ {i} ^ {+} \bigg / \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Z _ {i} ^ {2}} \\ & {- \int x J (\hat {F} _ {0} ^ {-} (x)) d \hat {F} _ {0} ^ {-} (x) \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Z _ {i} ^ {-} \bigg / \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} Z _ {i} ^ {2}.} \end{array}
$$

For a general p-vector $Z _ { i }$ , let $z _ { i j }$ be the jth component of $Z _ { i } , j = 1 , . . . , p$ Let $z _ { i j } ^ { + } = \operatorname* { m a x } \{ z _ { i j } , 0 \} , z _ { i j } ^ { - } = z _ { i j } ^ { + } - z _ { i j }$ , and $\hat { F } _ { 0 j } ^ { \pm }$ be the c.d.f. putting mass $z _ { i j } ^ { \pm } / \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } z _ { i j } ^ { \pm }$ at $r _ { i } , i = 1 , . . . , n$ . For any $j .$ , if $z _ { i j } \geq 0$ for all i (or $z _ { i j } \leq 0$ for all i), then we set $\hat { F } _ { 0 j } ^ { + } \equiv 0 \ ( \mathrm { o r } \ \hat { F } _ { 0 j } ^ { - } \equiv 0 )$ . An L-estimator of $\beta$ is defined to be 

$$
\hat {\beta} _ {L} = \hat {\beta} + (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {- 1} (A ^ {+} - A ^ {-}),\tag{5.82}
$$

where 

$$
A ^ {\pm} = \left(\int x J (\hat {F} _ {0 1} ^ {\pm} (x)) d \hat {F} _ {0 1} ^ {\pm} (x) \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} z _ {i 1} ^ {\pm},..., \int x J (\hat {F} _ {0 p} ^ {\pm} (x)) d \hat {F} _ {0 p} ^ {\pm} (x) \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} z _ {i p} ^ {\pm}\right)
$$

Obviously, $\hat { \beta } _ { L }$ in (5.82) reduces to the previously defined $\hat { \beta } _ { L }$ when $\beta$ and $Z _ { i }$ are univariate. 

Theorem 5.12. Assume model (5.80) with i.i.d. $\varepsilon _ { i } \mathrm { { ^ { s } } }$ from a c.d.f. $F _ { 0 }$ satisfying (5.81) for a given J. Suppose that $F _ { 0 }$ has a uniformly continuous, positive, and bounded derivative on the range of $\varepsilon _ { 1 }$ . Suppose further that the conditions on $Z _ { i } \mathrm { ^ { * } s }$ in Theorem 3.12 are satisfied. 

(i) If the function J is continuous on $\left( \alpha _ { 1 } , \alpha _ { 2 } \right)$ and equals 0 on $[ 0 , \alpha _ { 1 } ] \cup [ \alpha _ { 2 } , 1 ]$ , where $0 < \alpha _ { 1 } < \alpha _ { 2 } < 1$ are constants, then 

$$
\sigma_ {F _ {0}} ^ {- 1} (Z ^ {\tau} Z) ^ {1 / 2} (\hat {\beta} _ {L} - \beta) \rightarrow_ {d} N _ {p} (0, I _ {p}),\tag{5.83}
$$

where $\sigma _ { F _ { 0 } } ^ { 2 }$ is given by (5.79) with $F = F _ { 0 }$ (ii) Result (5.83) also holds if $J ^ { \prime }$ is bounded on $[ 0 , 1 ] , E | \varepsilon _ { 1 } | < \infty$ , and $\sigma _ { F _ { 0 } } ^ { 2 }$ is finite. 

The proof of this theorem can be found in Bickel (1973). Robustness and eficiency comparisons between the LSE $\hat { \beta }$ and L-estimators $\hat { \beta } _ { L }$ can be made in a way similar to those in 5.3.2. 

## 5.4 Generalized Estimating Equations

The method of generalized estimating equations (GEE) is a powerful and general method of deriving point estimators, which includes many previously described methods as special cases. In 5.4.1, we begin with a description of this method and, to motivate the idea, we discuss its relationship with other methods that have been studied. Consistency and asymptotic normality of estimators derived from generalized estimating equations are studied in 5.4.2 and 5.4.3. 

Throughout this section, we assume that $X _ { 1 } , . . . , X _ { n }$ are independent (not necessarily identically distributed) random vectors, where the dimension of $X _ { i }$ is $d _ { i } , \ i = 1 , . . . , n \ ( \mathrm { s u p } _ { i } d _ { i } < \infty )$ , and that we are interested in estimating θ, a k-vector of unknown parameters related to the unknown population. 

## 5.4.1 The GEE method and its relationship with others

The sample mean and, more generally, the LSE in linear models are solutions of equations of the form 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} (X _ {i} - \gamma^ {\tau} Z _ {i}) Z _ {i} = 0.
$$

Also, MLE’s (or RLE’s) in 4.4 and, more generally, M-estimators in 5.2.2 are solutions to equations of the form 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \psi (X _ {i}, \gamma) = 0.
$$

This leads to the following general estimation method. Let $\Theta \subset \mathcal { R } ^ { k }$ be the range of $\theta , \psi _ { i }$ be a Borel function from $\mathcal { R } ^ { d _ { i } } \times \Theta$ to $\mathcal { R } ^ { k } , i = 1 , . . . , n$ , and 

$$
s _ {n} (\gamma) = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \psi_ {i} (X _ {i}, \gamma), \quad \gamma \in \Theta .\tag{5.84}
$$

If $\theta$ is estimated by $\hat { \theta } \in \Theta$ satisfying $s _ { n } ( { \hat { \theta } } ) = 0$ , then $\hat { \theta }$ is called a GEE estimator. The equation $s _ { n } ( \gamma ) = 0$ is called a GEE. Apparently, the LSE’s, RLE’s, MQLE’s, and M-estimators are special cases of GEE estimators. 

Usually GEE’s are chosen so that 

$$
E [ s _ {n} (\theta) ] = \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} E [ \psi_ {i} (X _ {i}, \theta) ] = 0,\tag{5.85}
$$

where the expectation $E$ may be replaced by an asymptotic expectation defined in 2.5.2 if the exact expectation does not exist. If this is true, then $\hat { \theta }$ is motivated by the fact that $s _ { n } ( { \hat { \theta } } ) = 0$ is a sample analogue of $E [ s _ { n } ( \theta ) ] = 0$ 

To motivate the idea, let us study the relationship between the GEE method and other methods that have been introduced. 

## M-estimators

The M-estimators defined in 5.2.2 for univariate $\theta = \mathtt { T } ( F )$ in the i.i.d. case are special cases of GEE estimators. Huber (1981) also considers regression M-estimators in the linear model (5.80). A regression M-estimator of $\beta$ is defined as a solution to the GEE 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \psi (X _ {i} - \gamma^ {\tau} Z _ {i}) Z _ {i} = 0,
$$

where $\psi$ is one of the functions given in Example 5.7. 

## LSE’s in linear and nonlinear regression models

Suppose that 

$$
X _ {i} = f (Z _ {i}, \theta) + \varepsilon_ {i}, \qquad i = 1, \dots , n,\tag{5.86}
$$

where $Z _ { i } \mathrm { ^ { * } s }$ are the same as those in (5.80), θ is an unknown k-vector of parameters, f is a known function, and $\varepsilon _ { i } \mathrm { { ^ { s } } }$ are independent random variables. Model (5.86) is the same as model (5.80) if f is linear in θ and is called a nonlinear regression model otherwise. Note that model (4.64) is a special case of model (5.86). The LSE under model (5.86) is any point in Θ minimizing $\textstyle \sum _ { i = 1 } ^ { n } [ X _ { i } - f ( Z _ { i } , \gamma ) ] ^ { 2 }$ over $\gamma \in \Theta$ . If f is diferentiable, then the LSE is a solution to the GEE 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} [ X _ {i} - f (Z _ {i}, \gamma) ] \frac {\partial f (Z _ {i} , \gamma)}{\partial \gamma} = 0.
$$

## Quasi-likelihoods

This is a continuation of the discussion of the quasi-likelihoods introduced in 4.4.3. Assume first that $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are univariate $( d _ { i } \equiv 1 )$ . If $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ follow a GLM, i.e., $X _ { i }$ has the p.d.f. in (4.55) and (4.57) holds, and if (4.58) holds, then the likelihood equation (4.59) can be written as 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} \frac {x _ {i} - \mu_ {i} (\gamma)}{v _ {i} (\gamma)} G _ {i} (\gamma) = 0,\tag{5.87}
$$

where $\mu _ { i } ( \gamma ) = \mu ( \psi ( \gamma ^ { \tau } Z _ { i } ) ) , G _ { i } ( \gamma ) = \partial \mu _ { i } ( \gamma ) / \partial \gamma , v _ { i } ( \gamma ) = \mathrm { V a r } ( X _ { i } ) / \phi$ , and we have used the following fact: 

$$
\psi^ {\prime} (t) = (\mu^ {- 1}) ^ {\prime} (g ^ {- 1} (t)) (g ^ {- 1}) ^ {\prime} (t) = (g ^ {- 1}) ^ {\prime} (t) / \zeta^ {\prime \prime} (\psi (t)).
$$

Equation (5.87) is a quasi-likelihood equation if either $X _ { i }$ does not have the p.d.f. in (4.55) or (4.58) does not hold. Note that this generalizes the discussion in 4.4.3. If $X _ { i }$ does not have the p.d.f. in (4.55), then the problem is often nonparametric. Let $s _ { n } ( \gamma )$ be the left-hand side of (5.87). Then $s _ { n } ( \gamma ) = 0$ is a GEE and $E [ s _ { n } ( \beta ) ] = 0$ is satisfied as long as the first condition in (4.56), $E ( X _ { i } ) = \mu _ { i } ( \beta )$ , is satisfied. 

For general $d _ { i } \mathrm {  ~ s ~ } _ { \cdot }$ , let $X _ { i } = ( X _ { i 1 } , . . . , X _ { i d _ { i } } ) , i = 1 , . . . , n$ , where each $X _ { i t }$ satisfies (4.56) and (4.57), i.e., 

$$
E (X _ {i t}) = \mu (\eta_ {i t}) = g ^ {- 1} (\beta^ {\tau} Z _ {i t}) \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \operatorname{Var} (X _ {i t}) = \phi_ {i} \mu^ {\prime} (\eta_ {i t}),
$$

and $Z _ { i t } \mathrm { ^ { > } s }$ are k-vector values of covariates. In biostatistics and life-time testing problems, components of $X _ { i }$ are repeated measurements at diferent times from subject i and are called longitudinal data. Although $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are assumed independent, $X _ { i t }$ ’s are likely to be dependent for each i. Let $R _ { i }$ be the $d _ { i } \times d _ { i }$ correlation matrix whose $( t , l )$ th element is the correlatior coeficient between $X _ { i t }$ and $X _ { i l }$ . Then 

$$
\operatorname{Var} (X _ {i}) = \phi_ {i} [ D _ {i} (\beta) ] ^ {1 / 2} R _ {i} [ D _ {i} (\beta) ] ^ {1 / 2},\tag{5.88}
$$

where $D _ { i } ( \gamma )$ is the $d _ { i } \times d _ { i }$ diagonal matrix with the tth diagonal element $( g ^ { - 1 } ) ^ { \prime } ( \gamma ^ { \tau } \bar { Z } _ { i t } )$ . If $R _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ in (5.88) are known, then an extension of (5.87) to the multivariate $x _ { i } \mathrm { { ' s } }$ is 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} G _ {i} (\gamma) \{[ D _ {i} (\gamma) ] ^ {1 / 2} R _ {i} [ D _ {i} (\gamma) ] ^ {1 / 2} \} ^ {- 1} [ x _ {i} - \mu_ {i} (\gamma) ] = 0,\tag{5.89}
$$

where $\mu _ { i } ( \gamma ) = ( \mu ( \psi ( \gamma ^ { \tau } Z _ { i 1 } ) ) , . . . , \mu ( \psi ( \gamma ^ { \tau } Z _ { i d _ { i } } ) ) )$ and $G _ { i } ( \gamma ) = \partial \mu _ { i } ( \gamma ) / \partial \gamma$ . In most applications, $R _ { i }$ is unknown and its form is hard to model. Let $\tilde { R } _ { i }$ be a known correlation matrix (called a working correlation matrix). Replacing $R _ { i }$ in (5.89) by $\tilde { R } _ { i }$ leads to the quasi-likelihood equation 

$$
\sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} G _ {i} (\gamma) \{[ D _ {i} (\gamma) ] ^ {1 / 2} \tilde {R} _ {i} [ D _ {i} (\gamma) ] ^ {1 / 2} \} ^ {- 1} [ x _ {i} - \mu_ {i} (\gamma) ] = 0.\tag{5.90}
$$

For example, we may assume that the components of $X _ { i }$ are independent and take $\tilde { R } _ { i } = I _ { d _ { i } }$ . Although the working correlation matrix ${ \tilde { R } } _ { i }$ may not be the same as the true unknown correlation matrix $R _ { i }$ , an MQLE obtained from (5.90) is still consistent and asymptotically normal ( 5.4.2 and 5.4.3). Of course, MQLE’s are asymptotically more eficient if $\ddot { R } _ { i }$ is closer to $R _ { i }$ Even if ${ \tilde { R } } _ { i } = R _ { i }$ and $\phi _ { i } \equiv \phi$ , (5.90) is still a quasi-likelihood equation, since the covariance matrix of $X _ { i }$ cannot determine the distribution of $X _ { i }$ unless $X _ { i }$ is normal. 

Since an ${ \tilde { R } } _ { i }$ closer to $R _ { i }$ results in a better MQLE, sometimes it is suggested to replace $\tilde { R } _ { i }$ in (5.90) by $\hat { R } _ { i }$ , an estimator of $R _ { i }$ (Liang and Zeger, 1986). The resulting equation is called a pseudo-likelihood equation. As long as max $_ { i \leq n } \left\| \hat { R } _ { i } - U _ { i } \right\| \to _ { p } 0$ as $n \to \infty$ , where $\| A \| = { \sqrt { \operatorname { t r } ( A ^ { \tau } A ) } }$ for a matrix A and $U _ { i }$ is a correlation matrix (not necessarily the same as $R _ { i } )$ , $i = 1 , . . . , n$ , MQLE’s are consistent and asymptotically normal. 

## Empirical likelihoods

The previous discussion shows that the GEE method coincides with the method of deriving M-estimators, LSE’s, MLE’s, or MQLE’s. The following discussion indicates that the GEE method is also closely related to the method of empirical likelihoods introduced in 5.1.4. 

Assume that $X _ { i } { } ^ { \ ' } \mathrm { s }$ are i.i.d. from a c.d.f. F on $\mathcal { R } ^ { d }$ and $\psi _ { i } = \psi$ for all i. Then condition (5.85) reduces to $E [ \psi ( X _ { 1 } , \theta ) ] = 0$ . Hence, we can consider 

the empirical likelihood 

$$
\ell (G) = \prod_ {i = 1} ^ {n} P _ {G} (\{x _ {i} \}), \qquad G \in \mathfrak {F}
$$

subject to 

$$
p _ {i} \geq 0, \quad \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} = 1, \quad \text { and } \quad \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {n} p _ {i} \psi (x _ {i}, \theta) = 0,\tag{5.91}
$$

where $p _ { i } = P _ { G } ( \{ x _ { i } \} )$ .
